# NOTICE
<note>original: "Avertissement"; a common term in 17th-19th century books for an introductory editorial note or foreword.</note>

In 1662, there appeared in Leiden, from the house of *Francis Moyard & Peter Leffen* <note>original: "apud Franciscum Moyardum & Petrum Leffen"</note>, a small quarto of 121 pages (plus 34 pages of an unpaginated Preface), under the following title: *René Descartes on Man, provided with figures and Latin translation by Florent Schuyl, Senator of the Illustrious City of 's-Hertogenbosch, and Professor of Philosophy in the same place* <note>original: "Renatus Des Cartes De Homine, figuris & latinitate donatus à Florentio Schuyl, Inclytæ Urbis Sylvæ Ducis Senatore, & ibidem Philosophiæ Professore"</note>. The editor, Florent Schuyl, explained at the end of his Preface that he had produced this Latin translation from two copies of the French original, both preserved in Holland and placed at his disposal by two old friends of Descartes: Alphonse Pollot (whom he calls *Alphonsus Palotti*), and Antoine Studler van Surck, Lord of Bergen. Furthermore, Clerselier, having been informed of this project, reportedly strongly urged the author to carry it out.

In 1664, a bookseller in Paris, Jacques Le Gras, published a small octavo, the title of which is as follows: *The World by Mr. Descartes, or The Treatise on Light, & the other principal objects of the Senses. With a Discourse on Local Motion, and another on Fevers, composed according to the principles of the same Author* <note>original: "Le Monde de Mr Descartes, ou Le Traitté de la Lumiere, & des autres principaux objets des Sens..."</note>, (260 pages for the first Treatise, and only 31 for the two Discourses, neither of which, moreover, is by Descartes). The privilege <note>A "privilège du roi" was a legal grant of exclusive publication rights, an early form of copyright.</note> for this small volume is dated October 18, 1663, "registered in the Book of the Community" of Booksellers on the following October 27. A Preface, signed D. R., informs us that the gift of this work to the public is the generosity of "Mr. D. A." (undoubtedly d’ALIBERT), who sent for the text of this treatise *On the World*, "almost at the ends of the Earth...

# AVERTISSEMENT
<note>Foreword/Notice</note>

...Northern [parts]," <note>original: "Septentrionales"</note> that is to say, apparently as far as Sweden (unless it was simply Holland).

Shortly after, Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’ brother-in-law and his primary literary executor. He dedicated years to organizing and publishing Descartes’ unfinished manuscripts.</note> published a volume in his turn, which he had announced as early as the Preface to volume II of the *Letters of Descartes* in 1659. (See volume V of the present edition, pp. 635-636.) The printing was completed on April 12, 1664, under the title: **MAN by RENÉ DESCARTES, & A TREATISE ON THE FORMATION OF THE FETUS** <note>original: "L'HOMME de RENÉ DESCARTES, & UN TRAITÉ DE LA FORMATION DU FŒTUS"</note> *by the same Author. With the Remarks of Louis de la Forge, Doctor of Medicine, residing at La Flèche, on the Treatise on Man by René Descartes, & on the Figures invented by him.* (In Paris, at the house of Theodore Girard, 1664. Large quarto, 448 pages, plus 68 pages for an unpaginated *Epistle* and *Preface*.) *Man*, pp. 1-107. *Formation of the Fetus*, pp. 109-170. *Remarks by Louis de la Forge*, pp. 171-408. French translation of Schuyl's *Preface* to his Latin edition of 1662, pp. 409-448.

Clerselier, whose name does not appear in the title, but only at the bottom of the dedicatory Epistle "to Monseigneur de Colbert," <note>Jean-Baptiste Colbert (1619–1683), the powerful Minister of Finances under King Louis XIV and a great patron of the sciences.</note> returns, at the beginning of his Preface, to the two previous editions of 1662 and 1664. He regrets that they were produced with too much haste. Regarding the *Treatise on Man*, Schuyl <note>Florentius Schuyl, who published the first Latin version of "Man" in 1662.</note> had only obtained copies, whereas Clerselier possessed the original, which certainly should have been printed first. From the very first lines, one would have seen that it was not a separate Treatise, but a sequel to the work of which Descartes speaks in his *Discourse on Method* and which he elsewhere calls his *World* <note>original: "Monde"</note>. The chapters on *Man* must therefore come after those of the *Treatise on Light*, which form the first part of that work. Clerselier also regrets that the *Treatise on Light* was released too quickly in 1664, as he says he possessed "a more faithful text, with better-made figures," and he had intended to join it to the *Treatise on Man* in the same volume, since they were effectively two parts of the same whole. However, as we have seen, he did not do so in his 1664 publication.

It explains Clerselier's editorial frustrations with earlier "hasty" editions and his clarification that these texts were intended as components of a larger work titled "The World."</summary>

# THE WORLD.

...and the reason for it is easy to guess: the small volume of *The World*, which had just been published, mentions that Jacques Le Gras, the printer, shared his privilege <note>In the 17th century, a "privilege" was a royal license granting exclusive rights to print and sell a specific book for a set number of years, acting as an early form of copyright.</note> with Michel Bobin, Nicolas Le Gras, and Théodore Girard, "to enjoy it according to the agreement made between them." But Théodore Girard is precisely the name of the printer we find at the head of the volume of *Man*: to also print the *Treatise on Light* in the same volume in 1664 would have abruptly stopped the sale of the small octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves (16 pages); these were typically smaller, more portable, and more affordable volumes.</note> copies, which offered this Treatise separately, and which, having only recently appeared, were still far from being sold out.

But thirteen years later, in a second edition in 1677, there were no longer the same reasons to hold back, and the volume bears this new title: **MAN by RENÉ DESCARTES, and the FORMATION OF THE FETUS, with the Remarks of Louis de la Forge. To which has been added THE WORLD, or TREATISE ON LIGHT, by the same Author.** (In Paris, at the house of Michel Bobin & Nicolas Le Gras, 1677. <note>original: "M. DC. LXXVII."</note> Quarto, <note>A larger book format where each sheet is folded twice to form four leaves (8 pages).</note> 511 pages. Plus 66 pages of the *Epistle and Preface, unpaginated*.) *Man*, pp. 1-98. *The Description of the Human Body (or Formation of the Fetus)*, pp. 99-154. *Remarks by Louis de la Forge*, pp. 155-368. *Translation of the Preface by Monsieur Schuyl*, <note>Florentius Schuyl (1619–1669) was a Dutch physician who produced the first Latin edition of Descartes' "Man" in 1662.</note> pp. 369-404. *The World*, pp. 405-511. Plus 8 pages of the *Table of Contents*. Clerselier did not reproduce the text published in 1664 for *The World*, which was only a copy, but, naturally, the one he had in his possession—that is to say, the original.

These are the four documents, all printed, that we will use to publish both the *Treatise on Light* and the *Treatise on Man*.

First, we will publish them one after the other, beginning with the *Treatise on Light*. Not only do Clerselier's statements authorize us to do so, but they do not allow us to do otherwise. The original Manuscript of the *Treatise on Man*, which he offered to show to anyone who wished, was, in fact, titled, he says: *Chapter 18*. In truth, the *Treatise on Light*, as he gives it to us, only contains...

->### NOTICE.<-

15 chapters; there would therefore be a gap of two chapters, 16 and 17. But this should not give us pause: especially as the first sentence of the *Treatise on Man*—the meaning of which Schuyl <note>Florentius Schuyl (1619–1669) was a Dutch physician who produced the first Latin translation of Descartes' work on physiology, *De Homine*, in 1662.</note> misunderstood in his translation for lack of grasping this connection—clearly shows that he is still discussing this artificial World, which Descartes constructs from scratch in imaginary spaces, and not the real World in which we live; finally—and this is no less decisive—at a certain point in the same *Treatise on Man*, regarding the parts of the second element, <note>In Cartesian physics, the "second element" refers to the subtle matter that makes up the heavens and transmits light.</note> he recalls "what was said above," referring precisely to the *Treatise on Light*.

Furthermore, the first edition of the *Treatise on Light*, published in 1664, informs us that the manuscript <note>original: "MS."</note> copy used at the time did indeed show a division into chapters (likely 1 through 15), but these chapters lacked titles. Those found throughout the small 1664 volume were added by the editor, as was the second part of the general title: *Treatise on Light* AND OF THE OTHER PRINCIPAL OBJECTS OF THE SENSES, as the editor himself admits. We will therefore provide all these titles, along with the 1664 *Preface* signed D. R., after this *Notice*; hereafter, we will only reproduce the chapter numbers within the text itself.

However, in his 1677 edition, Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was a friend and the primary literary executor of Descartes, responsible for publishing much of his posthumous work.</note> also included titles; these are not the same as the 1664 titles, though they are equivalent. Had he found them in the original manuscript? He does not say, and it is hardly likely, for the earlier copy would have reproduced them as well. To preserve Descartes' text in its full purity, it is best to provide these titles only in the margin and within parentheses—especially since, when inserted before each chapter, they break the flow of the discourse. This is a very important matter, and one we were wrong to overlook when printing the French text of the *Principles* in Volume IX of the present edition: the first edition <note>original: "édition princeps"</note> presented this text, as is proper, as a single continuous flow, with the titles placed in the margins. With even greater reason, the

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the editorial "Notice" regarding the publication history of René Descartes' posthumous works, specifically focusing on the "Treatise on Light" and the "Treatise on Man," which together comprise "The World." It discusses the differences between the 1664 and 1677 editions and the justification for the current edition's formatting.</meta>

-># THE WORLD.<-

*Treatise on Light*, which dates from an earlier period, when Descartes still preferred the form of the *Discourse* <note>A reference to Descartes' famous *Discourse on Method*, published in 1637, which established his style of philosophical presentation.</note>, as seen in the 1637 publication.

For the *Treatise on Man*, which follows, we shall do the same; and we will be all the more justified in doing so because any division into chapters was missing there, both in the copies and in the original. This is what the editors declare, and to be convinced of it, one need only compare the numbering that Schuyl <note>Florentius Schuyl (1619–1669), who published the first Latin translation of this work.</note> added regardless (without, moreover, providing titles for the 33 chapters he thus distinguishes), and that of Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), Descartes' friend and literary executor.</note>, in 93 chapters, which are much better justified, and which we reproduce, along with the conjectured titles—though we place them at the end (p. 203-209), as they are not by Descartes himself.

The general arrangement thus being decided, which text shall we choose? For the *Treatise on Light*, we cannot, following what Clerselier declared, fail to prefer the edition of 1677, which reproduces the original manuscript, over that of 1664, which only reproduces a copy. However, the difference between the two is not as great as Clerselier announced in his *Preface* to the *Treatise on Man* in 1664. And indeed, to tell the truth, neither one seems to us a faithful reproduction of Descartes' own text, at least regarding the spelling and certain idioms <term>locutions familières</term> <note>These are characteristic ways of speaking or turns of phrase unique to Descartes' 17th-century French style.</note> familiar to the philosopher. In this regard, both substitute the more fashionable forms that had replaced them for ways of speaking and writing that were already a bit outdated in 1664 and even more so in 1677. What is curious, however, is that on certain points the 1677 text is rather behind the times, while on others, that of 1664 is ahead. Here are some examples. Descartes usually wrote *pour ce que* <note>original: "pour ce que"</note> and *d’autant que* <note>original: "d’autant que"</note> <note>These are archaic French conjunctions meaning "because" or "inasmuch as."</note>: this form *d'autant que* is generally preserved in the 1677 edition; but that of 1664 replaces it everywhere, not even with the phrase *pource que*, which likely seemed to also need modernizing, but with the quite recent form of *parce que* <note>original: "parce que"</note>: only once had the typesetter left *pource* (p. 102); but *parce* is caref—

<summary>The editor explains the choice to use the 1677 edition of Descartes' work as a base text, while noting that both the 1664 and 1677 editions modernized Descartes' original 17th-century spelling and phrasing.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Treatise on Light, Treatise on Man, Clerselier, Schuyl, textual criticism, 17th-century orthography, publishing history</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the editorial discussion regarding the textual variations between the 1664 and 1677 editions of Descartes' works. # ADVISORY.

...properly restored in the errata. On the other hand, the 1664 volume almost always prints the letter *i* for *j* in the word *I* <note>original: "ie"</note> (as Descartes used to write); the 1677 edition uniformly gives *I* <note>original: "je"</note>. Finally, once—doubtless by oversight—the 1664 typographer printed *this one* <note>original: "cetuy-cy"</note> (p. 19); but one finds, restored in the errata, *this one* <note>original: "celuy-cy"</note>, which is the form also adopted in 1677, although Descartes very probably wrote *this* <note>original: "cetuy"</note> instead. It is enough now that the reader be warned. We cannot take it upon ourselves to retouch the texts in one direction or the other. We will therefore publish, with these reservations, the text given in 1677 by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), Descartes' friend and the primary editor of his posthumous papers.</note> based on the original manuscript, followed, at the bottom of the pages, by all the variants offered by the 1664 text printed from a simple copy. As for the figures <note>The scientific diagrams and illustrations accompanying the text.</note>, we will reproduce those that go with Clerselier's text; he declares them, moreover, to be "better made," and we easily believe him.

For the *Treatise on Man*, we do not have such a difficult choice: only one text has been preserved for us, the one Clerselier published in 1664; we will therefore provide it as it is. At most, a comparison of this French text—which is the original—with the Latin translation by Schuyl <note>Florentius Schuyl (1619–1669), a Dutch physician who produced the first published version of this work in Latin.</note>, made from two copies, will reveal a few differences in those two copies: we will not fail to point them out.

But the most interesting question regarding this *Treatise on Man* is that of the figures. Descartes left none behind, except for two, which will be indicated in their respective places. All the others in the 1662 edition are by Florent Schuyl. And he was not content merely to adapt them as much as possible to the text; he wanted them to be as beautiful as possible, and one feels the hand of a true artist in them. But Clerselier rightly thought that, although these figures "are much superior, if one simply considers the engraving and the printing," they are, for the most part, "less intelligible" than those he proposes, and "less suited for understanding the text." Two scholars had provided him, each on his own...

VII
-> THE WORLD. <-

...and without having had knowledge of Schuyl’s volume, [produced] new figures: Louis de la Forge, a doctor of medicine at La Flèche, and Gérard van Gutschoven, a professor at Louvain. Their figures are indeed simpler and clearer than those of Schuyl; they are certainly less artistic, and present rather the character of a *diagram* <note>original: "schema" — a simplified or symbolic representation rather than a realistic drawing.</note>, as is appropriate. We will therefore reproduce them, doing moreover as Clerselier did, who, having been embarrassed more than once by certain figures between the model of one and that of the other, retained both, designating them by the letters F and G (de la Forge and Gutschoven). We will add the letter D for the two figures by Descartes, which we will provide because of their authenticity.

# CLERSELIER’S PREFACE
## 1664

> "If I had not been obliged to provide a Preface, to make known to everyone how little a part I have in this whole Work, and to give the honor due to those who have taken the trouble to work on the Figures and the Remarks that accompany it, I would have been satisfied with the one that <term>Mr. Schuyl</term> <note>Florentius Schuyl (1619–1669) was a Dutch physician and professor. He published the first edition of Descartes' *Treatise on Man* in Latin in 1662, two years before this French edition.</note> has already placed before the Latin version he made of the *Treatise on Man* by Mr. Descartes; for it is so full and so beautiful that, besides leaving me almost nothing to say, it has entirely taken away my hope of doing better... If he had been as successful in the figures of the muscles and the brain which he invented, as he was in his Preface, and if he had worked from a more faithful copy to produce his version, I would have wanted to do nothing more than to return this Treatise to its <term>Natural language</term> <note>Meaning the original French in which Descartes wrote, as opposed to the Latin translation.</note>, and would have used his own figures, which are undoubtedly far superior to those I have had placed here, if one considers only the engraving and the printing; but which I believe for the most part to be less intelligible than these, and less suited to the understanding of the text."

> "As these Figures are not by me, I can speak my mind more freely about them, and that will not prevent others from making their own judgment. This is why I beg him to excuse me if, after having thanked him for the overly kind praises with which he overwhelmed and honored me in his Preface, I must nonetheless say here that he was a bit too hasty in the printing of this Treatise, and that if he had done me the favor of alerting me, I would have asked him to postpone it (as was, it seems to me, quite reasonable) until I had it printed here in French—I, who possessed the original manuscript; and I would have at the same time prevented him from falling, as he did, into several errors that were inevitable for him due to the flaws in his copy, which undoubtedly would have made his Book better."

> "I do not wish to list them all here: those who take the trouble to confront his Latin with the French will easily be able to notice them. I will only say that, for having wanted to correct the..."

> » I had requested; for along with all these **Illustrations**, he sent me a copy of the treatise that he had used to devise them. > » spread, the <term>muscle</term><note>A bundle of fibrous tissue in the body that can contract or expand to produce movement.</note> T also swells, and by the same means helps to open the upper <term>eyelid</term><note>original: "paupiere"</note>. Conversely, when the branches *s* fill with <term>Spirits</term><note>Descartes used the term "animal spirits" to describe a very fine fluid or wind that he believed flowed through hollow nerves to inflate muscles and cause movement.</note>, since they cannot pull the corner of the eye toward themselves because it is immobile, their middle section or "belly" swells; and by swelling on both sides at the same time, they cause the eyelids to draw together and close. And so that this may be better understood and executed, one must conceive that between the branches of the <term>nerve</term> *pr* and those of the nerve *qs*, there are communication channels with <term>valves</term>, which produce the ordinary effect they have in <term>Antagonistic</term><note>Muscles that work in opposition to each other; when one contracts, the other relaxes.</note> muscles, so that these branches can mutually provide each other with Spirits in large enough quantities to be sufficiently swollen, and so that some do not hinder the effect of others. And besides this, one must conceive that between the branches of the nerve *pr*, some of which go into muscle T and others into muscle V, there is communication; but this communication is always open, so that the branches going into muscle T, through the communication they have with the others spread throughout muscle V, can also provide Spirits to the branches of the nerve *qs* spread throughout muscle V, and also receive from them when necessary; and also so that by this means muscle T swells and deflates with the branches *r* spread in muscle V, and that it does not hinder, but rather favors the effect of the branches of the nerve *qs*. This being thus explained, it seems to me (as I have said) that it is easy to understand what the thought of <term>Monsieur Descartes</term><note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the philosopher and mathematician whose physiological theories are the subject of this book.</note> was concerning the movement of muscles, and concerning the insertion of the fibers or branches of the nerves into the body of each muscle, and that this makes it clear enough how this action or movement occurs, which is the principal function of all this <term>machine</term><note>Descartes famously viewed the human body as a complex biological machine governed by mechanical laws.</note>. »

[*On the difference between our sensations and the things that produce them.*]

In proposing to treat here of Light, the first thing of which I wish to warn you is that there may be a difference between the sensation <term>sensation <note>Descartes uses the word "sentiment," which in the 17th century referred to any sensory perception or feeling, rather than just an emotion.</note></term> we have of it—that is to say, the idea formed in our imagination through the mediation of our eyes—and what is in the objects that produce this sensation in us—that is to say, what is in the flame or in the Sun, which is called by the name of Light. For although everyone is commonly persuaded that the ideas we have in our thought are entirely similar to the objects from which they proceed, I see no reason at all that assures us that this is so; but

Now, among the particles of air, if there are some that are very large in comparison to others—such as those atoms <note>original: "atomes." In the 17th century, "atoms" often referred to the visible dust motes seen dancing in a beam of light, rather than the modern concept of subatomic particles.</note> that are seen there—they also move very slowly; and if there are some that move faster, they are also smaller. But, among the particles of flame, while there may be some smaller than those in the air, there are also larger ones, or at least a greater number equal to the largest of those in the air, <margin>5</margin> which moreover move much faster; and it is only these latter ones that have the power to burn. <margin>10</margin>

That there are smaller ones can be conjectured from the fact that they penetrate through many bodies whose pores <term>pores: tiny, invisible openings or passages within the structure of a material</term> are so narrow that even air itself cannot enter them. That there are either larger ones, or just as many large ones in greater number, is clearly seen in the fact that air alone is not enough to sustain it <note>Descartes is referring to the "nourishment" or fuel of the flame.</note>. <margin>15</margin> That they move faster, the violence of their action makes us experience it clearly enough. And finally, that it is the largest of these particles which have the power to burn, and not the others, is evident in the fact that the flame which comes from brandy <note>original: "eau de vie," literally "water of life"—a high-proof distilled spirit.</note>, or other very subtle <term>subtle: here meaning refined, thin, or composed of exceptionally small and fast-moving particles</term> bodies, hardly burns at all; and that on the contrary, the flame produced in hard and heavy bodies is very hot. <margin>20</margin>

Nature, you will easily recognize that all these spaces, which the common people <term>the common people: (original: "le peuple") referring to those who rely solely on their senses rather than philosophical reasoning.</term> estimate to be empty, and where we sense only air, are at the very least just as full, and filled with the same matter, as those where we <margin>5</margin> sense other bodies.

Could one really believe that the water in a well must rise upwards against its natural inclination, only so that the pipe of a pump may be filled, <margin>20</margin> and yet think that the water in the clouds should not descend, to finish filling the spaces that are down here, if there were even the slightest vacuum between the parts of the bodies they contain?

I suppose as a second Rule: That when one body pushes another, it cannot give it any motion without losing at the same time as much of its own; nor can it take away any from it, without its own motion increasing by just as much. This Rule, joined with the preceding one <note>The "preceding rule" is Descartes's first law of nature: that each thing remains in the state it is in (motion or rest) as long as it does not collide with another.</note>, relates very well to all those experiences in which we see a body begin or cease to move because it is pushed or stopped by some other. For, having supposed the preceding rule, we are exempt from the difficulty in which the Learned <note>Descartes uses "the Learned" (original French: *les Doctes*) to refer to the Scholastic professors who followed Aristotle. But the reason is easy to give. For who is there who can deny that the air in which it moves offers it some resistance? One hears it whistle when it divides the air; and if one moves a fan, or some other very light and very broad body, one can even feel by the weight in one's hand that the air hinders the movement, far from continuing it, as some have wished to say <note>Aristotle's "antiperistasis" theory suggested that air actually rushes behind a stone to push it forward; Descartes is explicitly debunking this here.</note>. Then, because the parts of the second Element surrounding it toward *Y* move faster—and are even a little smaller, or at least are not any larger, than those toward *K*—they would give it even more <margin>20</margin> force to pass further toward *F*: so that it would go as far as the circumference of this Heaven, without being able to stop in any place in between; then from there, it would easily pass into another Heaven; and thus, instead of being a Planet, it would become a <margin>25</margin> Comet.

That is to say, just as one side of a balance cannot be raised or lowered without the other doing the exact opposite at the same instant, and the heavier side always prevailing over the other; so the stone R, for example, is so opposed to the quantity of air (exactly equal to its size) which is above it, and whose place it would occupy if it moved further from the center T, that this air would necessarily have to descend as the stone rose. And likewise, it is so opposed to another equal quantity of air which is below it, and whose place it must occupy if it approaches this center, that the stone must descend when that air rises.

But, to make it turn toward the East, it is the *entirety* of the matter of the Heavens contained within the circle **R** that acts against it, and jointly against all the earthly parts of the air contained in this same circle. Thus, since there is no more of it acting against the stone than against that air, it should not turn any faster than the air does in that direction.

# THE WORLD. 473-474.

And you can understand from this that the reasons used by many Philosophers <note>Descartes refers here to the Scholastic followers of Aristotle who argued for a stationary Earth.</note> to refute the movement of the real Earth have no force against the movement of the Earth I am describing to you. These only take place if one supposes that the Earth is not carried along by the course of the Heaven <note>term: Heaven (Ciel). In Cartesian physics, this refers to the fluid "ether" or celestial matter that fills space and carries planets in vortices.</note> that surrounds it, but that it is moved by some other force, and in some other direction than this Heaven.

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.
*On Light.*</margin> I have already said several times that bodies which turn in a circle always tend to move away from the centers of the circles they describe; but I must here determine more particularly toward which sides the parts of the matter, of which the Heavens and the Stars are composed, tend.

And for this, it must be known that when I say a body "tends" toward some side, I do not want one to imagine that it has within itself a thought or a will that carries it there, but only that it is disposed to move that way: whether it truly moves there, or rather that some other body prevents it from doing so; and it is principally in this latter sense that I use the word *tending* <note>original: "tendre"</note>, because it seems to signify some effort, and every effort presupposes resistance. But I reply to this, that they cannot advance so little toward that point without it being enough to perfectly prove what I have said: namely, that all the space there, being already full of some body <note>Descartes uses "body" here to mean any physical substance or matter</note>, whatever it may be, they continually press upon this body and exert force against it, as if to drive it out of its place.

Then, besides that, I reply that their other movements, which continue within them while they advance in this way toward E, do not allow them to remain arranged in the same way for a single moment; this prevents them from touching one another, or else ensures that after having touched, they immediately separate again. Thus, they do not fail to advance without interruption toward space E until it is entirely filled. So that one can conclude nothing else from this, except that the force with which they tend toward E is perhaps like a trembling, and increases and relaxes with various small shocks as they change their positions: which seems to be a property very well suited to Light.

### The principal properties of Light are:
1. That it extends in a circle on all sides around the bodies named Luminous. 2. And to any kind of distance. 3. And in an instant. 4. <margin>CHAPTER XV.
That the appearance of the Heavens of this new World must appear to its Inhabitants entirely similar to that of Our Own.</margin>

Having thus explained the nature and the properties of the action that I have taken to be Light, I must also explain how, by its means, the Inhabitants of the Planet that I have supposed to be the Earth can see the face of their Heavens entirely similar to that of our own.

Firstly, there is no doubt that they must see the body marked **S** <note>In Descartes' diagrams, 'S' typically represents the Sun at the center of a vortex.</note> as being full of Light, and similar to our Sun; seeing as this body sends rays from every point of its surface toward their eyes. And because it is much closer to them than the Stars, it must appear much larger to them. It is true that the parts of the small Heaven **A B C D** <note>The 'small heaven' refers to the local vortex or atmosphere surrounding the Earth.</note>, which turns around the Earth, offer some resistance to these rays; but because all those parts of the great Heaven, which are between **S** and **D**, strengthen them, those which are between **D** and **T**, being only few in number by comparison, can only take away a small amount of their force. And even the entire action of the parts of the great Heaven **F G G F** is not sufficient to prevent the rays of several fixed Stars from reaching as far as the Earth, on the side that is not illuminated by the Sun.

...so large, or so many joined together, that they can resist the action of Light: it is easy to understand that they must appear by means of the rays that the Sun sends toward them, and which are reflected from there toward the Earth. Just as opaque or dark objects that are in a room can be seen there by means of the rays that the torch <note>The author uses "flambeau" (torch/candle) as a terrestrial point of light to contrast with the Sun.</note> which illuminates it sends toward them, and which return from there toward the eyes of the onlookers. And with that, the rays of the Sun have a very remarkable advantage over those of a torch: which consists in the fact that their force is preserved, or even increases more and more, as they move away from the Sun, until they have reached the outer surface of its Heaven <note>In this Cartesian cosmology, "Heaven" refers to the vortex of subtle matter surrounding a star.</note>, because all the matter of this Heaven tends toward there; whereas the rays of a torch weaken as they move away, in proportion to the size of the spherical surfaces they illuminate, and even a little more, because of the resistance of the air through which they pass. From this it follows that objects which are close to this torch are notably more enlightened by it than those which are far away; and that the lower Planets are not, in the same proportion, more illuminated by the Sun than the higher ones, nor even than the Comets, which are incomparably further away.

Now experience shows us that the same happens also in the true World; and nevertheless I do not believe it is possible to give a reason for it, if one supposes that Light is anything else in objects than an action or disposition such as I have explained it. I say...

Then, as these drops of blood rarefy <note>The author, René Descartes, believed the heart acted like a furnace, causing blood to expand rapidly through heat rather than muscular contraction.</note> and expand suddenly into a space incomparably larger than that which they occupied before, they push against and close those little doors <note>valves</note> located at the entrances of the two veins. But immediately afterward, this rarefied blood condenses again, or penetrates into other parts; and thus the heart and the arteries deflate. The little doors at the two entrances of the arteries close again, and those at the entrances of the two veins reopen, providing passage for two more drops of blood, which once again cause the heart and arteries to swell, just like the preceding ones.

But what must be principally remarked upon here is that all the most lively, the strongest, and the most subtle parts of this blood betake themselves into the cavities of the brain; insofar as the arteries which carry them there are those which come from the heart in the most direct line of all, and because, as you know, all bodies that move tend, as much as is possible, to continue their movement in a straight line.

See, for example, the heart **A** (Fig. 1), and consider that, when the blood exits it with force through the opening **B**, there are none of its parts which do not tend toward **C**, where the cavities of the brain are located; but since the passage is not large enough to carry them all there, the weakest among them are diverted by the strongest, which by this means betake themselves there alone.

You may also remark in passing that, after those which enter the brain, there are none stronger nor more lively than those which betake themselves to the vessels destined for generation <note>Descartes is referring to the reproductive organs</note>. For, for example, if those which have the strength to reach as far as **D** cannot go further toward **C**, because there is not enough room for all, they return toward **E** rather than toward **F** or **G**, insofar as the passage there is straighter. Following which, I could perhaps show you how, from the humor <note>term: humor; in this context, a bodily fluid or secretion</note> which assembles toward **E**, another machine <note>term: machine; Descartes famously viewed the animal and human body as a complex biological machine</note> can be formed, entirely similar to this one; but I do not wish to enter further into this matter.

From this it is easy for you to judge how the soul will be able to feel all the other kinds of tastes, if you consider in how many other ways the small particles of terrestrial bodies can act against the tongue.

But what must be principally remarked here is that these are the same small particles of food <note>original: "viandes," used here in the archaic sense of any sustenance or foodstuff</note> which, being in the mouth, can enter the pores of the tongue and there excite the sensation of taste, and which, being in the stomach, can pass into the blood, and from there go to join and unite with all the limbs; and even, that there are only those which tickle the tongue moderately, and which can by this means make the soul feel an agreeable taste, that are entirely suited for this purpose.

For, as for those that act too much or too little, just as they can only make one feel a taste that is too sharp or too bland, so too are they either too penetrating or too soft to enter into the composition of the blood.

If no **refraction** <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, like the fluids of the eye.</note> occurred within this eye, the object **R** would send only a single one of its rays to point **S**, and the others would spread out here and there across the entire space **V, Y**; and likewise the points **T** and **X**, and all those located between them, would each send one of their rays toward this same point **S**.

Now, it is quite evident that object **R** must act more strongly against the part of the nerve located at point **S** when it sends a great number of rays there, than if it sent only one; and that this part of the nerve **S** must report the action of this object **R** more distinctly and faithfully to the **brain** when it receives rays from it alone, than if it received them from various others.

The change in size that happens to the pupil serves to moderate the force of vision; for it is necessary that it be smaller when the light is too vivid, so that not so many rays enter the eye that the nerve might be harmed by them; and that it be larger when the light is too weak, so that enough of them enter to be felt. And furthermore, assuming that the light remains equal, it is necessary that the pupil be larger when the object the eye looks at is distant than when it is near: for, for example (**Fig. 12**), if only as many rays from point **R** enter through the pupil of eye **7** as are needed to be felt, it is necessary that just as many enter into eye **8**, and consequently that its pupil be larger.

The smallness of the pupil <note>original: "prunelle"; here referring to the opening of the iris</note> also serves to make vision more distinct; for you must know that, whatever shape the crystalline humor <note>the lens of the eye</note> may have, it is impossible for it to cause the rays coming from different points of the object to assemble all exactly in as many other different points. Instead, if those from point R, for example (*Fig. 10*), assemble precisely at point S, there will be, from point T, only those which pass through the circumference and through the center of one of the circles that can be described on the surface of this crystalline humor, which can assemble exactly at point V. Consequently, the others—which will be fewer in number as the pupil is smaller—striking the nerve <note>the retina/optic nerve complex</note> at other points, cannot fail to bring confusion there. From this it follows that, if the vision of the same eye is less strong at one time than another, it will also be less distinct, whether this comes from the distance of the object or from the weakness of the light; because, the pupil being larger when the light is less strong, this also makes the vision more confused.

From this it also follows that the soul <note>Descartes uses "the soul" to refer to the conscious perceiving mind</note> can never see more than a single point of the object very distinctly at each time—namely, that point toward which all parts of the eye are directed at that moment—and that the others will appear to it all the more confused as they are further removed from this one. Now, insofar as I want you to conceive of these movements as being similar to those toward which we are naturally inclined by the various actions of the objects that move our senses, I desire here that you consider six different kinds of circumstances upon which they may depend. The first is the place from which the action proceeds, which opens some of the small <term>tubes</term> <note>tubes: Small channels within the brain through which the animal spirits flow.</note> through which the spirits first enter. The second consists of the force and all the other qualities of this action. The third is the disposition of the small filaments that compose the substance of the brain. The fourth is the unequal force that the small particles of the spirits may possess. The fifth is the varying position of the external limbs. And the sixth is the meeting of several actions that move the senses at the same time.

Regarding the place from which the action proceeds, you already know that, if the object **A B C** (<term>Fig. 36</term> <note>Fig. 36: A diagram illustrating how light from an object hits the eyes and is mapped onto the interior of the brain.</note>), for example, acted against another sense than that of sight, it would open other tubes on the interior surface of the brain than those marked 2, 4, and 6. Regarding the various positions of the external limbs, one must only consider that they change the pores which immediately carry these <term>spirits</term> <note>animal spirits: In Descartes' physiology, these are not "ghosts" but a very subtle wind or fluid that flows through the nerves to move the body.</note> into the nerves. <summary>Descartes argues that his mechanical model of the body is highly plausible because it relies on simple, observable structures like fibers and valves found throughout nature. He maintains that his "Machine" theory is simpler and more likely to be correct than more complex traditional anatomical theories.</summary>

...of the heart and arteries, the nourishment and growth of the limbs, respiration, waking and sleep; the reception of light, sounds, smells, tastes, heat, and other such qualities, in

->THE END<-

<summary>In this concluding passage of his physiological treatise, Descartes argues that all bodily functions—including sensation, memory, and movement—are purely mechanical and require no supernatural "soul" to operate. He famously compares the human body to a clock or automaton, driven by the physical heat of the heart and the flow of "animal spirits."</summary>

### III.

## AUTOMATA.

->Pages 130-132.<-

Descartes is likely referring to machines that he might have seen, for example, at Fontainebleau <note>The Royal Palace of Fontainebleau was famous for its complex water features and mechanical grottoes</note>. But there were also such machines mentioned in the works of the time, which he may have seen during his travels. Montaigne, who traveled in 1580-1581 through Upper Germany and Italy, describes wonders of this kind that he admired particularly in Augsburg, at Prattelino or Pratolino near Florence, and at Tivoli near Rome. (*Journal of Montaigne's Travels*, published by Louis Lautrey, 1906, pp. 125, 187-9 and 195-6, 269-271.) Here are a few other interesting texts on this subject:

<meta>This page serves as an editorial introduction or "Notice" to Descartes' anatomical writings, establishing the provenance and authenticating the manuscript titled "The Description of the Human Body." It connects this work to previous editions by Claude Clerselier.</meta>

# NOTICE

The inventory of Descartes' papers indicates, under the letter **G**, a manuscript <note>The abbreviation MS. stands for manuscript, a handwritten document.</note> titled: THE DESCRIPTION OF THE HUMAN BODY. (See volume 10, page 9, line 17.) A manuscript letter from Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was a friend of Descartes and the editor responsible for publishing many of his works after his death.</note>, which we have also printed (ibid., pages 13-14), provides its beginning. Now, this beginning is identical to the first pages of a Treatise that Clerselier published in his 1664 volume, following the *Treatise on Man*, under the same initial title of *The Description of the Human Body*, although he prints this different title at the top of the pages: *On the Formation of the Fetus* <note>original Latin/French: "De la Formation du Fœtus"</note>. The authenticity of this publication is therefore beyond doubt.

Truth be told, this double title from Clerselier requires explanation. It is because the Treatise, which remains unfinished, comprises two distinct parts: the first indeed undertakes a description of the human body, or rather its functions, with a complete program that Descartes had mapped out for himself (pages 112-113, Clerselier edition), and which he only began; the second appears as a digression, and that is precisely how Clerselier presents it (ibid., page 137); it explains the formation of the animal. But a link exists between the two, and not an artificial link: Descartes created it himself with his own hand. However, Clerselier’s second title: *On the Formation of the Fetus*, seems to belong to the editor; besides the fact that it does not suit the treatise as a whole, and only really designates the second part—the "digression"—Descartes would have titled this part *On the Formation of the Animal* <note>original Latin/French: "De la Formation de l'animal"</note>; and this is also the title...

<summary>This preface explains the editorial history and authenticity of Descartes' unfinished manuscript "The Description of the Human Body," clarifying why it was sometimes published under the title "On the Formation of the Fetus."</summary>

<keywords>René Descartes, Claude Clerselier, anatomy, manuscript history, Treatise on Man, human physiology, embryology</keywords>

## THE DESCRIPTION

*Body.*

In what state was the MS. <note>MS. is a standard abbreviation for "manuscript," meaning a hand-written document rather than a printed one.</note> of this Treatise found? Descartes
"himself had already begun to distinguish it by parts
and by articles," says Clerselier in his 1664 Preface
(unpaginated page 28). "And that," continues the editor, "gave
me the thought to complete what he had begun." These articles
number 74 in Clerselier’s edition. We
have just seen that Descartes had not numbered them this
way to the end; but where did he stop, and from which
number do we have Clerselier’s divisions, and no longer
Descartes’? This is impossible to determine. Therefore,
we will provide the indication of these 74 articles, while
maintaining all our reservations. — Furthermore, the beginning of the Treatise, of
which we have found a MS. copy (vol. X, p. 13-14), indeed
gives the words: "*1st Art.*" and "*2nd Artic.*", but without giving a title
to either one. We can conclude from this that the titles, which are
found in full in the 1664 edition, are not by
Descartes: it is Clerselier who added them, as he says
he also did for the *Treatise on Man*. We will
therefore relegate all these titles to the end of the present Treatise,
not believing we have the right to insert them into the phi-
losopher's text, nor even to place them alongside the
articles as they appear. However, as Descartes had divided this Treatise
"by parts," Clerselier assures us, we will at least
preserve this division: namely five parts, of which the 1st is only a *Pre-*
*face*, the 2nd and 3rd deal with *The movement of the Heart & the blood*,
then *Of nutrition*, and the last two, 4th and 5th, *Of the for-*
*mation of the animal.*

What is the date of this Treatise now? We can
determine it with a certain approximation.

First, Descartes, on several occasions (pp. 133, 140, 159,
Clerselier edition), refers to his *Principles*; and he indeed says *Prin-*
*ciples* in French, and not *Principia Philosophiæ* <note>original Latin: "Principia Philosophiæ"; this refers to Descartes' major work "Principles of Philosophy," first published in Latin in 1644.</note>, which

<summary>This page discusses the editorial history of Descartes' manuscript, noting that while Descartes began dividing the work into sections, the specific titles and many of the article numbers were likely added by his posthumous editor, Claude Clerselier.</summary>
<keywords>manuscript history, Claude Clerselier, Principles of Philosophy, anatomical treatise, editorial methodology, Descartes</keywords>

--- Page 255 ---
<meta>This page continues the editorial analysis of the manuscript’s history, moving from the physical state of the document to establishing a precise timeline for its composition through Descartes’ correspondence.</meta>

<header>OF THE HUMAN BODY.</header>

suggests that the translation has already appeared, and that the Treatise is later than 1647, and not only later than 1644.

Furthermore, in a letter to Princess Elizabeth <note>Princess Elizabeth of the Palatinate (1618–1680) was a close friend and long-term correspondent of Descartes; her insightful questions often pushed him to refine his theories on physics and ethics.</note>, dated January 25, 1648, Descartes declares "that he now has a writing in his hands," for which he even gives the subject, if not the title: "it is the description of the functions of the animal and of man." (*Volume V*, p. 112, l. 12-15.) This corresponds exactly to the first three parts that we have seen. But Descartes adds this significant phrase: "And I have even ventured" (but only for eight or ten days now) "to want to explain the way in which the animal is formed from the very beginning of its origin." (*Ibid.*, l. 19-22.) This clearly indicates the "digression" in our Treatise, concerning the "formation of the Animal," and gives us its date to within a few days. Finally, Descartes ends with a phrase that we find almost word for word in the Treatise (p. 161, Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes' literary executor who published many of his works after his death.</note> edition):

> "I say the animal in general; for, as for man in particular,
> "I would not dare undertake it, for lack of having enough experiments
> "for that purpose." (*Volume V*, p. 112, l. 22-25.)

This decisive text is confirmed by two others from the same year, 1648. The first is taken from the very interesting interview between Descartes and Burman <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679) was a Dutch theologian who visited Descartes; the record of their conversation is a vital source for understanding Descartes' later views.</note>, dated April 16, 1648. In it, there is mention of a *Treatise on the Animal*, on which Descartes worked "this winter." Characteristic details follow: the philosopher initially wanted to explain only the functions of the animal; but he saw that he absolutely could not do so without explaining the formation of the animal from the egg <note>original: "ab ovo"</note>. (*Volume V*, p. 170-171.) Indeed, Descartes, in his Treatise, after having spoken of the *movement of the heart & blood*, then of *nutrition*, deals with the *formation of the animal*. Finally, in a later letter, from the end of 1648 or the beginning of 1649, he explains, in almost the same terms, his double design: *description of the animal*, the first design, which was moreover abandoned "because he now has a better one," which is, instead of dealing "with the functions of the animal,"

to find "*the causes of its formation*." And he does not despair of succeeding, "*provided that he has the leisure and the convenience to conduct some experiments*." (Volume V, p. 260-261.)

We can therefore fix, with complete certainty, the date of the present Treatise to the year 1648. (Perhaps it was already begun in 1647.) And we shall not call it the "Second Treatise," as Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes' friend and literary executor; he was responsible for the first posthumous editions of many of Descartes' works.</note> does, who also called the *Treatise on Man* the "First Treatise." The two are independent of each other, and are separated, as we can see, by a fairly long interval.

the stomach, and the like, which contain no thought in themselves, are nothing but bodily movements; and since it is more common for one body to be moved by another body than for it to be moved by a soul, we <margin>5</margin> have less reason to attribute them to the soul than to the body.

<margin>IV.</margin> We can also see that, when some parts of our body are injured—for example, when a nerve is pricked—this causes them no longer to obey our will, as they were accustomed to do, and even that they often have <margin>10</margin> convulsive movements <term>convulsion<note>A sudden, involuntary muscle contraction. Descartes argues these prove the body has its own internal "springs" of motion independent of the soul's command.</note></term> which are contrary to it. This shows that the soul cannot excite any movement in the body unless all the bodily organs required for that movement are well-disposed; <margin>15</margin> but that, on the contrary, when the body has all its organs disposed for some movement, it does not need the soul to produce it. Consequently, all movements that we do not experience as depending on our thought must not be <margin>20</margin> attributed to the soul, but solely to the disposition of the organs; and even those movements called *voluntary* proceed principally from this disposition of the organs, since they cannot be excited without it, regardless of the will we have for them, although <margin>25</margin> it is the soul that determines them <note>Descartes uses the term "determines" to suggest the soul acts like a steersman who directs a ship that is already in motion by its own engines.</note>.

<margin>V.</margin> And although all these movements cease in the body when it dies and the soul leaves it, one must not infer from this that it is the soul that produces them; but only that it is one and the same cause which makes <margin>30</margin> the body no longer fit to produce them, and which also causes the soul to depart from it.

## *On the movement of the Heart & the blood.*]

<margin>VIII.</margin> | One cannot doubt that there is heat in the heart, for one can even feel it with the hand when opening the body of some living animal. And there is <margin>5</margin> no need to imagine that this heat is of any other nature than that which is generally caused by the mixing of some liquid, or some leaven <note>The author uses "leaven" (ferment) to describe a chemical reaction similar to fermentation or yeast rising</note>, which causes the body where it is located to dilate.

<margin>IX.</margin> But, because the dilation of the blood caused by <margin>10</margin> this heat is the first and the principal spring <note>The "spring" or "prime mover" of the body's mechanical system</note> of our entire machine, I would wish that those who have never studied Anatomy would take the trouble to see the heart of some terrestrial animal, large enough (for they <margin>15</margin> are all nearly similar to that of man), and that having first cut the tip of this heart, they would notice that there are inside it two caverns, or cavities, which can contain much blood. [one would be forced] to posit, besides that, other faculties <note>In 17th-century science, "faculties" were mysterious innate powers that older philosophers used to explain biological functions. Descartes, a mechanical philosopher, sought to replace these with physics and geometry.</note> that would change the qualities of the blood while it is in the heart. Instead, by considering only the expansion <term>dilatation: the swelling or increasing in volume of the blood</term> of this blood, which must necessarily follow from the heat—which everyone acknowledges is greater in the heart than in all other parts of the body—one clearly sees that this expansion alone is sufficient to move the heart in the way I have described. At the same time, it is sufficient to change the nature of the blood as much as experience shows it changes; and indeed, as much as one might imagine it must be changed, so that this blood is prepared and made more suitable to serve as nourishment for all the limbs, and to be used for all the other purposes it serves in the body. Consequently, there is no need to suppose any unknown or foreign faculties for this purpose.

For what preparation could one imagine to be greater and more rapid than that which is performed by fire or by heat, which is the strongest agent we know in nature? When it rarefies <note>Rarefaction is the process where a substance increases in volume, similar to how boiling water turns into expanding steam.</note> the blood in the heart, it separates its tiny parts from one another, and even divides them and changes their shapes in every imaginable way.

Aristotle's Greek text translates as: "This affection is like boiling; for boiling occurs when a liquid is turned to vapor by heat."</note>; and also that what creates the pulse is that the juice of the food <note>The original French "suç des viandes" refers to the nutritious liquid, or chyle, extracted from food during digestion.</note> one has eaten, entering continually into the heart, lifts its outer skin<sup>b</sup> <note>original: "Ἐν δὲ τῇ καρδίᾳ ἡ τοῦ ἀεὶ προσιόντος ἐκ τῆς τροφῆς ὑγροῦ διὰ τῆς θερμότητος ὄγκωσις ποιεῖ σφυγμὸν, αἰρομένη πρὸς τὸν ἔσχατον χιτῶνα τῆς καρδίας." This translates as: "In the heart, the swelling of the fluid constantly arriving from food, caused by heat, produces the pulse by rising against the outermost membrane of the heart."</note>: however, because he makes no mention there of the blood, nor of the structure of the heart, one sees that it is only by chance that he happened to say something approaching the truth, and that he had no certain knowledge of it. Likewise, his opinion was followed by no one in this matter, despite the fact that he has had the good fortune of being followed by many in many other matters that are less plausible.

And nevertheless, it is so important to know the true cause of the heart's movement that, without it, it is impossible to know anything concerning the Theory of Medicine, because all the other functions of the animal depend on it, as will be clearly seen from what follows.

<margin>XX.</margin>
But to understand this distinctly, one must consider that the parts of all bodies that have life, and which sustain themselves by nourishment—that is to say, animals and plants—are in continual change; so much so that there is no other difference between those named *fluids*, such as the blood, the humors <note>In 17th-century medicine, "humors" referred to the various bodily fluids like phlegm or bile.</note>, and the spirits <note>Descartes uses "animal spirits" to describe very subtle, fast-moving particles that travel through the nerves to move the muscles; they were thought of as a physical fluid, not a supernatural soul.</note>, and those named *solids*, such as the bones, the flesh, the nerves, and the skins; except that each particle of the latter moves much more slowly than those of the former.

And to conceive how these particles move, one must imagine that all the solid parts are composed only of small threads <note>original: "petits filets." Descartes envisioned biological tissues as mechanical structures made of microscopic filaments.</note> variously extended and folded, and sometimes also interwoven, each of which emerges from some point on one of the branches of an artery; and that the fluid parts, that is to say, the humors and the spirits, flow along these small threads through the | spaces found around them, and there form an infinity of little streams, which all have their source in the arteries, and ordinarily exit from the pores of these arteries that are closest to the root of the small threads they accompany; and that after various turns and returns that they make with these threads in the body, they finally come to the surface of the skin, through the pores of which these humors and spirits evaporate into the air.

<margin>XXXVIII.</margin>
At the same time that the blood coming from the right cavity begins to form the lungs, that which exits from the left begins also to form the other parts; and the first of all, after the heart, is the
<margin>5</margin> brain. For one must consider that, while the coarsest parts of the blood leaving the heart travel first in a straight line to the area of the seed <note>The "seed" refers to the formative fluid or the early-stage embryo before distinct organs are visible.</note> where the lower parts of the head are later formed, the most subtle [parts], which compose the spirits, 
<margin>10</margin> advance a little further and place themselves in the spot where the brain is later to be. <margin>15</margin> the spinal cord <note>Original: "moëlle de l'eſpine du dos," literally the marrow of the spine of the back.</note> is later located; this is because the movement of the blood in the part of the great artery descending from the heart—to which they are close at that time—agitates the neighboring seed and facilitates their course toward that side.

<margin>XXXIX. 20</margin>

<margin>25</margin> they flow little by little, and from there spread into all the other areas of the seed—those of their particles which exceed the others in some quality separate from the main body [of spirits] and turn off to the right and left toward the base of the brain and toward the
<margin>30</margin> front, where they begin to form the organs of the senses.

<margin>5</margin> though one does not commonly see as many arteries as veins in the bodies of animals. For reason dictates that the latter should appear much more than the former, because the blood is accustomed to remaining in the small veins, just as in the larger ones,
<margin>10</margin> even after the animal is dead, because the skin <note>In this context, Descartes refers to the "tunic" or membrane wall of the vessels.</note> of all of them contracts more or less equally. Instead, the blood of the arteries never stops in their small branches; for being pushed there by the *Diastole* <term>Diastole: the phase of the heartbeat where the chambers dilate; Descartes attributed this to the blood heating up and expanding like steam</term>, it passes promptly into the veins, or else it
<margin>15</margin> falls back into the larger arteries at the moment of the *Systole* <term>Systole: the phase where the heart's motion subsides; unlike modern medicine, Descartes viewed this as a passive collapse after the "vaporized" blood exited</term>, because their tubes remain open; and thus their smallest branches cannot be seen, any more than the white veins, called lacteals, which *Asellius* <term>Gaspare Aselli (c. 1581–1625), an Italian anatomist famous for discovering the lacteal vessels which carry nutrients (chyle) from the digestive tract</term><gloss>a</gloss> has recently discovered in the Mesen-
<margin>20</margin> tery <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, where they are never perceived unless one opens animals while they are still living, a few hours after they have eaten.

<margin>LV.</margin>
I have no need to explain the formation of the other veins and arteries at greater length, for I see nothing particular to remark upon there; they are all produced by this general principle: whenever some small part of the seed <note>the primordial fluid from which the embryo develops</note> travels toward the heart, the stream it creates in going there is a vein, and the stream made by the blood that comes from the heart to take its place is an artery. Thus, when these streams are somewhat distant from one another, the vein and artery seem separate, because the extremities of the artery are not visible.

And several various causes can, in this beginning, make these streams turn away, or cause one to divide into two, or two to join into one; this creates the difference we see between the distribution of the veins and that of the arteries. But this does not prevent them from always maintaining the same communication through the ends of their branches, because the course of the blood, which passes continually through these branches, keeps it open.

<margin>LVI.</margin>
And since the branches through which this communication occurs are found in every part of the body, and not only at its extremities, even if a foot or a hand is cut off, one does not thereby stop it <note>the flow of blood</note> in the leg or the arm.

blood leaves the heart at the time of **diastole** <term>diastole: the phase of the heartbeat where the chambers expand; Descartes believed this was caused by the blood "boiling" and expanding due to heat</term>, those of its particles that remain there enter into its flesh, where they find pores so arranged, and fibers so strongly agitated, that there is nothing but the matter of the **first Element** <term>first element: in Cartesian physics, the smallest, fastest-moving particles that fill all gaps and constitute fire</term> surrounding them; and that at the time of **systole** <term>systole: the phase where the heart contracts and pumps blood out</term> these pores change their shape, because the heart elongates, which causes the particles of blood that remained there—as if to serve as a **leaven** <term>leaven: a substance like yeast that causes expansion; Descartes uses this to explain how a small amount of "hot" blood triggers the expansion of the "new" blood</term> <note>original: "leuuain"</note>—to exit with great speed, and by this means, penetrating easily into the new blood entering the heart, they cause its particles to move away from one another, and in this distancing, they acquire the form of fire.

Now, while the fibers of the heart are agitated by the heat of this fire, they are so disposed to open and close their pores alternately, to produce the movements of **diastole** and **systole**, that even after the heart is removed from the body of the animal, and cut into pieces, provided that it is still warm, it requires only a very small amount of blood vapors presenting themselves to enter its pores to compel it to the movement of **diastole**; but when it is completely cooled, the shape of its pores, which depended on the agitation of the **first Element**, is changed, so that the vapors of the blood no longer enter; and because its fibers are stiff and hard, they are no longer so easy to bend.

# NOTICE

THE PASSIONS OF THE SOUL. By *René Descartes*. (In Paris, at the shop of Henry Le Gras, at the third Pillar of the Great Hall of the Palace, at the sign of the Crowned L. 1649. *With the King's Privilege*.) <note>original: "Avec Privilege du Roy" — a legal document granting exclusive rights to print a book.</note> Such is the title of the small octavo <term>octavo: a book size resulting from folding a printed sheet into eight leaves.</term> of 286 pages, plus 44 unnumbered introductory pages, which was the last work by Descartes printed during his lifetime. Despite bearing the name of a Parisian bookseller, it actually originated in Holland, as evidenced by the marking on a large number of copies: *In Amsterdam, at the shop of Louys Elzevier*, etc. Printer's mark: *Minerva*. However, due to an agreement between the two booksellers, copies were sent to France and bear the address we mentioned first.

Descartes was already in Sweden when this work appeared. He received several copies before his death; and Chanut, the executor of his final wishes, gave one to Chancellor Oxenstiern (letter of February 22, 1650) ᵃ. Furthermore, the distribution in France was handled by the Abbé Picot, to whom Descartes sent instructions on two occasions from Stockholm, on December 4, 1649, and January 15, 1650 ᵇ. The book had already been distributed in Holland, and Brasset received two copies in The Hague on November 26, 1649—one for himself and the other for his daughter ᶜ.

Descartes indeed announces to Carcavi <note>Pierre de Carcavi (c. 1600–1684), a mathematician and royal librarian who acted as a bridge between Descartes and the Parisian scientific community.</note>, in a letter of August 17, 1649, that he is to send his *Treatise* to a friend, who will take charge of printing it; and one finds, upon opening the volume, a *Warning* <note>original: "Avertiſſement"</note> by one of the friends of the *Author* <note>original: "Autheur"</note>, who declares that he will provide no other preface than to place here "the same letters, which he had previously written to him, in order to obtain that from him" <note>original: "les meſmes lettres, qu’il luy a cy-devant eſcrites, affin d’obtenir cela de luy"</note>. # FOREWORD.

The earliest date for the work would be the winter of 1645-46. In September and October 1645, Descartes was already thinking about it: he spoke of it to Chanut <note>Pierre Chanut (1601–1662), a French ambassador and close friend of Descartes.</note> and even wrote to Princess Elisabeth about it; by April 1646, he was able to deliver his Treatise to her. Princess Elisabeth <gloss>a</gloss> even wished to take it with her to Germany (letter of July 1646), and prior to that (letter of April 25, 1646) she had offered a slight critique of it, to which Descartes responded twice in May 1646 <gloss>b</gloss>. The princess's remarks and the philosopher's explanations concern only the first two parts of the Treatise, which would lead one to believe that the third part was still missing. Indeed, Elisabeth first takes issue with the general definition of the passions, and Descartes' response to this is a summary of the first part; Elisabeth then makes several observations on details, based on her personal experience, regarding certain passages of the second part. However, there is also a question of a passage that we had previously attributed to the *third* part, specifically article 170, or so we believed. But we were mistaken in this: article 170 speaks only "of Irresolution," and Elisabeth's remark concerns "a certain languor." "Languor" (*langeur* <note>original: "langeur," an archaic spelling of *langueur*</note>) is indeed the title of an article and even of several articles of the Treatise; but these are articles 119, 120, and 121 of the *second* part. And it even seems that Descartes gave satisfaction to the princess on this point: the sentence she complained about is no longer found in the printed text; the philosopher appears to have deleted it. But—and this is what matters most for our purposes—the Treatise, at that date, still had only two parts, and not three. Furthermore, other traces remain of these successive drafts: the inventory of Descartes' papers, made in Stockholm on February 14, 1650, mentions it twice: **K** *The Draft of the second part of the treatise on passions.* — **N** *On the nature of the passions of the soul. A draft heavily crossed out by the hand of the said Mr. Descartes* <gloss>c</gloss>.

<meta>This page continues the editorial introduction regarding the publication history of "The Passions of the Soul." It transitions from discussing the drafting of the manuscript to the specific typographical choices made for the printed edition of 1649.</meta>

->### OF THE PASSIONS.<-

Whatever the case may be, we currently possess only the text printed in 1649. And it is this very text that we shall reproduce, following the original edition with the most scrupulous fidelity, both for the typographical arrangement (division by articles, with their titles placed above the text rather than in the margin) and for the spelling. The latter is not exactly that of Descartes; it is rather the style of the printing house of <term>Louis Elzevier<note>A member of a famous Dutch family of printers and booksellers, renowned for their high-quality editions of scholarly works during the 17th century.</note></term>. However, Descartes accepted it, since he undoubtedly reviewed the proofs himself before his departure for Sweden on September 1st or 2nd, 1649, the text having already been sent by him to Paris on August 14th, fully printed. And in fact, except for the distinction between the letters *i* and *j*, which the Elzeviers differentiate (though they still print the capital as *Ie* and not *Je*), and that of the *u* and *v* which they also distinguish, the rest is fairly consistent with the rules the philosopher had imposed upon himself. The primary rule was the omission of double consonants, particularly the consonant *n* (writing *viene* instead of *vienne* <note>original: "viene" for "vienne" (comes); "comprene" for "comprenne" (understands)</note>, *comprene*, etc.). All things considered, in the absence of any original manuscript, and allowing for a few small details, we have a sufficient approximation of the way of writing words adopted by the philosopher.

Let us finally add that the original edition, published in 1649 under the name of Louis Elzevier in Amsterdam and in Paris under the name of Henry Le Gras, can still be found with other indications. Some copies of the same edition, a small <term>octavo<note>A book size resulting from folding a sheet of paper three times to create eight leaves; approximately 6 by 9 inches.</note></term>, bear the following: *At Amsterdam, by Louis Elzevier, and sold in Paris at the house of Henry Le Gras, 1650.* <note>original: "A Amſterdam, par Lovis Elzevier, & ſe vendent à Paris chez Henry Le Gras, 1650."</note> Or: *Amsterdam, by Louis Elzevier, 1650.* Or: *Amsterdam, and sold in Paris at the house of Thomas Joly, 1650.* Or finally, without a date: *At Paris, at the house of Guillaume Angot.* However, Alphonse Willems adds—to whom we owe all this information (*The Elzeviers*, Brussels, 1880, p. 270)—that "while the 1649 title pages in the name of L. Elzevier and H. Le Gras are of Elzevirian printing, the other titles we have just cited were executed in Paris." No doubt Le Gras had transferred a portion of the edition to two of his Parisian colleagues. As for

### ARTICLE III.

->*What rule one must follow for this purpose.*<-

<margin>5</margin>In this, one will not find great difficulty, if one takes care that everything we experience as being in us, and which we also see can exist in entirely inanimate bodies, must be attributed only to our body; and on the contrary, that everything that is in us, and which we do not conceive in any way to belong to a body, must be attributed to <margin>10</margin>our soul.

### ARTICLE IV.

->*That heat and the movement of the limbs proceed*<-
->*from the body; thoughts, from the soul.*<-

<margin>15</margin>Thus, because we do not conceive that the body thinks in any way, we have reason to believe that all the kinds <note>original: "fortes," likely a typesetting variant or error for "sortes" (kinds/sorts)</note> of thoughts that are in us belong to the soul. And because we do not doubt that there are inanimate bodies that can move in as many or more various ways <margin>20</margin>than ours, and which have as much or more heat (as experience shows in a flame, which alone has much more heat and movement than any of our limbs), we must believe that all the heat and all the movements that are in us, in <margin>25</margin>so far as they do not depend on thought, belong only to the body.

<meta>WORKS. VI.</meta>

<summary>Descartes establishes a foundational rule for distinguishing between the soul and the body: physical processes found in inanimate objects (like heat and motion) belong to the body, while thinking belongs exclusively to the soul. This allows him to argue that the body functions like a self-moving machine, independent of the soul's influence for its basic biological operations.</summary>

### ARTICLE V.

## *That it is an error to believe that the soul gives movement and heat to the body.*

By this means we will avoid a very significant error, into <margin>5</margin>
which many have fallen; so much so that I believe it is the 
primary cause that has prevented anyone from being able 
to properly explain the Passions and other things 
belonging to the soul until now. This error consists in 
the fact that, seeing that all dead bodies are deprived <margin>10</margin>
of heat, and subsequently of movement, people 
imagined that it was the absence of the soul that 
caused these movements and this heat to cease. And 
thus they believed, without reason, that our natural 
heat <note>Descartes refers to the "innate heat" or "vital flame," a concept from ancient medicine that he reinterprets here as a purely mechanical, thermodynamic process rather than a spiritual one.</note> and all the movements of our bodies <margin>15</margin>
depend on the soul; whereas one should think, on the 
contrary, that the soul only departs when one dies 
because this heat ceases and the organs that serve 
to move the body decay.

---

### ARTICLE VI.

<margin>20</margin> ## *What difference there is between a living body and a dead body.*

In order, then, that we may avoid this error, let us 
consider that death never occurs through the fault 
of the soul, but only because some of the principal 
parts of the body decay; and let us judge that the body <margin>25</margin>
of a living man differs as much from that of a [dead] man <note>The text cuts off here, but Descartes is beginning a famous analogy comparing the living body to a functioning watch and a dead body to a broken one.</note>

<summary>Descartes corrects the common mistake of thinking the soul provides the body's heat and motion; instead, he argues that the soul only leaves the body because the body’s physical mechanisms have broken down.</summary>

small threads or small tubes that all come

## ARTICLE XIII.

### ARTICLE XVII.
