### ARTICLE XIX.
#### *Of Perception.*

<margin>10</margin> Our perceptions are also of two kinds, and some have the soul as their cause, the others the body. Those which have the soul as their cause are the perceptions of our acts of will, and of all the imaginations or other <margin>15</margin> thoughts that depend on them. For it is certain that we could not will anything without perceiving, by that same means, that we will it. And although, with regard to our soul, it is an <term>action<note>In Cartesian philosophy, an "action" is something the soul does or initiates; a "passion" is something the soul receives or undergoes.</note></term> to will something, one can say that it is also in the soul a <margin>20</margin> <term>passion<note>Descartes is making a subtle point here: even when we are being "active" by making a choice, we "passively" notice or feel ourselves making that choice.</note></term> to perceive that it wills. However, because this perception and this will are in effect only one and the same thing, the naming is always done according to that which is most noble; and thus we are not <margin>25</margin> accustomed to calling it a passion, but only an action.

## ARTICLE XXX.

### *That the soul is united to all parts of the body collectively.*

But, to understand all these
<margin>5</margin> things more perfectly, it is necessary to know that the soul is truly joined to the entire body, and that one cannot properly say that it is in any one of its parts, to the exclusion | of the others, because the body is one and in some way indivisible, due to the arrangement of
<margin>10</margin> its organs, which are all so related to one another that when any one of them is removed, it renders the whole body defective; and because the soul is of a nature that has no relation to <term>extension<note>original: "l’eſtendue." In Cartesian philosophy, "extension" refers to the primary attribute of matter—the fact that it occupies physical space. Descartes argues the soul, being purely thought, has no physical size or shape.</note></term>, nor to the dimensions or other properties of the matter of which the body
<margin>15</margin> is composed, but only to the whole assembly of its organs. As it appears from the fact that we cannot in any way conceive of half or a third of a soul, nor what space it occupies, and that it does not become any smaller when one cuts away some
<margin>20</margin> part of the body, but rather it separates from it entirely when the assembly of its organs is dissolved.

## THE ORDER & THE ENUMERATION OF THE PASSIONS <note>original: "passions" — in Cartesian philosophy, these are perceptions or emotions caused by the body's influence on the soul.</note>.

### ARTICLE LIII.

### *Wonder.*

<margin>5</margin> When the first encounter with some object surprises us, and we judge it to be new, or very different from what we knew before, or even from what we supposed it ought to be, this causes us to wonder at it and be
<margin>10</margin> astonished by it. And because this can happen before we know in any way whether this object is | suitable to us or if it is not, it seems to me that Wonder <note>original: "Admiration" — Descartes uses this term to mean a neutral intellectual surprise or wonder, rather than modern "admiration" which implies liking something.</note> is the first of all the passions. And it has no contrary, because if the object which
<margin>15</margin> presents itself has nothing in it that surprises us, we are not moved by it at all, and we consider it without passion.

### ARTICLE LIV.

### *Esteem & Scorn, Generosity or Pride, & Humility or Abjection.*

<margin>20</margin> To Wonder is joined Esteem or Scorn, according to whether it is the greatness of an object or its smallness that we wonder at. And we can thus esteem or scorn ourselves: from which come

## ARTICLE LXVIII.

### *Why this enumeration of the Passions is different from the one commonly received.*

This is the order that seems to me to be the best for
<margin>5</margin>enumerating the Passions. In this, I know well that
I am departing from the opinion of all those who have
previously written on the subject. But this is not without great reason.
For they derive their enumeration from the fact that they distin-
guish two appetites in the sensitive part of the soul,
<margin>10</margin>which they name, one *Concupiscible* <note>The "desiring" faculty focused on seeking pleasure and avoiding pain</note>, the other *Irascible* <note>The "spirited" faculty focused on overcoming obstacles or resisting threats</note>.
And because I do not recognize in the soul any distin-
ction of parts, as I have said above<gloss>a</gloss>, that
seems to me to signify nothing else, except that it has two
faculties: one for desiring, the other for getting angry; and
<margin>15</margin>because it has in the same way the faculties for wondering,
loving, hoping, fearing, and thus for receiving into
itself each of the other passions, or for performing the actions
to which these passions push it, I do not see
why they wanted to relate them all to Con-
<margin>20</margin>cupiscence or to Anger. Besides, their enumera-
tion does not include all the principal pas-
sions, as I believe this one does. I speak
only of the principal ones, because one could
still distinguish many other more specific ones,
<margin>25</margin>and their number is indefinite.

---

<margin>a. Article 47, page 364, lines 23-24.</margin>

<margin>10</margin> knowledge of it. This is what is commonly called

### ARTICLE LXXIV.

->*What all the passions are useful for,*<-
<margin>15</margin> ->*and how they are harmful.*<-

Now it is easy to know, from what has been said
above, that the utility of all the passions consists
only in that they strengthen and prolong thoughts in the soul,
which it is good for the soul to preserve, and which
<margin>20</margin> might easily without this be erased from it.
Just as all the evil they can cause consists
in their strengthening and preserving these thoughts
more than is necessary; or else that they strengthen and
preserve others, upon which it is not good to
<margin>25</margin> dwell.

<summary>Descartes defines astonishment as an excessive form of wonder that paralyzes the body and mind, and concludes that the general purpose of passions is to reinforce useful thoughts.</summary>

## *What Wonder is particularly useful for.*

And it can be said specifically of Wonder <note>original: "l’Admiration" — as noted previously, this refers to the intellectual surprise at something new or rare.</note>,

also by the application of our understanding, which

And the other passions can serve
to make one notice things that appear
<margin>20</margin> good or evil; but we have only wonder
for those that appear merely rare.
Thus we see that those who have no natural
inclination toward this passion are usually
<margin>25</margin> very ignorant.

### ARTICLE LXXVI.

#### *How it can be harmful: and how one can compensate for its deficiency and correct its excess.*

<margin>5 10 15 20</margin>
But it happens much more often that one wonders too much, and is astonished upon perceiving things that deserve little | or no consideration, than that one wonders too little. And this can entirely take away or pervert the use of reason. This is why, although it is good to be born with some inclination toward this passion, because that disposes us toward the acquisition of the sciences, we must nevertheless try afterward to deliver ourselves from it as much as possible. For it is easy to compensate for its deficiency by a particular reflection and attention, to which our will can always oblige our understanding <term>understanding: the faculty of the mind that perceives and processes ideas</term>, when we judge that the thing presenting itself is worth the trouble; but there is no other remedy to prevent oneself from wondering to excess, than to acquire the knowledge of many things, and to practice the consideration of all those which may seem the rarest and the strangest.

### ARTICLE LXXVIII.

->*That its excess can turn into a habit, when*<-
->*one fails to correct it.*<-

And although this passion seems to diminish through
<margin>10</margin>use—because the more one encounters rare things
that one wonders at, the more one becomes accustomed to ceasing

that is to say, those who seek out rarities only to
wonder at them, and not at all to know them; for they
become little by little so prone to wonder, that things of
<margin>25</margin>no importance are no less capable of
arresting them than those whose investigation is more useful.

<summary>Descartes explains that while experience usually reduces wonder, an uncorrected habit of excessive wonder leads to "blind curiosity," where one fixates on novelty without seeking actual knowledge.</summary>

<header>Second Part.</header>

### ARTICLE LXXIX.
### *The definitions of Love and Hatred.*

<margin>5, 10, 15</margin>Love is an emotion of the soul, caused by the movement of the spirits <note>original: "esprits"; referring to "animal spirits," which 17th-century physiology imagined as very subtle fluids or wind that carried signals through the nerves</note>, which incites it to join itself by will to objects that appear to be suitable to it. And Hatred is an emotion, caused by the spirits, which incites the soul to want to be separated from objects that present themselves to it as harmful. I say that these emotions are caused by the spirits, in order to distinguish Love and Hatred, which are passions and depend upon the body, as much from the judgments which also lead the soul to join itself by will with the things it esteems good, and to separate itself from those it esteems bad, as from the emotions that these judgments alone excite in the soul.

### ARTICLE LXXX.
### *What it is to join or separate oneself by will.*

<margin>20, 25</margin>Furthermore, by the word "will" <note>original: "volonté"</note>, I do not intend to speak here of desire, which is a passion apart and relates to the future, but of the consent by which one considers oneself from this moment as joined with what one loves: in such a way that one imagines a whole, of which one thinks oneself to be only a part, and that the thing loved is another part. Just as, on the contrary, in Hatred one considers oneself alone as a whole, entirely separated from the thing for which one has an aversion.

<summary>Descartes defines Love and Hatred as physiological passions driven by "animal spirits," distinguishing them from purely intellectual judgments, and explains "will" as a sense of unity with the beloved object.</summary>
<keywords>Love, Hatred, animal spirits, will, soul and body, physiological psychology, aversion</keywords>

# ARTICLE LXXXI.

## *On the distinction commonly made between the Love of concupiscence and the Love of benevolence<gloss>a</gloss>.*

<note>original: "Amour de concupiscence & de bienveillance"; these are traditional Scholastic terms. "Concupiscence" refers to a love of desire or self-interest, while "benevolence" refers to wishing well to another.</note>

Now, it is common to distinguish two kinds
<margin>5</margin>of Love: one is named the Love of bene-
volence, that is to say, which incites one to wish for the good of
what one loves; the other is named the Love of concu-
piscence, that is to say, which makes one desire the thing
one loves. But it seems to me that this distinction concerns
<margin>10</margin>only the effects of Love, and not at all its
essence. For as soon as one has joined oneself by will to some
object, of whatever nature it may be, one feels for it
benevolence; that is to say, one also joins to it by will
the things one believes to be suitable to it: which is
one of the principal effects of Love. And | if one judges that
<margin>15</margin>it would be a good to possess it, or to be associated with
it in some way other than by will, one desires it: which
is also one of the most ordinary effects of love.

### ARTICLE LXXXIV.

## *That there are not as many species of Hatred as of Love.*

Furthermore, although Hatred is directly opposed to Love, it is not distinguished into as many species; this is because we do not notice <margin>10</margin> the difference between the evils from which we are separated by will as much as we do the difference between the goods to which we are joined.

### ARTICLE LXXXVI.
<margin>20</margin>
#### *The Definition of Desire.*

The passion of **Desire** is an agitation of the soul, caused
by the spirits <note>referring to "animal spirits," which Descartes believed were physical fluids in the nerves that moved the body and affected the soul</note>, which disposes it to wish for the future
those things it represents to itself as being suitable. Thus
one does not only desire the presence of an absent good,
<margin>25</margin>but also the conservation of the present; and furthermore the absence
of evil, as much of that which one already has, as of that
which one believes one might receive in the time to come.

<summary>Descartes distinguishes between love/hatred based on reason versus those based on sensory attraction (Likability and Horror), warning that sensory passions are more violent but less truthful. He then defines Desire as a physical agitation of the soul directed toward future goods or the avoidance of evils.</summary>

### | ARTICLE LXXXVII.
## *That it is a passion which has no contrary.*

I know well that commonly in the Schools <note>referring to "Scholasticism," the traditional philosophy taught in universities based on Aristotle</note> one opposes the passion that tends toward the pursuit of good, which alone is named **Desire**, to that which tends toward the flight from evil, which is named **Aversion**. But insofar as there is no good whose deprivation is not an evil, nor any evil, considered as a positive thing, whose deprivation is not a good; and since in seeking, for example, riches, one necessarily flees poverty, and in fleeing diseases one seeks health, and so with the others: it seems to me that it is always one and the same movement that carries one toward the pursuit of good, and simultaneously toward the flight from the evil which is its contrary. I notice there only this difference: that the **Desire** one has when tending toward some good is accompanied by **Love**, and subsequently by **Hope** and **Joy**; whereas the same **Desire**, when one tends to move away from the evil contrary to that good, is accompanied by **Hatred**, **Fear**, and **Sadness**: which is the reason why one judges it to be contrary to itself. But if one wishes to consider it when it relates equally and at the same time to some good in order to seek it, and to the opposite evil in order to avoid it, one can see very evidently that it is only a single passion <note>Desire is thus a unified force for Descartes, whether it is "pulling" toward a benefit or "pushing" away from a harm</note> which performs both.

<summary>Descartes argues against the traditional philosophical distinction between Desire and Aversion, claiming they are actually a single passion directed toward a good and away from its corresponding evil simultaneously.</summary>
<keywords>Desire, Aversion, Scholasticism, Good and Evil, Unity of Passion, Love, Hatred, Animal Spirits</keywords>

## ARTICLE LXXXVIII.

### *What its various species are.*

There would be more reason to distinguish **Desire** into as many different species as there are different objects 
<margin>5</margin> that one seeks. For, | example, **Curiosity**, which is nothing other than a desire to know, differs greatly from the desire for glory, and this latter from the desire for vengeance, and so with the others. But it suffices here to know that there are as many as there are species of **Love** or of 
<margin>10</margin> **Hatred**, and that the most significant and the strongest are those which arise from **Attraction** <note>original: "Agreément," referring to the soul's sense of something being pleasing or suitable</note> and from **Horror**.

## ARTICLE LXXXIX.

### *What the Desire is that arises from Horror.*

<margin>15</margin> is contrary to it, as has been said: the **Desire** that arises from **Attraction** is nonetheless very different from that which arises from **Horror**. For this **Attraction** and this **Horror**, which truly are contraries, are not the good and the evil which serve as objects to these **Desires**,

### ARTICLE XCII.

->*The definition of Sadness.*<-

<margin>20</margin> **Sadness** is a disagreeable languor, in
which consists the discomfort that the soul receives from
the evil, or from the defect, which the impressions of the brain
represent to it as belonging to it. And there is also
<margin>25</margin> an intellectual **Sadness**, which is not the **passion**,
but which hardly fails to be accompanied by it.

### | ARTICLE XCIII.

## *What are the causes of these two Passions.*

<margin>5 10 15</margin>
Now, when intellectual **Joy** or **Sadness** thus excites the kind that is a **passion**, their cause is quite evident; and one sees from their definitions that **Joy** comes from the opinion one has of possessing some good, and **Sadness** from the opinion one has of having some evil or some defect. But it often happens that one feels sad or joyful without being able to distinctly notice the good or the evil that are the causes: namely, when this good or this evil make their impressions in the brain without the mediation of the soul <note>Descartes argues that the body can sometimes trigger emotional states through purely mechanical processes in the brain before the conscious mind processes the reason why.</note>, sometimes because they belong only to the body; and sometimes also, even though they belong to the soul, because the soul does not consider them as good and evil, but under some other form, the impression of which is joined with that of good and evil in the brain.

### ARTICLE XCVI.

# *What are the movements of the blood and the spirits that cause the five preceding passions* <note>original: "cinq paſſions precedentes." These are Love, Hatred, Desire, Joy, and Sadness, as established in Article 69.</note>.

<margin>5</margin>The five passions that I have begun to explain here are so joined or opposed to one another that it is easier to consider them all together than to treat each separately, as was done with Wonder <note>original: "l'Admiration." Descartes treats Wonder differently because it does not involve the heart or blood, only the brain.</note>. And their cause is not, like that of Wonder, in the brain alone, but also in the heart, <margin>10</margin>in the spleen, in the liver, and in all the other parts of the body, insofar as they serve in the production of the blood, and consequently of the spirits <note>term: "esprits" (animal spirits). In 17th-century physiology, these were thought to be very fine, subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to move the body.</note>. For, although all the veins conduct the blood they contain toward the heart, it nevertheless happens sometimes <margin>15</margin>that the blood from some veins is pushed there with more force than that from others; and it also happens that the openings through which it enters the heart, or those through which it leaves, are more enlarged or more constricted at one time than at another.

### ARTICLE CXIII.

## *On the actions of the eyes and the face.*

<margin>5, 10, 15, 20, 25</margin> There is no Passion that some particular action of the eyes does not declare: and this is so manifest in some, that even the most stupid servants can notice by the eye of their master whether he is angry with them, or if he is not. But even though one easily perceives these actions of the eyes, and knows what they signify, it is not easy for all that to describe them, because each one is composed of several changes which happen to the movement and the shape of the eye, which are so specific and so small that each of them cannot be perceived separately, although what results from their conjunction is very easy to notice. One can say almost the same of the actions of the face, which also accompany the passions: for although they are larger than those of the eyes, it is nevertheless difficult to distinguish them; and they are so little different, that there are men who make almost the same face when they weep as others do when they laugh. It is true that there are some which are quite remarkable, such as the wrinkles of the forehead in anger, and certain movements of the nose and the lips in indignation and in mockery; but they do not seem so much to be natural as voluntary <note>voluntary: Descartes suggests these specific expressions might be consciously controlled or learned behaviors rather than automatic biological responses.</note>. ### ARTICLE CXIV.

<margin>5</margin> ### *On changes of color.*

One cannot so easily prevent oneself from blushing or turning pale when some passion disposes one to it: because these changes do not depend on the nerves and the muscles, as the preceding ones do; and because they come <margin>10</margin> more immediately from the heart, which one can name the source of the passions, insofar as it prepares the blood and the spirits <note>spirits: referring to "animal spirits," which Descartes believed were subtle physical fluids that traveled through the nerves to move the body.</note> to produce them. Now it is certain that the color of the face comes only from the blood, which, flowing continually from the heart through the arteries into all the <margin>15</margin> veins, and from all the veins into the heart, colors the face more or less, according as it fills more or less the small veins which are toward its surface.

---

### ARTICLE CXV.

### *How Joy causes blushing.*

<margin>20</margin> Thus Joy makes the color more vivid and more ruddy, because by opening the sluices of the heart, it causes the blood to flow more quickly into all the veins; and because, becoming warmer and more subtle <note>subtle: in 17th-century science, this refers to matter that is refined, thin, or composed of very small, fast-moving particles.</note>, it moderately swells all the parts of the face: which <margin>25</margin> renders the air <note>air: the general appearance or look of a person.</note> more smiling and more gay.

<summary>Descartes explains that while facial expressions can be faked, changes in skin color like blushing are involuntary because they result directly from the heart's influence on blood flow. He specifically notes that joy causes a ruddy complexion by warming the blood and increasing its circulation to the face.</summary>

### ARTICLE CXVI.

### *How Sadness causes paleness.*

Sadness, on the contrary, by narrowing the orifices
of the heart, causes the blood to flow more slowly into
<margin>5</margin> the veins, and as it becomes colder and thicker,
it needs to occupy less space there: so that,
withdrawing into the largest veins, which are those
closest to the heart, it leaves the more distant ones; of
which the most visible being those of the face, this makes
<margin>10</margin> it appear pale and gaunt, especially when the
Sadness is great, or when it comes on suddenly:
as is seen in Terror <note>original: "l'Eſpouvante"</note>, where the surprise increases
the action that constricts the heart.

### ARTICLE CXX.

->*How it is caused by Love and by Desire.*<-

And the Passion <note>term: Passion — in 17th-century philosophy, a "passion" is an emotion or state of mind caused by external stimuli acting upon the soul</note> which most commonly causes this effect is Love, joined with the Desire for a thing whose <margin>5</margin>acquisition is not imagined as possible for the present time. For Love so occupies the soul in considering the beloved object, that it employs all the spirits <note>term: spirits — "animal spirits," which Descartes believed were subtle fluids in the blood that traveled through nerves to move muscles</note> that are in the brain to represent its image to it, and halts all the movements of the gland <margin>10</margin>which do not serve this purpose. And it must be noted, regarding Desire, that the property I have attributed to it of making the body more mobile only belongs to it when one imagines | the desired object to be such that one can, from that moment, do something that serves to <margin>15</margin>acquire it. For if, on the contrary, one imagines that it is impossible at that time to do anything useful toward it, all the agitation of Desire remains in the brain without passing into the nerves at all; and being entirely employed in strengthening the idea of the desired object there, <margin>20</margin>it leaves the rest of the body languishing.

### ARTICLE CXXII. <margin>10</margin>

### *On Fainting.*

Fainting <note>original: "Pasmoison" — a swoon or loss of consciousness</note> is not very far removed from death. For
one dies when the fire that is in the heart is extinguished
entirely; and one only falls into a faint when
it is smothered in such a way that there still remain <margin>15</margin>
some remnants of heat, which can afterwards
rekindle it. Now there are several indispositions of the body
which can cause one to fall thus into a failing state;
but among the passions, it is only extreme Joy
that is observed to have the power to do so. And the way in <margin>20</margin>
which I believe it causes this effect is that, by opening
extraordinarily the orifices of the heart, the blood from the veins
enters there so suddenly and in such great quantity that it cannot
be rarefied <note>term: rarefied — the process of heating and expanding the blood, which Descartes believed created the pressure necessary for circulation</note> by the heat quickly enough
to lift the little membranes <note>original: "petites peaux" — referring to the heart valves</note> that close the entrances of these <margin>25</margin>
veins: by means of which it smothers the fire, which it
is accustomed to maintain when it enters the heart
only in measured amounts.

SECOND PART.

### ARTICLE CXXIII.

->*Why one does not faint from Sadness.*<-

It seems that a great Sadness, which occurs unexpectedly, ought to so tightly constrict the orifices of the heart <margin>5</margin> that it could also extinguish its fire; but nevertheless, one does not observe this to happen, or if it does happen, it is very rarely: of which I believe the reason is, that there can hardly be so little blood in the heart that it does not suffice to maintain the heat, even when its orifices <margin>10</margin> are almost closed.

### ARTICLE CXXIV.

->*Of Laughter <insert>a</insert>.*<-

Laughter consists in the fact that the blood coming from the right cavity of the heart through the arterial vein <note>original: "vene arterieuse" — what we now call the pulmonary artery</note>, swelling the lungs suddenly and at various intervals, <margin>15</margin> forces the air they contain to exit with impetuosity through the windpipe <note>original: "sifflet" — literally "whistle," referring to the trachea or larynx</note>, where it forms an inarticulate and piercing voice; and both the lungs in swelling, and this air in exiting, push all the muscles of the diaphragm, the chest, and the throat: <margin>20</margin> by means of which they cause the muscles of the face which have some connection with them to move. And it is only this action of the face, with this inarticulate and piercing voice, that is called Laughter.

### ARTICLE CXXV.

*Why it does not accompany the greatest Joys.*

Now, although it seems that Laughter is one of the principal signs of Joy, it can nevertheless only <margin>5</margin> cause it when that Joy is merely moderate, and when there is some wonder <note>original: "admiration" — in the 17th century, this meant a sense of surprise or being struck by novelty</note> or some hatred mixed with it. For we find by experience that when we are extraordinarily joyful, the subject of that <margin>10</margin> joy never causes us to burst out laughing; and we cannot even be as easily invited to it by some other cause as when we are sad. The reason for this is that, in great Joys, the lung is always so full of blood that it cannot be further swollen by <margin>15</margin> repeated bursts.

The other is the mixture of some liquid which increases the rarefaction of the blood. And I find none suitable for that except the most fluid part of

than their use. Regarding which it is to be remarked that, according to the institution of Nature, they all relate to the body, and are given to the soul only insofar as it is joined with it: so that their <margin>5</margin> natural use is to incite the soul to consent and contribute to the actions which can serve to preserve the body, or to render it in some way more perfect. And in this sense, Sadness and Joy are the first two that are employed. For the soul is not immediately <margin>10</margin> warned of things which harm the body, except by the feeling it has of pain, which produces in it first the passion of Sadness, then following that, Hatred of what causes this pain, and in the third place, the Desire to be delivered from it. Just as <margin>15</margin> the soul is not immediately warned of things useful to the body, except by some sort of tickling <note>original: "chatoüillement" — Descartes uses this term to describe a pleasant physical stimulation or "titillation" that signals a beneficial state for the body.</note>, which, exciting Joy within it, then gives birth to the love of what one believes to be the cause, and finally the desire <margin>20</margin> to acquire what can make one continue in this Joy, or else enjoy a similar one again afterward. This shows that all five are very useful in regard to the body; and even, that Sadness is in some way primary and more necessary than Joy, and Hatred than Love: because <margin>25</margin> it is of greater importance to repel things which harm and can destroy, than to acquire those which add some perfection without which one can subsist.

<summary>Descartes argues that the primary passions (Joy, Sadness, Love, Hatred, and Desire) serve a biological purpose by signaling what is harmful or beneficial to the body's survival. He posits that negative passions like Sadness and Hatred are more essential for survival than positive ones because avoiding destruction is more critical than gaining non-essential improvements.</summary>

### ARTICLE CXXXVIII.

->*Of their defects, and the means of correcting them.*<-

But even though this use of the passions is the most natural they can have, and although all <margin>5</margin> animals without reason <note>Descartes refers to non-human animals, which he famously viewed as "automata" lacking a rational soul.</note> conduct their lives only by bodily movements similar to those which usually follow the passions in us, and to which the passions incite our soul to consent: it is nevertheless <margin>10</margin> not always good, insofar as there are many things harmful to the body which at the beginning cause no Sadness, or even give Joy; and others which are useful to it, although at first they are inconvenient. And besides that, they almost always make <margin>15</margin> both the goods and the evils they represent appear much greater and more important than they are; so that they incite us to seek the ones and flee the others with more ardor and more care than is suitable: just as <margin>20</margin> we also see that beasts are often deceived by baits, and that to avoid small evils, they plunge into greater ones. This is why we must make use of experience and reason to distinguish good from evil, and <margin>25</margin> to know their true value, so as not to take one for the other, and not to be carried toward anything with excess.

<gloss>passions: the emotions or perceptions of the soul caused by the body; reason: the faculty of the soul to judge truth; bodily movements: the physiological responses triggered by the animal spirits; soul: the thinking substance; Sadness: a passion signaling harm; Joy: a passion signaling benefit; experience: empirical knowledge gained over time; excess: an immoderate response beyond what reason dictates.</gloss>

<summary>Descartes explains that while passions are natural guides for survival, they are often deceptive by exaggerating the importance of objects or masking harm with pleasure. He concludes that human reason and experience are necessary to moderate these impulses and avoid harmful excesses.</summary>

# Of the Passions.

### ARTICLE CXXXIX.

#### *Of the use of these same Passions, insofar as they belong to the soul; and first, of Love.*

This would be sufficient if we had nothing but the <margin>5</margin> body within us, or if it were our better part; but since it is only the lesser part, we must principally consider the Passions insofar as they belong to the soul. In regard to the soul, Love and Hatred proceed from knowledge and precede Joy <margin>10</margin> and Sadness—except when these latter two take the place of knowledge, of which they are species <note>Descartes suggests that sometimes we feel joy or sadness before we intellectually understand why, making the feeling itself a type of "confused" knowledge.</note>. And when this knowledge is true—that is to say, when the things it leads us to love are truly good, and those it leads us to <margin>15</margin> hate are truly evil—Love is incomparably better than Hatred; it can never be too great, and it never fails to produce Joy. I say that this Love is extremely good because, by joining us to true goods, <margin>20</margin> it perfects us by that much. I also say that it cannot be too great; for all that the most excessive Love can do is to join us so perfectly to these goods that the Love we have particularly for ourselves makes no <margin>25</margin> distinction between them <note>This refers to Descartes' idea that when we love something truly good, we consider ourselves and that object as a single "whole," seeking its benefit as much as our own.</note>; which I believe can never be bad. And it is necessarily followed by Joy, because it represents what we love to us as a good that belongs to us.

<summary>Descartes shifts focus from the body to the soul, arguing that Love based on true knowledge is always beneficial and can never be excessive because it unites the soul with genuine goods. He establishes a hierarchy where Love and Hatred are primary intellectual judgments that then trigger Joy or Sadness.</summary>
<keywords>Love, Hatred, Joy, Sadness, knowledge, soul, perfection, union with the good, René Descartes</keywords>

### ARTICLE CXL.

#### *Of Hatred.*

Hatred, on the contrary, can never be so small
that it does not cause harm; and it is never without Sadness. I
<margin>5</margin> say that it cannot be too small, because
we are never incited to any action by the Hatred
of evil that we could not be even better incited to
by the Love of the good to which it is contrary: at least
when this good and this evil are sufficiently known. For
<margin>10</margin> I admit that the Hatred of evil which is manifested only
by pain, is necessary with regard to the body;
but I am speaking here only of that which comes from a
clearer | knowledge, and I relate it only to the soul.
I say also that it is never without Sadness, because,
<margin>15</margin> since evil is only a privation <note>Descartes follows the philosophical tradition (like that of Augustine) viewing evil not as a positive force, but as the absence or "privation" of a good that should be there.</note>, it cannot be
conceived without some real subject in which it exists; and
there is nothing real which does not have in itself some goodness,
so that the Hatred which distances us from some evil,
distances us by the same means from the good to which it is
<margin>20</margin> joined, and the privation of this good, being represented to
our soul as a defect belonging to it,
excites Sadness within it. For example, the Hatred which
distances us from someone's bad character,
distances us by the same means from their conversation <note>In this context, "conversation" refers to social interaction or keeping company with someone.</note>, in
<margin>25</margin> which we might otherwise find some
good, of which we are sorry to be deprived. And
thus in all other Hatreds, one can remark
some subject of Sadness.

<summary>Descartes argues that Hatred is always harmful and accompanied by Sadness because it involves rejecting a real object which, despite its flaws, contains some inherent good.</summary>

# ON THE PASSIONS.

## | ARTICLE CXLI.

### *Of Desire, Joy, and Sadness.*

As for Desire, it is evident that when it proceeds from true knowledge, it cannot be bad, provided that it is not excessive and that this <margin>5</margin> knowledge regulates it. It is also evident that Joy cannot fail to be good, nor Sadness to be bad, in respect to the soul: because it is in the latter that all the discomfort <note>original: "incommodité"</note> consists which the soul receives from evil, and in the former that all the <margin>10</margin> enjoyment <note>original: "joüissance"</note> of the good which belongs to it consists. So that if we had no body, I would dare to say that we could not abandon ourselves too much to Love and to Joy, nor avoid Hatred and Sadness too much. But the bodily movements that accompany them can <margin>15</margin> all be harmful to health when they are very violent; and on the contrary, be useful to it when they are only moderate.

### ARTICLE 146.

->*On those things which depend on us and on others.*<-

We must therefore entirely reject the common opinion that there is a Fortune <note>original: "Fortune." Referring to the personified concept of luck or chance.</note> outside of us which causes things to happen or not happen according to its pleasure; and we must know that everything is guided by divine Providence, whose eternal decree is so infallible and immutable that, except for the things which this same <margin>10</margin> decree has willed to depend on our free will <note>original: "libre arbitre." The capacity of the soul to choose its own actions.</note>, we must think that, as far as we are concerned, nothing happens which is not necessary and, as it were, fated <note>original: "fatal." In the sense of being determined by fate or destiny.</note>, so that we cannot without error desire that it happen in any other way. But because most of our Desires extend to things which do not depend entirely on us, <margin>15</margin> nor entirely on others, we must carefully distinguish in them what depends only on us, so as to extend our Desire to that alone. And as for the rest, although we must consider its success to be entirely fated and unchangeable, so that our Desire <margin>20</margin> does not occupy itself with it, we must nonetheless consider the reasons which make us more or less hopeful for it, so that they may serve to regulate our actions. For example, if we have business in some place to which we can go by two different roads, one <margin>25</margin> of which is usually much safer than the other: although perhaps the decree of Providence is such that if we go by the road we consider safest, we shall not fail to be robbed there,

## ARTICLE 152.

<margin>10</margin> ### *For what cause one may esteem oneself.*

And because one of the principal parts of wisdom is to know in what way and for what cause each person ought to esteem or despise themselves, I shall try here to state my opinion on the matter. I notice in us <margin>15</margin> only one single thing which can give us just reason to esteem ourselves: namely, the use of our free will <note>original: "libre arbitre."</note> and the dominion we have over our volitions. For it is only the actions that depend on this free will for which we can with reason <margin>20</margin> be praised or blamed; and it makes us in some way similar to God by making us masters of ourselves, provided that we do not lose through cowardice the rights it gives us.

### ARTICLE 155.

## In what virtuous Humility consists.

Thus, the most generous are usually the most humble; and virtuous humility consists only in
<margin>10</margin> this: that the reflection we make on the infirmity of our nature, and on the faults we may have previously committed, or are capable of committing—which are no less than those that can be committed by others—causes

### ARTICLE 159.

### *On Vicious Humility.*

As for Abjectness, or Vicious Humility <note>original: "Baſſeſſe, ou Humilité vitieuſe"</note>, it consists principally in one feeling weak or <margin>5</margin> irresolute, and that, as if one did not have the full use of one's free will <term>free will: the power of the mind to choose its own actions, which Descartes views as the core of human dignity</term>, one cannot prevent oneself from doing things which one knows one will repent of later; then also, in that one believes one cannot subsist by oneself, nor do without several things whose ac- <margin>10</margin> quisition depends on others. Thus it is directly opposed to Generosity <term>Generosity: the virtue of knowing one's own worth based on the right use of the will</term>; and it often happens that those who have the lowest spirit are the most arrogant and proud, in the same way that the most generous are the most modest and the most humble. But <margin>15</margin> whereas those who have a strong and generous spirit do not change their mood because of the prosperities or adversities that happen to them, those who have a weak and abject spirit are led only by fortune <note>original: "fortune" - here meaning luck or external circumstances beyond one's control</note>; and prosperity inflates them no less than adversity <margin>20</margin> makes them humble. Indeed, one often sees that they abase themselves shamefully before those from whom they expect some profit or fear some harm; and that at the same time they rise up insolently above those from whom they neither hope for nor fear any <margin>25</margin> thing.

<summary>Descartes defines "vicious humility" or abjectness as a lack of self-reliance and control over one's will, leading to a character that fluctuates between servility and insolence depending on external circumstances.</summary>

### ARTICLE CLXI.

### *How Generosity can be acquired.*

And it must be noted that what are commonly called virtues are habits in the soul which <margin>10</margin> dispose it to certain thoughts, so that they are different from those thoughts, but they can produce them, and reciprocally be produced by them. It must also be noted that these thoughts can be produced by the soul alone, but it often happens <margin>15</margin> that some movement of the spirits <note>original: "esprits" - the "animal spirits" or subtle fluids Descartes believed moved through the nerves to mediate between body and soul</note> strengthens them, and that then they are actions of virtue, and at the same time Passions of the soul. ### ARTICLE CLXII.

#### *Of Veneration.*

Veneration or Respect is an inclination of the soul, not only to esteem the object which it reveres, <margin>15</margin> but also to submit to it with some fear, in order to try to make it favorable to oneself. In such a way that we have Veneration only for free causes <note>original: "causes libres" - agents capable of independent choice, like humans or God</note>, which we judge capable of doing us good or evil, without our knowing which of the <margin>20</margin> two they will do. For we have Love and Devotion, rather than a simple Veneration, for those from whom we expect only good; and we have Hatred for those from whom we expect only evil; and if we do not judge that the cause <margin>25</margin> of this good or evil is free, we do not submit ourselves to it to try to have it favorable. ### ARTICLE CLXV.

## Of Hope and Fear.

<margin>15</margin>
Hope is a disposition of the soul to persuade itself that what it desires will happen, which is caused by a particular movement of the spirits <term>animal spirits: the subtle fluids Descartes believed traveled through the nerves to move the body and stimulate the soul</term>, namely by that of Joy and Desire mixed together. And Fear is another disposition of <margin>20</margin> the soul, which persuades it that it will not happen. And it is to be remarked that, although these two Passions are contrary, one can nevertheless have them both together, namely when one represents to oneself at the same time various reasons, of which some make one judge that <margin>25</margin> the fulfillment of the Desire is easy, and others make it appear difficult.

<summary>Descartes explains how a weak character fluctuates between superstition and impiety, then defines Hope and Fear as conflicting expectations regarding the fulfillment of a desire.</summary>

### ARTICLE CLXVI.

#### *Of Security and Despair.*

And never does one of these Passions accompany
Desire without leaving some room for the other. For
<margin>5</margin>when Hope is so strong that it entirely drives away
Fear, it changes its nature and is called
Security or Assurance. And when one is assured that what
one desires will happen, although one continues to want
it to happen, one nevertheless ceases to be agitated by the
<margin>10</margin>passion of Desire, which caused one to seek the outcome
with anxiety. In the same way, when Fear
is so extreme that it leaves no room for Hope, it
converts into Despair; and this Despair, represent-
ing the thing as impossible, entirely extinguishes
<margin>15</margin>Desire, which only directs itself toward possible things.

### ARTICLE CLXVII.

#### *Of Jealousy.*

Jealousy is a species of Fear, which re-
lates to the Desire one has to preserve the possession of
<margin>20</margin>some good; and it comes not so much from the strength of the
reasons that lead one to judge that it could be lost, as from the
great esteem in which one holds it, which is the cause of one
examining even the smallest subjects of suspicion, and
taking them for very significant reasons.

### ARTICLE CLXXI. <margin>15</margin>

## *On Courage and Boldness.*

Courage, when it is a Passion and not a habit or natural inclination, is a certain heat or agitation which disposes the soul to apply itself <margin>20</margin> powerfully to the execution of the things it wants to do, of whatever nature they may be. And Boldness is a species of Courage which disposes the soul to the execution of things that are the most dangerous.

## ARTICLE CLXXVII.

### *On Remorse.*

Remorse of conscience is a species of Sadness,
which comes from the doubt one has that a thing one is doing, or
has done, is not good. And it necessarily presupposes
doubt. For if one were entirely assured
<margin>5</margin>that what one is doing were bad, one would abstain from
doing it; insofar as the will only carries itself toward things
that have some appearance of goodness. And if one were
assured that what one has already done was bad, one
would feel repentance; not | merely Remorse. Now
<margin>10</margin>the use of this Passion is to make one examine whether the
thing one doubts is good or not, and to prevent
one from doing it another time, as long as one is
not assured that it is good. But because it pre-
supposes evil, the best would be that one never had
<margin>15</margin>reason to feel it; and one can prevent it by the same
means by which one can exempt oneself from Irre-
solution <note>Descartes previously defined irresolution as a lack of firm judgment that leaves the soul wavering between different actions.</note>.

### ARTICLE CLXXXV.

->Of Pity.<-

<margin>5</margin>Pity is a species of Sadness, mixed with Love or goodwill toward those whom we see suffering some evil which we judge them to be undeserving of. Thus, it is the opposite of Envy, by reason of its object, and to Mockery, because it considers that object in a <margin>10</margin>different way.

### ARTICLE CLXXXVI.

->*Who are the most prone to pity.*<-

Those who feel themselves to be very weak, and very subject to the adversities of fortune, seem to be more inclined toward <margin>15</margin>this Passion than others, because they represent the evil of another to themselves as something that could happen to them; and thus they are moved to Pity more by the Love they bear for themselves than by that which they have for others.

### *Of Favor.*

### ARTICLE CXCIV.

### <margin>10</margin>*Of Ingratitude.*

As for Ingratitude, it is not a Passion: for

<margin>15</margin>is always virtuous and one of the principal bonds of

### ARTICLE CXCV.

#### *Of Indignation.* <note>original: "De l'Indignation"</note>

### ARTICLE CCIII.

->*That Generosity serves as a remedy against its excesses.*<-

Furthermore, although this Passion is useful for <margin>10</margin> giving us the vigor to repel injuries, there is nevertheless none whose excesses one should avoid with more care: because, by troubling the judgment, they often cause one to commit faults which one later repents; and even sometimes they <margin>15</margin> prevent one from repelling these injuries as well as one could do if one had less emotion. But as there is nothing that makes it more excessive than Pride, so I believe that **Generosity** <term>Generosity: In Descartes's philosophy, this is the virtue of knowing one's own free will and resolving to use it well.</term> is the best remedy that one can find against its excesses: <margin>20</margin> because, by making one value very little all the goods that can be taken away, and on the contrary making one value greatly the liberty and absolute command over oneself—which one ceases to have when one can be offended by someone—it causes one to have only contempt, or <margin>25</margin> at most indignation, for the injuries by which others are accustomed to be offended.

<summary>Descartes explains that while anger can provide energy to defend oneself, its excesses are dangerous and rooted in pride; the virtue of Generosity acts as a cure by prioritizing self-mastery over external goods.</summary>
<keywords>Anger, Pride, Generosity, self-mastery, passions, moral philosophy, René Descartes</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on how Generosity acts as a remedy for the excesses of pride and anger, Descartes now moves to define the social passions of Glory and Shame.</meta>

### ARTICLE CCIV.
### *On Glory.*

What I call here by the name of Glory <note>original: "Gloire". In the 17th century, this term often referred to the joy of being honored or recognized by others, rather than just "fame."</note> is a species of Joy, founded upon the Love that one has for oneself, and which comes from the opinion or the hope that one has <margin>5</margin> of being praised by some others. Thus it is different from internal Satisfaction, which comes from the opinion that one has of having done some good action. For one is sometimes praised for things that one does not believe <margin>10</margin> to be good at all, and blamed for those that one believes to be better. But they are both species of the esteem that one has for oneself, as well as species of Joy. For it is a reason to esteem <margin>15</margin> oneself, to see that one is esteemed by others.

### ARTICLE CCV.
### *On Shame.*

Shame, on the contrary, is a species of Sadness, founded also upon the Love of oneself, and which comes from the opinion or the fear that one has of being blamed. It <margin>20</margin> is, besides that, a species of modesty or humility, and a lack of confidence in oneself. For when one esteems oneself so highly that one cannot imagine being despised by anyone, one cannot easily be ashamed.

### ARTICLE CCX.

*On Alacrity.* <note>original: "l’Allegreſſe." While often translated as "mirth" or "cheerfulness," Descartes specifically defines it here as the lightness felt after a burden is removed.</note>

Finally, what I call Alacrity is a species of Joy, in which there is this particularity: that its <margin>10</margin> sweetness is increased by the memory of the evils one has suffered, and from which one feels relieved <note>original: "allegé." And I see nothing very remarkable in these three Passions; thus I have only placed them here to follow the order of the enumeration that I made above. But it seems to me that this enumeration was useful to show that we were omitting none which <margin>20</margin> was worthy of any particular consideration.

And now that we know them all, we have much less reason to fear them than we had before. For we see <margin>25</margin> that they are all good by their nature, and that

As when one is unexpectedly attacked by some enemy, the occasion does not permit that one employ any time to deliberate. ->*That it is on them alone that all the good and evil of this life depends.*<-

<margin>10</margin>Furthermore, the soul can have its pleasures apart; but as for those which are common to it and the body, they depend entirely on the Passions <note>Descartes uses "Passions" to refer to the emotions or "commotions" of the soul caused by the body.</note>, so that the men whom they can most move are capable of tasting the most sweetness in this life. <margin>15</margin>It is true that they can also find the most bitterness there, when they do not know how to employ them well, and when fortune is against them. # APPENDIX
---

The *Passions of the Soul* were immediately translated into Latin. The translation first appeared in a separate volume:
**The Passions of the Soul**, by **René Descartes**: *Written by himself in French, but now, for the benefit of foreigners, granted Latin citizenship <note>A metaphorical way of saying "translated into Latin."</note>. By H. D. M. I. v. L. (Amsterdam, at the house of Louis Elzevier, 1650, small duodecimo. Printer's mark: Minerva. 28 preliminary leaves, 242 pages, 13 unnumbered pages of index.)*

In the same year, 1650, Louis Elzevier also published this translation as the third part of a quarto volume, of which the first two parts were Descartes' *Principles of Philosophy* and the *Samples of Philosophy* <note>original: "Specimina Philosophiæ," which included the Dioptrics, Meteors, and Geometry.</note>.

This translation was made without the involvement of Descartes, who had no knowledge of it. We will therefore content ourselves with providing the Translator's Preface. He was a Frenchman, as he himself declares—perhaps Habert de Montmort? <note>Henri Louis Habert de Montmort (1600–1679) was a French scholar and patron of Descartes.</note>

---

### THE TRANSLATOR'S
## BRIEF PREFACE
#### TO THE READER

As the saying goes, *Dear Reader*, "good wine needs no ivy bush" <note>original Latin: "Vino vendibili... hederâ suspensâ non est opus." An old proverb meaning that a good product needs no advertisement; ivy was traditionally hung outside taverns.</note>: therefore you should not expect me to say much, either in recommendation of this Pathological Treatise <note>In this context, "Pathological" refers to the study of the passions or emotions (from the Greek 'pathos'), not disease.</note>, or in praise of the Author. Read the former, and mourn the latter, whom a premature death snatched away from the literary world a few months ago in Sweden. The Most Serene Queen of the Swedes <note>Queen Christina of Sweden (1626–1689), who invited Descartes to her court.</note>, a Daughter no less great than her exalted Father <note>King Gustavus Adolphus.</note>, who has long since added to the three Crowns of her lineage a fourth far more august—one of astounding erudition, profound wisdom, and magnificent liberality toward the learned of every...

<column-break/>

<vocab>René Descartes, Passions of the Soul, Principles of Philosophy, Samples of Philosophy, Louis Elzevier, Habert de Montmort, Christina of Sweden, Pathology, Latin translation</vocab>

<summary>This appendix introduces the first Latin translation of Descartes' "Passions of the Soul," published in 1650 by Elzevier, and includes the beginning of a preface mourning Descartes' recent death in Sweden.</summary>

--- Page 524 ---
<meta>Continuing from the Translator's Preface, specifically the discussion of the work's merit and the circumstances of Descartes' invitation to the Swedish court.</meta>

# ON THE PASSIONS

->**PREFACE** (continued)<-

...of her station, the most noble Descartes was most kindly invited to her presence. She had seen his philosophical writings, which are worthy of cedar oil <note>original: "cedro dignis" — a Roman expression meaning a work is worthy of preservation for eternity, as cedar oil was used to protect papyrus from decay</note>, and was enticed, as they say, by the reading and admiration of this very Treatise on the Emotions. But he had scarcely set foot in Sweden when, seized by a sudden illness, he departed from this life's station. How much that most wise Queen—the armed Pallas <note>The Greek goddess of wisdom and war</note> of the Gothic people—valued him while he lived is said to have been testified by her very tears upon hearing the news of his death. The judgment of such a great Queen regarding this man is sufficient to wash away whatever the zeal and fervor of certain rivals once wished to sprinkle upon him. There is not one of them whose memory will ever be honored with such precious funeral rites; nor could he fail to please the highest Princes, he who had displeased such lowly adversaries.

Such is the fate of Virtue and Erudition, that envy accompanies them no less than smoke follows fire. Whoever reads his works with their own emotions set aside will confess that he brought a great light to the Philosophical Disciplines, even if they do not admit his specific views—those who, having found the harvest of grain, still take pleasure in feeding upon acorns <note>A metaphor for those who cling to old, primitive ideas (the acorns) after better, modern ones (the grain) have been discovered</note>. This very Pathological Treatise <note>The study of the passions</note> sufficiently shows that he made no less progress in the knowledge of the Microcosm <note>The "small world," referring to the human body and soul</note> than in the contemplation of the Macrocosm <note>The "great world," referring to the universe or heavens</note>. It will come into no one's hands—even if they hold different opinions, as has always been permitted among good men—without them marveling at his sharpness, skill, clarity, and subtlety, and how conveniently he was able to investigate all the movements of this natural automaton <note>Descartes viewed the body as a self-moving machine or "automaton"</note> by the light of reason alone. For he considers man in the Philosophical manner, and does not penetrate into his native corruption—that most fertile mother of these anomalous and eccentric movements within us—which belongs instead to Theological inquiry.

Do not wonder, *Kind Reader*, that I have been unable to match the brilliance of the style he used in our native tongue <note>French</note> within this Latin discourse. The author himself ought to have been the interpreter of his own concepts. It was enough for me to express them as faithfully as I could; while doing so, I neglected elegance. And I would even dare to say that they could not be expressed happily enough by anyone other than a Frenchman. This moved me so that, although the term *Emotions* <note>original: "Affectuum"</note> might perhaps be used more purely in Latin, I preferred to retain the word *Passions* <note>original: "Passionum"</note>, so that I might stick more closely to the Author's own principles. Initially, I was preparing this Translation <note>original: "Metaphrasim"</note> for myself alone; but later, great men, whose authority I would have felt it a religious duty not to shun, authored the suggestion that I should permit it to the typesetter. To it, I have added the Letters prefixed to the French edition by that most learned man who had overseen it. Enjoy, therefore, this small labor of ours, *Friend Reader*, and learn from it to moderate your own emotions. Farewell.

<summary>The translator concludes his preface by recounting Descartes' final days in the court of Queen Christina of Sweden and defending the philosopher's legacy against critics. He explains his choice of Latin terminology and his focus on a faithful, rather than elegant, translation of the French original.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as a preface or "Warning" to the reader regarding the provenance of certain posthumous fragments attributed to René Descartes, specifically those concerning biology and the senses.</meta>

# WARNING

The Amsterdam Edition: *R. DES-CARTES Posthumous Minor Works, 1701*, provides, with a separate pagination, pp. 1-23, a fragment entitled: *First Thoughts on the Generation of Animals* <note>original: "Primæ Cogitationes circa Generationem Animalium"</note>; it is even followed by another fragment, much shorter, pp. 24-26: *On Flavors* <note>original: "De Saporibus"</note>. A note, placed on the back of the half-title page ᵃ, indicates their origin rather vaguely: these few pages were delivered to the publisher with the assertion that they are indeed by Descartes; they are, moreover, consistent with a translation in the Flemish language <note>Dutch</note> which had already been released. The publisher does not otherwise guarantee their authenticity; and even in the Preface at the head of the volume, when he mentions these *First Thoughts*, he does not dare to assert that they are authentic ᵇ. Later, Victor Cousin, in volume XI of his—

---

a. **TO THE READER.** <note>original: "AD LECTOREM"</note> *Since these First Thoughts on the Generation of Animals, with the attached notes On Flavors, were sent to us, and it was affirmed that they were the offspring of Descartes, we considered it useful to insert them among the rest of the posthumous dissertations of that author. We did this primarily so that nothing found in the editions of Descartes' works published in the Belgian tongue <note>Dutch</note> would be missing from our edition. Our Latin copy agrees entirely with the Belgian one, and we present it in its entirety, with no changes made, although many things may perhaps be found in it that suffer from errors. Furthermore, whether these truly have Descartes as their Author, or whether they are forged, let that be the judgment of others. It is possible that some things were interpolated here and there by the person who transcribed them, which the learned know happens not infrequently with posthumous works, especially those to which the Authors did not apply the final polish. Meanwhile, you, Blessed Reader, enjoy these, and farewell.*

b. Following the passage of the Preface, reproduced in volume X, p. 492, one reads:
"*All these are followed by the First Thoughts on the Generation of Animals, & Some Notes on Flavors, which we give in their entirety in Latin, just as they were.*"
"Regarding these, Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet, Descartes' early biographer</note> says not even a jot, although among many other—"

<summary>This preface discusses the questionable authenticity of two posthumous fragments attributed to Descartes regarding animal generation and flavors, first published in the 1701 Amsterdam edition.</summary>

But a new fact has emerged since then, which seems to allow the matter to be settled. The notes of Descartes, copied in Paris in 1675 and 1676 at the home of Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier, the primary editor of Descartes' literary estate</note> by Leibniz and Tschirnhaus (see our vol. X, p. 208-209), and of which the <term>manuscript</term> <note>original: "MS."</note> copy, rediscovered in Hanover, was published by Foucher de Careil in 1859 and 1860: these notes, I say, contain several passages identical to the last three pages, pp. 21-23, of the *First Thoughts* <note>original: "Primæ Cogitationes"</note> printed in 1701. Except for slight variations, and very few in number, it is word for word exactly the same text. Several consequences can be inferred from this.

First, this identity is proof that at least two pages of the 1701 publication are authentic, and undoubtedly also all those preceding them, pp. 3-21. A copy had remained in Holland, which some <term>Cartesian</term> <note>a follower of Descartes' philosophy</note> must have communicated to the Amsterdam publisher. During this time, the original had traveled from Egmond to Stockholm, then had come to Paris: a copy, taken there, had been brought back to Hanover. The conformity of the two texts—one of which was supported by Descartes' own handwriting and the testimony of Clerselier, and the other by the testimony of a Dutchman faithful to the philosopher's memory—should remove our slightest doubt: we truly have here a frag-

Furthermore, the manuscript copy from Hanover gives a precise date for one of the passages identified in this way: *Feb. 1648*. Undoubtedly, this date does not even apply to all three of our pages, but only to the paragraph it precedes; even more so, it cannot apply to the entirety of the fragment, pages 3-23. But one can already conclude that the title given by the editor, *First Thoughts* <note>original: "Primae Cogitationes"</note>, does not apply to the entire fragment either. Descartes' first thoughts on generation certainly do not date from 1648. If one looks through the philosopher's correspondence, one sees that this question preoccupied him as early as the end of 1629, and also in 1630 in Amsterdam, then in 1632 and 1633, then at Santporte near Haarlem in 1637-38, then at Endegeest from 1642 to 1643 (vol. III, p. 352-3, and vol. IV, p. 247-8), finally at Egmond in 1647 and 1648, and doubtless until the end in 1649, as we stated in our *Foreword* to the preceding treatise. Therefore, the word *First* <note>original: "Primae"</note> at the very least is superfluous; and it would have been enough to say: *Thoughts on Generation* <note>original: "Cogitationes circa Generationem"</note>—unless the 1701 editor did not use this word in a chronological sense, but only to indicate that these were notes jotted down on paper, the first drafts of treatises that would be completed later <sup>a</sup>.

A final remark confirms this view: the paragraphs on the three pages, 21, 22, and 23, of the Amsterdam edition, although they follow one another continuously in the printed text, refer to separate passages in the Hanover manuscript copy; and even a rather long interval,

Now, what is true of these last three pages seems to be equally true of all those that precede them: we likely have here, brought together and placed end to end, several pages of notes which do not form—far from it—a continuous sequence. The continuity of the text printed in the 1701 edition <note>The first posthumous collection of Descartes' unpublished works, printed in Amsterdam.</note> must not deceive us: these are notes, written at different dates and on different questions, although all relating to generation <term>génération: the biological process of reproduction and development</term>. We are preserving its continuity, but while warning the reader that it is entirely artificial, so that they may know with what reservations they can reasonably rely upon it.

<margin>5</margin> Generation must be considered in two ways: one without seed or a womb, the other from seed.

There are, indeed, certain things common to all living creatures, such as moving spontaneously, being nourished, etc.; these ought to come first<sup>a</sup> into consideration. There are then
<margin>10</margin> others which belong to almost all, such as seeing, hearing, etc.; these are to be examined in the second place, along with why they are not present in all. There are certain traits subordinate to an entire genus, such as being two-footed for all birds, four-footed for wild beasts, having fins for fish, many-footed for insects, etc.;
<margin>15</margin> these will be weighed in the third order. Fourthly and finally, we shall arrive at the individual lowest species <term>species infimas: the most specific level of biological classification</term>.

Every animal that arises without a womb requires only this principle: namely, that two subjects, not very far removed from one another, are excited in different ways by the same force
<margin>20</margin> of heat, so that from one, subtle parts (which I shall hereafter call vital spirits <term>spiritus vitales: in Cartesian physiology, these were highly refined particles of blood that acted as the messengers of the nervous system</term>) [emerge], and from...

# ON ANIMALS.

That which is more refined moves more quickly and is more easily secreted from the bodies of the parents. Afterward follows the remaining seed, which is a little thicker and tends more toward the mouth of the womb. For instance, let the mouth of the womb be D; the purer seed occupies 
<margin>5</margin> the base A, while the thicker seed is toward the orifice B. 
Now, if that seed were only from one parent, it would easily slide back out by the same path it entered, for there is nothing to retain it there. Therefore, the seed of one is not sufficient for generation.
<margin>10</margin> If, however, the seeds of both parents are mixed together at the same time, then because they cannot be mixed without rarefaction <term>rarefaction: the process of becoming less dense or expanding, usually due to heat</term>, as they grow warmer and warmer in the womb, they become more inflated. Furthermore, the composition and structure of the womb is such that the more it is dilated, the more its 
<margin>15</margin> orifice is closed; but when it is constricted, its mouth is opened. Hence it happens that it opens during intercourse; but when it has conceived and the seed is inflated within it, it is tightly closed.
Now the seed, thus enclosed in the womb, is in a certain way fermented by the passage of time and is concocted <note>original: "concoquitur" - a term from old physiology meaning "ripened" or "processed" by heat</note> by the heat of the mother; 
<margin>20</margin> that is, its parts are more refinedly mixed among themselves. And indeed, then the parts that are most accurately mixed and tempered flow together toward the middle of the place where they are; namely, the greatest part that is found flows together into C and forms the brain; but along the entire tract from A and B, it flows 
<margin>25</margin> into the spinal cord <note>original: "spinæ medullam"</note>, so that this is like a stream from the thicker parts of the blood which are toward the mouth of the womb, through which the more refined parts that happen to exist among them are carried to the brain. But the remaining parts of the seed, which are not so refinedly mixed, but 
<margin>30</margin> yet sufficiently well and without great resistance, yield into the skin; of which, therefore, the greater part is toward B...

The seed swells by the power of heat (just as chestnuts swell in a fire); but it cannot swell forever, and these things happen in a short time, perhaps in one or two days, or perhaps in a single hour: for this is a question of fact and cannot be defined by pure reason. When the seed ceases to be inflated, the blood and spirit <note>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" were subtle fluids thought to carry life and sensation through the body.</note> nevertheless continue to flow toward the heart, since the momentum has already been established and the channels prepared for it. Thirdly, from the middle and interior ventricle of the brain, a double kind of material overflows on both sides, yet it is viscous and transparent like gum from trees; it drips down on both sides 
<margin>10</margin> and composes the eyes. Nor is it a wonder that they are afterwards contained within the cavities of the bones: for they are generated before any bones harden. Another waste product, which exits from the anterior parts of the brain, is drier: because that which was more moist passed into the eyes; and it is nothing else 
<margin>15</margin> than a vapor piercing the nostrils for itself on both sides.

All these things happen immediately and from the beginning, and before the skin is distinct from the flesh, the flesh from the bones, or these from the membranes and the brain and the marrow—or certainly at the same time. But no bones are hardened until much 
<margin>20</margin> later, before the child has urinated through the penis and emitted vapor <note>gas</note> through the anus, when he has his eyelids and lips divided; because he does not urinate except at intervals, on account of the capacity of the bladder, hence a muscle <note>the sphincter</note> naturally forms to constrict its opening.

<margin>25</margin> The division of the eyelids happens gradually, with a very thin fluid gliding down through the corners of the eyes on both sides, and gradually breathing out through the middle of the eyelids: so much so that, while their skin is being formed, that crack is gradually entirely covered. The same happens in the lips and the hymen. 
<margin>30</margin> Moreover, the fact that the lower jaws have different movements than the upper ones contributes especially to the slit of the mouth.

From this arise the umbilical arteries, at first one; but as the aorta grows, the place where the umbilical artery is <margin>15</margin> implanted is carried downward, and it pulls the umbilical artery along with it all the way to the flanks <note>original: "ilia"</note>; where, because the entire aorta is divided into two parts, the umbilical artery is also necessarily split into two. Moreover, the aorta follows the liver, because the aorta is growing at that time, and therefore it immediately occupies the place which it finds most suitable; <margin>20</margin> conversely, the liver becomes flaccid, and therefore leaves room both for the aorta and for the membranes <note>original: "tunicis"</note> in which it is wrapped, which are curved slightly inward until the navel is formed.

It must also be believed that a certain serous humor <note>a watery fluid</note> <margin>25</margin> is drawn from the lower part of the entire mass by the liver; this humor, once the navel is perforated, draws to itself the serum mixed with the blood and spirit coming through the navel: from which it happens that the water accumulated through it forms the bladder <note>original: "vesicam"</note>.

The kidneys, however, are generated before the umbilical tract is formed, at that time when—with the blood proceeding through the vena cava <margin>30</margin> and the spirit through the aorta—the liver nevertheless begins to grow flaccid.

## CONCERNING
# TASTES

There are as many differences of Tastes as there are types of particles which affect the nerves of the tongue in various ways. And there are
<margin>5</margin> nine principal ones: namely *insipid* or *soft*, *fatty* <note>original: "pinguis"; can also mean oily or unctuous</note>, *sweet*, *bitter*, *burning*, *acid*, *salty*, *sharp* <note>original: "acris"</note>, and *harsh* or *sour* <note>original: "austerus sive acerbus"</note>.

By *insipid*, I do not mean simply lacking in taste—for then it would not be numbered among the tastes—but
<margin>10</margin> that which is unpleasant to the palate because it moves the nerves of the tongue too weakly or softly. Indeed, all whole bodies, and those so hard or compact that their particles are not dissolved in the mouth, lack taste. Such
are metals, marbles, etc. Likewise, many things divided into par-
<margin>15</margin>ticles small enough to the sight, such as flour and the like; and under this genus of the insipid, both poisons, and purgatives, and every kind of quality can lie hidden. For in flour there are acidic parts and burning spirits, as
can be uncovered by various fermentation, distillation, and cooking.
<margin>20</margin> In arsenic there lie hidden sweet, sharp, and bitter parts; and likewise in scammony <note>a medicinal plant resin used as a purgative</note> and gamboge <note>original: "gutta gamba"; a mustard-yellow tree resin used as a drastic purgative</note>, but not of the same kind. There are also insipid particles which—

# PREFACE
<note>original: "AVERTISSEMENT"; a formal editorial notice or introduction</note>

In 1859-1860, Foucher de Careil published two octavo volumes of *Unpublished Works of Descartes*, based on the manuscripts of Leibniz held at the Royal Library of Hanover. We have already discussed these in Volume X of this edition, pages 207-212 and page 257. We even published, in that same Volume X, under the titles *Private Thoughts* <note>original: "Cogitationes privatæ"</note>, pages 213-248, and *On the Elements of Solids* <note>original: "De solidorum elementis"</note>, pages 265-276, several of these unpublished pieces. A good number still remain: some relating to anatomical observations, others titled *Remedies and the Potency of Medicines* <note>original: "Remedia et vires medicamentorum"</note>. To these, let us add a series of annotations that Descartes appears to have written himself regarding his Principles of Philosophy: *Annotations on the Principles of Philosophy which Descartes seems to have written on his own Principles of Philosophy* <note>original: "Ad Principia Philosophiæ annotationes quas videtur Des Cartes in sua Principia Philosophiæ scripsisse"</note>. These annotations are themselves preceded by other remarks, under the title *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>, which Foucher de Careil did not publish at all, even though they were part of the same manuscript.

The manuscript in Leibniz's hand, where the anatomical observations are found, currently comprises 15 sheets (it must have formerly comprised 17, according to an indication by Eduard Bodemann on page 52 of his catalog printed in 1895, *The Leibniz Manuscripts* <note>original: "Die Leibniz-Handschriften"</note>, etc.: "IV. Vol. 1, 4, b, excerpts from Descartes. 17 sheets. Folio."). Here is the description of these 15 sheets.

(Sheet I.) Folded in two, it forms two leaves, numbered 1 and 15; for these two leaves, which nevertheless must be read one after the other, serve as a cover or folder for all the others, which are found enclosed within. This is the mathematical fragment titled *On the Elements of Solids*— <note>original: "De solidorum ele-" (text breaks mid-word at the end of the page)</note>

<summary>This preface details the archival history of Descartes' unpublished manuscripts found in Leibniz's collection, listing specific anatomical, medical, and philosophical fragments. It provides a physical description of the 15-sheet manuscript held in Hanover.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Foucher de Careil, Eduard Bodemann, manuscripts, anatomy, medicine, Principles of Philosophy, bibliography</keywords>

(Sheet II.) This is not a full sheet, nor even a leaf, nor even a page; but only a fragment of a page with some written notes. It bears the number 2 in pencil.
