# ANATOMICAL MATTERS.

previous mention: *PART V of the anatomical excerpts from the manuscript of Descartes* <note>original: "PARS V excerptorum anatomicorum ex MS^o. Cartesii"</note>. Foucher de Careil also printed them in sequence, vol. I, pp. 132-140: *The arterial vein...* <note>original: "Vena arteriosa..."</note>; and pp. 140-156: *Six eggs having been cooked* <note>original: "Coctis sex ovis"</note>.

(Sheet VIII.) Two leaves, 13 and 14. After 18 lines, which Foucher de Careil did not reproduce—undoubtedly because one reads in the margin: <margin>These are deleted in the manuscript</margin> <note>original: "Hæc deleta in MS^o"</note>, but which Leibniz had copied nonetheless—one finds a whole series of observations or questions, which Foucher de Careil published, vol. I, pp. 72-100, though not without some omissions here and there. They begin thus: *Hail — I saw today in the month of December.* <note>original: "Grando — vidi hodie mense decembri."</note> — And after the hail, Descartes speaks a little about everything: about water entering cellars during floods, about the shape that vibrations give to a stretched string, about the mouth that blows both hot and cold, etc., etc.

One finds next on another sheet, in Leibniz's hand, some notes taken by him on the *Meditations* <note>Descartes' "Meditations on First Philosophy," his most famous metaphysical work</note>; but these are no longer excerpts from manuscripts, like everything that precedes them.

Now for a few remarks on the edition by Foucher de Careil. He began with this last series of observations and questions, as they were undoubtedly more curious, those of leaves 13 and 14, and published them, vol. I, pp. 72-100. On the other hand, he relegated everything that was purely mathematical to the very end, finding it perhaps a bit abstract for his readers: leaves 1 and 15 are found in vol. II, pp. 214-227. In the interval, Foucher de Careil inserted, following the order of the manuscript more or less, the anatomical observations and physiological theories. However, he still inverted this order. He prints leaves 3 and 4, 5 and 6, 7 and 8 all in a row in vol. II, pp. 86-210 (in the manuscript: *PART I, PART II, PART III*). But he prints in vol. I, pp. 100-156, leaves 9 and 10, 11 and 12, which bear the indications: *PART IV* and *PART V*. Furthermore, a kind of parenthesis, which is found on leaves 9 and 10, is relegated by him to vol. II, pp. 66-80.

But that would be only the least inconvenience of the edition

# EXCERPTS

by Foucher de Careil <note>Louis-Alexandre Foucher de Careil (1826–1891), a French scholar and diplomat who rediscovered many of Leibniz's manuscripts</note>, which is filled with errors on almost every page. Let us, however, offer two excuses in his favor here: 1st, the handwriting of Leibniz, in this copy taken in haste, is extremely difficult to decipher, and Foucher de Careil had the merit of first discovering it, then being the first to decipher it, which singularly facilitated a second reading for those who came after him; 2nd, the text he provided for printing was often good, as evidenced by the French translation placed alongside it: this translation accurately renders the manuscript copy from Hanover in more than one place, while failing to render the Latin text that accompanies it; many gaps and errors in the 1859-1860 edition would therefore be the fault not of the editor, but of the printer. Let us add, finally, that after the scrupulous collation <note>The process of comparing different versions of a text to identify variations</note> of the texts which was performed at the Royal Library of Hanover, one can be assured that, in this new edition of Descartes, the damage has been repaired as much as possible.

# EXCERPTS II, 86-90.

...entering into the vessel, it ended in fibers adhering to the walls toward the tip; and these fibers adhered more firmly in two places of the left chamber | and three of the right, so that what entered into the heart through those vessels could not easily return. I noted, moreover, that these two vessels at the entrance of the heart are shared with each other, and are not separated except by a very thin and loose membrane, which could be bent to either side. It was, however, still open in the lowest part (or perhaps accidentally broken by me); and it seemed that from that part which was open, fluid could glide down from the **hollow vein** <note>original: "vena cava"</note> into the **venous artery** <note>original: "arteriam venosam"; the pulmonary vein</note>, but not the other way around. If, however, the upper part of that membrane had been broken, then fluid could have flowed out from the artery into the vein, but not the other way around.

On both sides, moreover, above those two vessels, there were loose and cavernous extensions bent upward, which they call **auricles** <note>original: "auriculas"; the atria of the heart</note>, of a substance not unlike the vessels themselves, so that they were there only as if they were chambers in which the fluid, which could not enter into the heart, was collected. <margin>30</margin> have their extremities turned—not one to one side and the other to the other—but both turned toward the left side.

## II, 96-98. ANATOMICAL OBSERVATIONS.

In the heart of a younger calf <note>original: "vituli junioris"</note> I noted clearly that the middle wall <note>the septum</note> is composed of two ventricular walls. Likewise, the cavity of the right ventricle was curved, like *cd*, and that of the left *a* was triangular *e*. Likewise, there were as yet
<margin>5</margin> no valves of the **venous artery** <note>pulmonary vein</note> nor of the **hollow vein** <note>vena cava</note>; indeed, there were only their first beginnings <note>original: "rudimenta"</note>. But in the right chamber, that round little swelling <note>original: "tuberculum"</note> which joined two valves in the previous heart, was in this one like a column joining the middle wall with the outer wall
<margin>10</margin> of the right side: yet in such a way that it adhered to the middle wall toward the base, and to the outer wall toward the point <note>original: "mucronem"; the apex of the heart</note>. Likewise, the valves of the **aorta** and the **arterial vein** <note>pulmonary artery</note> were perfectly formed, as in the previous one. The point of the left side was extended much further than the right, and it was far more hollow at the
<margin>15</margin> end. It was open; that left side had been embraced by the right, folded in such a way, and it could still be unfolded. The flesh was much softer than the preceding one. The right side was higher, and positioned entirely toward the breastbone <note>original: "sternum"</note>; and the right auricle was also higher.
<margin>20</margin> The gullet <note>esophagus</note> descended more toward the left side of the **rough artery** <note>original: "asperae arteriae"; the trachea</note> than toward the right from its origin; and the trachea had a kind of crest on its back part, upon which the gullet lay from the left.
The **arterial vein** <note>pulmonary artery</note> thus proceeds at its beginning from the hollow vein through the
<margin>25</margin> spine *abc*, and is divided into three branches, of which two, *d* and *e*, go to each lung, and the third *f* with the aorta.

<margin>20</margin> of the vessels entering into them, two notable things, one on each side, placed in the same region, which seemed to be parts of the **pulmonary arteries** <note>original: "venae arteriosae"; literally 'arterial veins,' the historical term for pulmonary arteries</note>, and the left one was immediately below the trunk of the descending aorta; below these on each side there was also

## II. 134-136. ANATOMICAL OBSERVATIONS.

I also noted, in the **rough artery** <term>rough artery: the trachea or windpipe, so called in early anatomy due to its cartilaginous rings</term>, that two lower branches emerge from the same lowest and wider ring, but a third on the right emerges seven rings higher; and finally in the remainder of the artery, although I did not have the whole of it, I nevertheless counted 40

However, the fibers from which the very **flesh of the heart** consists are turned toward other parts,
<margin>10</margin> namely either all perpendicularly or certainly rather from the right toward the breast. Nor indeed is the **distinction of the ventricles** <term>ventricles: the lower pumping chambers of the heart</term> of any importance in those fibers; but to one considering it correctly, it seems the entire flesh of the heart was made by the impulse of the **vena cava** <term>cava: the large vein bringing deoxygenated blood to the heart</term>, which was sending blood toward the **tip** <note>original: "mucronem"; the apex or pointed end of the heart</note>, and from there the greater part of it was turned into the left side.
<margin>15</margin> But those **spirits** <term>spirits: in Cartesian physiology, "animal spirits" were subtle fluids thought to be refined from the blood to facilitate movement and sensation</term> which were more subtle were reflected more toward the middle of the heart, or the very origin of motion, into the **aorta**; those which were thicker were above, in the **arterial vein** <term>arterial vein: the pulmonary artery</term>; but those which were most subtle of all escaped through the flesh of the heart and
<margin>20</margin> were reflected downward into that tiny opening which I noted <gloss>b</gloss> <note>referring to the opening mentioned on page 564</note> to be below the cava, and there they followed the tracks of the first small vein (the only place in which the cutaneous-like vessels of the heart and its fibers keep the same path), and were then dispersed in the space contained within the **pericardium** <term>pericardium: the membrane or sac surrounding the heart</term>;
<margin>25</margin> and there, having been condensed, they either nourished the heart itself or certainly preserved it. Moreover, in that path of the first small vein, the fibers of the flesh, wider on both sides at the base of the heart, flowed together into it toward the tip; in a similar way on both sides, though not so accurately, but the left fibers were turned more toward the tip into the right.

<margin>15</margin> venous artery into the left [ventricle] was as if oval: hence only two [valves], and this necessarily followed from the joining of the sinuses.

Afterward, having opened the **aorta** and the **arterial vein** <term>arterial vein: the pulmonary artery</term>, besides all the common features, I noticed that the three valves of the vein could scarcely be opened entirely;
<margin>20</margin> but they were closed as tightly as possible, namely by the flesh protruding within them. Likewise, the valve of the aorta, which faced the chest, could scarcely be opened in the same way for the same reason; but the other two, on the contrary, could scarcely be closed: which helps in understanding why a greater
<margin>25</margin> force has gathered in the left side. Finally, I observed there a nerve (of the **sixth pair** <note>original: "sexti paris"; in older anatomical nomenclature, this often referred to the vagus nerve</note>, as I think) being consumed into the heart between the aorta and the vein toward the anterior part; moreover, the aorta and the vein were joined indissolubly in the common space between the valves.

<margin>30</margin> Then I examined the cutaneous veins and arteries: the veins were, first, a perpendicular one out of four small veins...

In a calf of two or three months, removed from the womb, I observed these things<gloss>b <note>original: "Voir figures IX." — See figures 9.</note></gloss>. The opening of the valve<gloss>c <note>original: "Lire peut-être uteri? ... Ou plutôt vulvæ." — Perhaps read "of the uterus"? Or rather "of the vulva." The translator notes that according to the anatomist Bauhin, the term "uterus" is properly used for women, while in other animals we call it the "vulva."</note></gloss> was very tightly closed at *b*; the vessels were on both sides at *f* and *g*. Of the horns *e* and *c*, the right one was far larger than the other, and the skin <margin>5</margin> of the fetus extended into it, but not into the left one. The head of the fetus was toward that side, but the **amnion** <term>amnion: the innermost membrane that encloses the embryo</term> did not extend so far, but was more of an oval shape in the middle, as at *a*. The back of the fetus was at *h*. The navel was at *i*, twisted like *m*, where the skin between the horns *c* and *e* was wrinkled, <margin>10</margin> because the uterus had grown toward *d*, but not toward *b*, and its opening was closed all the more tightly. Moreover, the fetus was floating in a great abundance of water <note>amniotic fluid</note> which was enclosed with it; its legs were straight, and it appeared that they had never yet been bent, but that as the <margin>15</margin> fetus gradually grows, the joints and articulations are formed. Furthermore, the cartilage in the knees and elsewhere was as long as the bone of the femur or tibia itself; however, the feet were perfectly formed. The tail was also longer than in adults; likewise the penis, which extended all the way <margin>20</margin> to the navel, and there it was turned back in a certain way into a hollow, so that it seemed its nerve <note>or "tendon/sinew"</note> had initially reached that far, but was now being reduced while the prepuce was growing there. The penis had no perceptible opening.

It also appeared how ridiculous it is to imagine that the water in which the fetus floats is its own sweat<sup>b</sup>, since it was so abundant, and without a doubt, as the fetus grows, it is diminished. # Anatomical Observations

...pulsating; the descending aorta <note>the main artery carrying blood from the heart to the lower body</note> was also very large, and the branches from it to the kidneys were very large; the ureters from the kidneys to the lowest part of the urachus <note>a duct connecting the fetal bladder to the umbilical cord</note> were remarkable. However, there was no bladder, but the urachus was very wide, like a hood or a funnel. <margin>5</margin> The umbilical arteries were very large; and some larger branches of the descending aorta were inserted into them, although these too were remarkable and would admit a stylus <note>a thin surgical probe</note>. The testes were white, quite conspicuous, and were even floating within the body. <margin>10</margin> The spleen, very vigorous and of a most brilliant red-to-blue color, was attached to the stomach.

In <gloss>a</gloss> a calf brought to me on the same day it was born, and although I was certain it had never eaten anything, it is marvelous to say, it had hay in its mouth, in its throat, and in its stomach, <margin>15</margin> even of such a length as is a hand <gloss>b</gloss>; while in the other intestines there was green dung, and in the anus and rectum it was yellowish. So much so that it was not only certain that it had eaten before it was born, but even that from the mother's esophagus or stomach, through the veins all the way to the <margin>20</margin> uterus, chaff and undigested food had flowed down, and were received there by the calf, all the membranes involving it having been broken; for the chaff could not have passed through the umbilicus to the gullet, especially since nothing appeared in the umbilical vein; while in the <margin>25</margin> umbilical arteries there was clotted blood. The left kidney was fixed to no place, but as if floating in the body...

# PART III

### *Anatomical excerpts from the Manuscript of Descartes*^a.

In the brain of a sheep, I first noticed^b that its lower shape—with the parts slightly loosened so it could be better distinguished—is roughly as follows: *a b* is the spinal cord, *c* is the process which they call the bridge of the cerebellum <note>term: pons varolii; a structure that links the medulla oblongata and the thalamus</note>, *d* is the cerebellum, *e* is the nerve of the fifth pair <note>the trigeminal nerve</note>, *f* is the nerve of the fourth pair <note>the trochlear nerve</note>. From *g* to *h* is a tiny cavity, above which a little hill-like structure *h* stands out. A valley follows this toward *i*; and there is <margin>10</margin> the opening which they call the "vulva" <note>original: "vulvam"; an archaic anatomical term for an opening below the pineal gland</note>, and at *l* is the meeting point of the optic nerves, marking the end of the vulva's slit; and there, on the outside, the spinal cord ends. *k* is a white protuberance which appears when the two parts of the brain are slightly separated, and it unites them; <margin>15</margin> *m* is the papillary process <note>the olfactory bulb</note>, *n* is a blackish point; this color is visible on the surface of the brain between the papillary processes. In the cavity at *h*, I saw no opening.

After the brain had sat in water overnight, I noted that the substance of the optic nerves was very soft; <margin>20</margin> on the other hand, the substance of all the others was very hard, insofar as they emerged outside the spinal cord. However, within the cord itself, they had no harder roots. The "pious mother" <note>term: pia mater; the delicate innermost membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord</note> was also far harder than before.

With the brain turned over, I noted at the top the Lambda-shaped press <note>original: "torcular Lambda"; likely referring to the confluence of sinuses at the back of the skull, named for the Greek letter Lambda (λ)</note>...

...to form between the two parts of the brain and the cerebellum, and to send out a distinguished vessel from the middle toward the basin <note>term: pelvis; here referring to the infundibulum or the area of the pituitary gland</note>, and a part of it is reflected above the arch <note>term: fornix; a C-shaped bundle of nerve fibers in the brain</note>. This arch begins above the third fold of the spinal cord; and the fibers of the cerebellum in the <margin>5</margin> middle were transverse, and almost even at the sides of the brain they were rather oblong. The marrow <note>term: medulla; the inner white matter</note> of the cerebellum, together with its bridge <note>term: pons; the pons Varolii</note>, which is also entirely made of marrow, seems to form a thick ring surrounding the entire spinal cord; but this ring adheres inseparably to it <margin>10</margin> everywhere, except for the upper part, where the spinal cord is hollowed out, and the worm-like process <note>term: processus vermiformis; the vermis of the cerebellum</note> is reflected downward so that it may fill that cavity; and this cavity is the ventricle of the cerebellum <note>the fourth ventricle</note>. This cavity is followed by an opening below the fourth fold, or protuberance of the spinal <margin>15</margin> cord, which is the smallest of all; nor are its two sides distinguished by a cleft like the others, but by a straight line, which is one of the bonds of the two sides of the spinal cordᵃ: *a* is the fundament <note>original: "podex"; an archaic term for the posterior part of the corpora quadrigemina</note>, *bb* is this bond, where *b* is the fourth interior fold of the spinal cord; and this fourth <margin>20</margin> fold meets directly between the brain and the cerebellum.

And for that reason, no cleft separates the second parts, because no excrements <note>note: in early modern anatomy, "excrements" referred to waste fluids or humors, such as cerebrospinal fluid, thought to be drained from the brain</note> ought to pass through there; but the third fold, which can properly be compared to the buttocks <note>original: "natibus"; the colliculi of the midbrain</note>, has a cleft in between; for it lies beneath the posterior part <margin>25</margin> of the brain, from which some excrements can glide down into the basin. Moreover, in this third fold, two reddish tubercles appear standing above the white floor, of which one part is *bb*, the other *dd*; *cc* are two tubercles, *e* is the "plugging penis" <note>original: "penis obturans"; likely referring to the pineal gland or a nearby structure acting as a valve</note> blocking the opening through which the <margin>30</margin> excrements glide down from the ventricles of the brain into the basin. # II. 176-178. ANATOMICAL OBSERVATIONS.

The opening, which I have called the fundament <note>original: "podicem"; referring to the posterior part of the corpora quadrigemina</note>, is a continuous straight channel from *a* to the basin <note>term: pelvis; the infundibulum or pituitary region</note> *e*, above which stands the white plane *ae*; finally, below *e*, between *e* and *f*, two parts of the second fold are joined together, so that the excrements <note>In 17th-century anatomy, "excrements" often referred to waste fluids or "serosities" rather than solid waste</note> of the anterior parts <margin>5</margin> can glide through *f* into the basin, and those of the posterior parts through *e*.

In the ear of a sheep there are three small bones <note>term: ossicula; the malleus, incus, and stapes</note>, but they are a little smaller <insert>correction in the manuscript from "larger"</insert> than in calves; except for the hammer <note>term: malleus</note>, which is proportionately larger. However, the stirrup <note>term: stapes</note> of both is clearly of the same <margin>10</margin> shape <note>See Figure XIII</note>, and it rests upon the small membrane closing one of the little windows <note>term: fenestella; the oval or round window of the ear</note> common to the cochlea and the labyrinth. I noted three branches of the auditory nerves, besides the hard part <note>term: pars dura; the facial nerve</note>, which was carried through its own channel: the principal branch was carried directly to the middle of the circles <margin>15</margin> of the cochlea; the second, much smaller, directly below the stirrup, where the thrice-revolved channel of the labyrinth began; the third, again, in the labyrinth between the first and second revolution of the channel, the first revolution of which was of such great size <note>See Figures XIV and XV</note> and shape. The cochlea is a <margin>20</margin> spiral channel gradually ending in a narrow point, or rather two joined channels; and it seems to allow <insert>perhaps read: "not only allow," the "not" being omitted in the manuscript</insert> entry from the oval window into the beginning of one of those channels, but from its end it again allows entry into the end or the narrower extremity of the other <margin>25</margin> channel; and finally from the other wider extremity of this [channel...]

# EXCERPTS II, 178-182

A certain path of the second channel lies open outside the stony bone <note>term: os petrosum; the petrous part of the temporal bone which houses the inner ear</note>, as it seems, towards the brain: whether that path be empty, or if a nerve or something else fills it, I do not yet know.

I clearly observed that the choroid plexuses <note>term: plexus choroides; networks of blood vessels in the ventricles of the brain</note> do not adhere to the ventricles, but are hung there like tapestries<gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "tapetiorum"; the author compares the vascular membranes to hanging rugs or curtains</note>, and specifically around the pineal gland, from which they hang like a canopy and cover the opening of the brain which receives the funnel <note>term: infundibulum; the stalk connecting the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland</note>: so that the spirits ascending through this funnel from the gland which they call the pituitary, may reach the pineal gland from there, provided they are strong enough. But if not, they are reflected first towards the fourth ventricle through the channel which is below the buttocks<gloss>b</gloss> <note>term: nates; the superior colliculi of the corpora quadrigemina, named for their rounded shape</note>, then towards the opening which is after the meeting of the optic nerves, from where they slip out of the brain. Their superfluous parts also follow these same paths when they are strong enough; and furthermore, they are purged from the ventricles towards the buttocks: for I noted accurately that one gland is placed upon the other, and the funnel is clearly of the same substance as the carotid arteries which sit upon it.

The work is only the development of these four parts: *Parts contained in the lower belly*, p. 27-94. *The Second Venter or Thorax*, p. 95-140. *The Third Venter or Head*, p. 141-212. *Concerning the Limbs and the Hand*, p. 213-242; *concerning the Foot*, p. 242-260.

# II, 194-196. ANATOMICAL STUDIES. 589

From this it is clear that this membrane is not produced until later.

The umbilical arteries <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "Arteriæ umbilicales"</note> coming from the iliac vessels to the navel, and the vein from the navel to the liver <note>original: "hepar"</note>, show that the blood first descended from the heart through the aorta to the flanks <note>the iliac region</note>, and from there returned to the navel joined to the placenta of the uterus; where, mixing itself with the mother's blood, it returned to the fetus's liver through the umbilical vein.

The urachus <gloss>b</gloss> <note>a structure connecting the bladder to the umbilical cord</note>, since in man it is not open <note>hollow or functional</note> as it is in beasts, shows that man has less serous fluid <note>watery residue</note> and approaches more to the nature of birds, which do not urinate; and for this reason, the fetus also lacks the allantoic membrane <note>original: "tunicâ allantoide"; a sac-like structure used by some mammals to collect liquid waste</note>.

These arteries are connected to the sides of the bladder <note>original: "vesicæ"</note>, which therefore seem to have arisen from it only because the blood of the fetus, by touching the mother's blood in the placenta, deposited some of its moisture there. The kidneys <note>original: "Renes"</note> were produced there for the same reason: indeed, since the intestines were not yet produced or at least not yet grown, the flanks, kidneys, and liver belonged together at the navel, and with it to the mother's placenta.

<margin>20</margin> The omentum <gloss>c</gloss> <note>the fatty tissue covering the stomach and intestines</note> is always connected to the stomach <note>original: "ventriculo"</note>, the spleen <note>original: "lieni"</note>, and the colon, and sometimes even to the diaphragm and the liver; the rest hangs down like a veil over the front of the intestine: nor does it seem to be made from anything other than the vessels which it receives and—

---

<margin>a.</margin> *Ibid.* <note>referring to Bauhin's text</note>: "THE UMBILICAL VESSELS. — ... They are double, one Vein, two Arteries... The umbilical vein... having exited the navel... But the Arteries, raised from the iliacs..." (Page 29-30.)

<margin>b.</margin> *Ibid.*: "The Urachus... In man, however, from the bottom of the bladder a cord arises in the shape of the Urachus, but in no way open..." (Page 30.)

<margin>c.</margin> *Ibid.*: "THE OMENTUM. — ... It consists of two membranes... the upper one, which is attached to the outer membrane of the stomach at the bottom; the lower one, which is always bound to the colon on the right, and to the spleen on the left, but more rarely grows to the fibers of the liver..." (Page 31.) "...The use of the membranes is to support the branches of the portal vein and the celiac artery, which are extended into the stomach, spleen, duodenum, and colon..." (Page 32.)

# EXCERPTS II, 206-208.

In the stomach, I observe that it has straight fibers inside, which reach there from the mouth through the **esophagus** <note>the food pipe</note>, but the intestines have transverse fibers ᵃ. Likewise, I note that it has many nerves, and there are also two recurrent nerves; likewise, I note <margin>5</margin> the history of a person who lacked a liver, but all the intestines were more fleshy; likewise, that in children many excrements <note>In this context, "excrements" refers to waste fluids or humors, not just fecal matter</note> fall down from the brain into the stomach. From these things I conjecture that the entire duct from the mouth to the **anus** <note>original: *podicem*</note> ᵇ had its origin from excrements falling down from the brain; and the very opening of the mouth <margin>10</margin> was formed by those same excrements regurgitating to that point. Moreover, those excrements remained stagnant below the liver, and therefore excavated the capacity of the stomach there, while the blood was also stagnant in the **renal vessels** <note>original: *emulgentibus*</note> ᶜ. Furthermore, because those excrements fell from the mouth into the throat and closed the path for the air attempting to exit from the **trachea** <note>original: *aspera arteria*</note>, <margin>15</margin> it happens that the nostrils are twin, because that air ascends upward through the sides of the throat ᵈ.

# ON GROWTH & NUTRITION.

->November 1637.<-

Growth <term>Accretio: the process of increasing in size by gradual external addition</term> is of two kinds: one pertains to dead things and those which are not
nourished; this occurs through the simple placement of parts
side-by-side, without any change in them, or at least without
<margin>5</margin>
much change. In this way metals grow in mines, as does honey in
beehives, etc., without any change of the parts; in this way also
stones and similar things grow, without much change of the parts <gloss>a</gloss>. | And even the transformation <note>original: "transmutatio"</note> of wood or another
<margin>10</margin>
body into stone occurs by way of such growth,
while the parts of the stone enter the pores of the wood, and
either assimilate the preceding parts to themselves, or thrust them out, or
partly one and partly the other.

The other kind of growth belongs to living things, or those which are
<margin>15</margin>
nourished, and it always occurs with some change of the parts.
Namely, various parts of various shapes, encountering one
another, are mixed together; and once mixed, they act upon
one another until they acquire certain determined shapes.
And sometimes the more fluid among these slip away,
<margin>20</margin>
while the less fluid remain: these latter, being impacted into one
another, compose a hard body, through which various little streams <note>Descartes often used the concept of "rivuli" or small channels to explain the movement of bodily fluids</note>
filled with all the mixed elements run everywhere; and the
thicker parts contained in those streams gradually take the place
of the surrounding parts, being pushed by the thinner ones,
<margin>25</margin>
and thus nutrition occurs; or one stream is divided into two or—

---

<margin>a. The manuscript adds: (*or even with a great change, nothing forbids it*), without it being known whether this parenthesis is an addition by Leibniz, or if it was already in the text of Descartes.</margin>

<summary>Descartes distinguishes between the mechanical growth of inanimate objects like minerals and the physiological process of nutrition in living beings, which involves the transformation of fluid particles within internal channels.</summary>
<keywords>growth, nutrition, minerals, petrification, physiology, Descartes, Leibniz, mechanical philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 631 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of growth and nutrition from the previous page, specifically detailing how the "little streams" or channels within a body facilitate the expansion of parts until old age or lack of flexibility halts the process.</meta>

<header>ANATOMICAL MATTERS.</header>

<margin>I, 110-114.</margin>
divide into many, and thus growth <term>accretio: increase in size</term> occurs. Truly, a body growing in this way is filled with countless little streams of this kind; and when, due to old age, the harder parts are so firmly packed together that the streams enclosed by them can no longer be dilated <margin>5</margin> so that two are made from one, growth ceases, and only nutrition remains. But if, in the course of time, those thicker parts are compressed even further, <insert>so</insert> that they cannot be pushed out of their place by other incoming parts, then nutrition and life itself also cease <gloss>a</gloss>. <note>original: "vita". Descartes links the mechanical failure of fluid movement directly to death.</note>
<margin>10</margin> | Furthermore, this growth or nutrition is either imperfect or perfect. It is imperfect when the matter filling those little streams arrives from elsewhere already so mixed or nearly arranged that it is simply blended and shaped. EXCERPTA II, 66-70.

Quite perfect as well, but lacking the extremes of thinness and solidity, is sticky phlegm <term>pituita: a thick, cool humor</term> and mucus. Finally, a perfect mixture produces flesh, nerves, and bones, according to whether there are more or fewer solid parts in it.

<margin>5</margin> Nails and hair are made of the same material as bones, yet they do not harden in the same way because their fluid parts evaporate too quickly. Teeth, however, are certainly of the same material as horns, yet they harden like other bones because, being covered by the mouth, they retain more moisture and <margin>10</margin> solidify more slowly.

Wasteful spirit <term>spiritus excrementitius: gaseous waste products of metabolism</term> evaporates through the ears: hence whistling and ringing <term>tinnitus</term>, namely when that spirit is prevented from exiting by earwax, and striking against it, then produces a sound.

<margin>15</margin> Spirit also evaporates through the eyes, as is evident in menstruating women, whose eyes are said to emit a vapor <note>original: "vaporem emittere dicuntur"; this reflects a common pre-modern belief that the gaze of a menstruating woman could physically affect her environment, such as dulling a mirror</note>: for the whole body of a woman swells with fluids when she menstruates, and indeed she is purged of thicker fluid through the womb, but of more subtle fluid through higher parts, namely <margin>20</margin> through the eyes.

All shivering <term>horror: the medical term for the "chills" or "rigors" that precede a fever</term> and cold in the body occur because the fluid parts flow together into a certain center <term>focus</term>, in which the heat is then at its peak. ### EXCERPTA II, 74-76.

...but not indeed a pure animal spirit <term>animal spirit: in early modern medicine, a subtle, fluid-like substance thought to travel through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement</term>. In that place, however, gas <term>flatus: internal wind or vapor</term> is generated, whether a nerve is pricked or if a sluggish vapor happens to penetrate there. This gas convulses the nerves because it somehow binds the parts of the spirits together and causes several to act in concert; thus, they overcome the strength of the nerve and arrange and determine themselves toward certain movements. Otherwise, they were accustomed to be arranged and determined by the nerves, because the individual particles of the nerve are more powerful than the individual particles of the spirit.

Gases are not usually produced by heat or cold alone, but only by cold following upon heat. For heat indeed thins the spirits, but it does not for that reason create gas: because, while it thins them, it simultaneously opens passages <term>meatus: pores or channels in the body</term> through which they may escape; and unless the heat is removed, these passages in the body always correspond proportionally to the quantity of the spirits that are becoming rarefied <term>rarefaction: the process of a substance becoming thinner or less dense, such as a liquid turning into vapor</term>. If, however, cold should supervene and block these passages, the spirit—which has already begun to be rarefied—continues to do so, both because the process has started and even more so with heat from other parts assisting it. Then that spirit, which cannot exhale, is turned into gas.

The same principle is evident in chestnuts placed over a fire on a perforated iron plate: for if they are not moved, the fire indeed thins the spirits trapped inside, but it also thins the skin closest to the fire, through which that spirit breathes out as a sweat <note>referring to the moisture or "spirit" escaping the shell</note>. If, however, they are moved, then the skin which was closest to the fire is turned to another side and exposed <note>original: "opponitur." In the manuscript, "ex" is rewritten above the first syllable, without "op" having been crossed out, suggesting a possible correction to "exponitur" (is exposed)</note> to the cold air, and its passages are therefore narrowed; meanwhile, the spirit inside is nonetheless thinned, both because it has already started and because the fire presses it from the other side. Nor...

II, 80-82. ANATOMICA. 607

...grind just as many leaves together, with a grain of salt added, and take it every morning on an empty stomach.

| If there is a tedious pricking in the soles of the feet and the palms of the hands while little morsels<sup>a</sup> <note>original: "morselli"; the editor suggests this refers to small pustules or bites, though the manuscript clearly reads "morbilli" (measles).</note> emerge, they should be
<margin>5</margin> be held for a long time in warm water.
The pulse increases immediately upon waking from sleep, because the blood, which was sluggish during rest in certain veins and in the flesh of the muscles, immediately flows toward the heart due to the movement of the whole body and the sudden entry of spirits <term>animal spirits: in early modern science, these were subtle fluids thought to carry sensation and motion through the nerves</term> into
<margin>10</margin> the muscles. From this, yawning and stretching sometimes occur simultaneously at that time.
Sneezing is the purging of the ventricles <note>cavities within the brain</note> of the brain through the nostrils. Yawning is the purging of vapors existing between both membranes <term>menynges: the meninges, or protective layers surrounding the brain</term> through the palate. Vapors,
<margin>15</margin> however, are collected there from a lack of agitation in the substance of the brain, or when—that space between the two membranes being full, as it always is—it is suddenly contracted because the brain is inflated. ### ANATOMICA.
<sig>*</sig>

<margin>I, 136-138.</margin>
...and the liver remain in the middle of the body. The stomach <term>ventriculus: the Latin term for both stomach and heart chamber; here referring to the digestive organ</term> adheres in its upper and posterior part to the spleen, and in its anterior part to the liver. By communicating certain arteries to the liver, the nearby blood has frothed over into bile, whence the gallbladder <margin>5</margin> was formed. Because it was joined to that part of the stomach, it caused a perforation there, and the intestines were produced, winding in countless ways as the bile, seeking an exit, rolled about.

The right ventricle of the heart seems to have been formed at almost the same <margin>10</margin> | time as the left. For it has its origin in the fact that, when the subtler or more mobile matter glided into the middle of the heart, and from there ascended in a straight line toward the head, the frothier and more airy matter turned around it. But why it turned from the spine toward <margin>15</margin> the right side (as appears from the flow <note>original: "fluxu"; a footnote in the manuscript suggests this may be "flexu," meaning "curve" or "winding"</note> of the coronary vein), rather than toward the left, is a difficulty that I have not been able to unravel until now.

This production of the right ventricle of the heart is not hindered by the fact that the umbilicus <term>umbilicus: the navel</term> was later formed exactly in the middle <margin>20</margin> | of the belly, and not on the right side. For before the ventricle was formed, the trunk of the aorta, from which the position of the umbilicus depended, nevertheless remained in the middle of the body, at least to the senses. For it is clear that it verged slightly more toward the left side than the right from the fact that it ascends from the vein <margin>25</margin> on the left side between the renal vessels <term>emulgentes: historical term for the renal arteries and veins</term> and the flanks <term>ilia: the lower abdominal or pelvic region</term>. From this, perhaps, it also follows that the right part of the body is usually stronger than the left, specifically because it is somewhat fleshier.

However, the second ventricle is necessarily formed <margin>30</margin> from the fact that there are many airy particles in the blood...

# EXCERPTA
### 144.

...much more curved than in a chick <note>The Latin text here is ambiguous; the editor suggests it might mean an "adult" bird or the "preceding" chick described on the previous page</note>, but whose outer wall seemed scarcely thinner than the walls of the left cavity <note>The left ventricle of the heart</note>; which, however, in adults are ten times thicker. Below the liver <term>hepar</term> appeared the stomach <term>ventriculus</term>, which was clearly white, and in which 
<margin>5</margin> some yellowish-green matter was observed after it had been opened; the intestines and the navel <term>umbilicus</term> were attached to it, and it was quite far from the rear <note>original: "podice"</note>. Near it, within the abdominal cavity, was contained the yolk <term>vitellus</term> of the egg, which had been reduced by barely a third; and once it was cooked, I found it to be of the same 
<margin>10</margin> flavor, but of a much harder substance than that of fresh eggs. Moreover, that yolk hung from a certain vessel mixed among the intestines, and I could not yet determine whether it terminated in the liver or elsewhere. I also saw no egg white <term>albumen</term>, for it was entirely consumed.

<margin>15</margin> Thus I judge that the animal spirits <term>spiritus animales: in Descartes's physics, these were highly refined fluids in the blood that acted as messengers for movement and sensation</term> are spread through the egg white; and in it, just as in the seed of four-legged animals, the limbs are formed first—at least in its chalaza <term>chalaza: the spiral strands of thickened egg white that hold the yolk in place</term> at the beginning, and then gradually in the rest, so much so that in its final 
<margin>20</margin> parts, the skin around the navel is formed last of all. 

Veins and arteries do not form except near the membranes <note>original: "tunicas"</note> of the yolk and egg white, which seem to be like the two membranes enveloping the fetus <term>foetus</term> of four-legged animals. The heart is not formed in the middle of the seed <note>original: "seminis"; referring here to the generative matter of the embryo</note>, but rather at 
<margin>25</margin> some extremity, just as we see in the seeds of plants that the part which sprouts <term>germinat</term> is always located at some extremity.

# ANATOMICAL OBSERVATIONS
### I, 146.

The course of the blood in the coronary vein and the right ventricle revolves in a circle, like all spiral shells; and from there like cranesbill <note>a type of geranium</note> and beans, but in the opposite manner than the bindweed <note>original: "convolvulus"</note>.

<margin>5</margin> In a <sup>a</sup> codfish <note>original: "cabeliau"; a Dutch-derived term for fresh cod</note> the throat was much wider than the esophagus, and the esophagus wider than the stomach. The intestines <sup>b</sup> were also quite narrow and twisted into only three folds: as in this figure, *a* being the stomach, *b* the anus. Moreover, the stomach consisted of very many fibers, just as in the palate of an ox <margin>10</margin> arising from the teeth <sup>c</sup>, and much longer. The bile <note>original: "fel"; refers to the gallbladder or bile</note> adhered partly to those fibers, partly to the intestine; the spleen was below the bile, and also adhered to the intestine; the liver was very white, and I did not note whether it adhered anywhere other than to the heart; however, it was attached to the heart by means of a very short vena cava, which <margin>15</margin> protruded considerably toward the heart, so that this swelling took the place of an auricle <note>the upper chamber of the heart</note>. What I just said about salt seems to be false. For water is just as transparent as salt. But instead of transparency <note>original: "diaphani"</note>, one must say that salt is accessible to the movement of heat because of its dryness; water, however, although it is accessible to the movement of light, is nevertheless not accessible to the movement of heat (which exists in parts that are a little more solid or larger) because of its moisture. From this, perhaps, a reason can be given why seawater glows at night <note>original: "luceat". This refers to bioluminescence or phosphorescence, a phenomenon that fascinated early modern scientists</note>. <margin>See volume VI, pp. 255-256; volume VIII, part 1, p. 255, and volume IX, part 2, pp. 249-250.</margin>

As far as I know, no salty fruits are produced: which sufficiently indicates that salt is very fixed <note>stable/non-volatile</note>, and is not raised into plants by the sun. But neither is any flesh salty, not even that of sea fish: which indicates that salt is very dry; <margin>5</margin> and indeed, nothing except glutinous substances can pass into flesh.

Most fruits are bitter <note>original: "Amari"</note>, <margin>10</margin> especially those that grow in somewhat warmer regions, such as the husks of nuts, golden apples <note>likely oranges or citrus fruits</note>, etc. Moreover, all bitter things wipe away <note>cleanse or abrade</note> most vehemently and dry things out; indeed, they even cause sores and cut back the ends of the veins. Therefore, I conclude that there are parts initially stirred into smoke by heat, and therefore opaque and black (as in the husk of a nut), but afterwards in the tree they are gradually separated by the fast-moving fluid parts and at the same time packed together (whence olives, the riper they are, the more bitter they become), and consequently they make the moist body very thick, which in its entirety is dry in respect to our flesh, and therefore it wipes away; <margin>15</margin> <margin>In the same way earwax is formed. <note>original: "aurium purgamenta". Marginal note by Leibniz.</note></margin> <margin>20</margin> <margin>25</margin>

...because elsewhere, if I remember correctly, I have seen such hail that was plainly round, but whose center was more whitish, while the edges were more transparent—that is, more dense. I think this happened then because the drops of water were smaller and the wind colder. And for that reason, they did not break apart. However, the hail that falls in summer becomes plainly transparent because the wind is more subtle <note>thinner or less dense</note>. Moreover, it often becomes clotted <margin>5</margin> <insert>or horned, or confused</insert> <note>original: "concreta... an cornuta, an confusa"; Leibniz notes these as possible alternative readings of the manuscript</note>, for no other reason, if I am not mistaken, than that the wind freezes it while casting it down, and very suddenly; <margin>10</margin> whence it happens that the parts which are first encountered by the wind harden more quickly, and no equality <note>symmetry or uniformity</note> is preserved.

It should also be noted that the grains of that cone-shaped hail were not as equal among themselves as the stars of snow <note>snowflakes</note> are. The reason for this is clear: because the stars of snow are formed in a continuous medium, and therefore they all ought to be equal; but the grains <margin>15</margin> of this hail are formed as only eight parts from a single drop, which ought to be equal to one another; yet from another larger drop, eight larger grains will be formed.

Why is it that when the water of a river rises or remains high, <margin>20</margin> it does not enter neighboring cellars as much as it does while it is falling? Nor does it enter as much while it quickly rises and falls, as when it does so slowly? Truly, it is for the same reason that if you plunge an empty vessel with a narrow opening into water, it will not be filled with water as much if you plunge it quickly <margin>25</margin> as if you do so slowly; nor will any water enter it as long as it is entirely submerged; but when you draw it out of the water again, if it is not yet full, new water [will enter].

# I, 76-78. ANATOMICAL OBSERVATIONS.

Why does a nerve, when plucked by a finger, appear double?
<margin>5</margin> | Surely because, while it is moved in a circular fashion, it remains longer in the same relation to the eye when it is at the top or the bottom than when it is ascending or descending: just as the planets appear when they are stationary <note>Descartes refers to "retrograde motion" where planets appear to pause at their furthest points</note>.

Why is the breath, when emitted with the mouth nearly closed, cold?
Because then it holds all the parts of the body which it touches motionless toward the <margin>10</margin> same part <note>original: "eandem partem"; the MS originally had "easd" (those) before being corrected</note>; on the other hand, however, when it is less forceful, it moves them, and is thus warm. As we see sometimes, when there is a great wind and it blows equally in the same direction, the trees of the forests and the sails of ships are not moved; but they are moved then, when its <margin>15</margin> force is relaxed or when it first begins; and more so, when only a light breeze blows. And this regarding the breath is demonstrated by the fact that, if we breathe with the mouth nearly closed toward <note>original: "versùs"; at this point in the manuscript, the author noted "turn the page" to continue the thought</note> our own hand, the same breath, which will be felt as cold on the rest of the hand, will be felt as warm in the gaps between the fingers <margin>20</margin> when they are not very tightly joined, so that the breath enters into them, because it will not be as forceful there. And from this it is clear why a cloth placed against the cracks of doors and windows best hinders the cold, even if it does not completely exclude the wind.

| Trees found beneath the earth in Holland are all overturned in such a way that the branches face the north. # EXCERPTS I, 84-86.

particles from the trunk move in a straight line, which are then reflected into a circle; and another circular motion occurs crosswise, by the mixing of which with the former, the particles are broken down more and more, and thus the fruit ripens. Gradually, indeed, <margin>5</margin>that circular motion gnaws at the very stem of the apple in a circle, until, the fruit being ripe, it is entirely separated and the fruit falls. Grafting <note>The practice of joining a shoot from one tree onto the trunk of another</note>, or even the cultivation of the soil alone, makes the fruit<gloss>a</gloss> milder: namely because the particles, carried through the channels <term>meatus</term> <note>Descartes uses this term to describe the microscopic pores or passages in organic matter</note> of two trees of different kinds, <margin>10</margin>are more thoroughly transformed. Likewise, from soil that is frequently turned, finer parts are drawn up: because, if the earth remains settled in the same place for a long time, its tiny particles will gradually combine into the same parts, so much so that the roots of the trees will go along similar paths; but when the clods are often turned, on the contrary, one part will enter the tree <margin>15</margin> in one way, another in another, and they will be better mixed there; for dissimilar things, in order to be mixed, must be broken into more parts. Hence all wild fruits become bitter.

In summary, all plants emerge from the earth in this way: <margin>20</margin>a copious vapor rises by the force of the sun through one part of the earth, and as the surrounding air resists its motion, it is partly dried, and partly its fibers, which were rising straight up, are turned crosswise, from which the bark is formed, having only transverse fibers, while on the contrary the <margin>25</margin>inner parts have straight ones. If any channels then occur in the bark, the vapor ascending between this and the wood takes on their shape through those oblong channels only in a transverse direction, and is formed into leaves. But that which penetrates from the very marrow <note>original: "medulla"; the pith or central core of the plant</note> of the wood through the wood and the bark,

# I, 86-88. ANATOMICAL OBSERVATIONS.
<note>original: "Anatomica"</note>

Since it emerges between fibers that are partly round and partly transverse, it becomes round; and from this, first the eye of the tree <note>The bud or germinal point of a plant</note> congeals, then the flower, and finally the fruit, as mentioned above in section a. <note>original: "ut supra a." referring to the previous pages describing the ripening of fruit</note> Furthermore, a cavity is formed in the middle of all plants, <margin>5</margin> filled either with air or with pith; because the parts of the vapor do not rise in a completely straight line, but obliquely here and there, as is evident from the fibers of wood: those which are more solid are carried toward the bark, and that which is lighter remains in the middle, like the sun among the planets. <note>Descartes uses a cosmological analogy to explain the distribution of matter in a plant stem</note>

<margin>10</margin> Plants < which > grow under water are more spongy and airy than others: because the vapor rising into the plant through the roots by the force of heat is almost entirely airy. In plants that grow in the air, however, the thinner parts of that vapor easily evaporate, and only the drier parts remain <margin>15</margin> to constitute the plant (which is also why a plant will be more solid on a mountain than in a valley). But under water, those airy parts are held back by the continuity of the water and by a certain stickiness <note>original: "lentore"</note> inherent to its nature, and they therefore make the plant more porous.

<margin>20</margin> If any body were driven or impelled to motion always by an equal force—namely, by a mind implanted within it (for no other such force can exist)—and it were moved in a vacuum, it would always take three times more time from the beginning of its motion to the midpoint of the space to be traversed than from the middle <margin>25</margin> to the end, and so on. # EXCERPTS I, 88-90.

...the speed may no longer increase perceptibly, and a certain other finite speed can be determined which it will never equal. <note>Descartes is describing the concept of terminal velocity or a limit that a moving body approaches but never reaches.</note>

Those things which are impelled by the force of gravity—since this gravity <margin>5</margin> does not always act equally like a soul <note>original: "anima"; here referring to a self-moving or constant internal force</note>, but is some other body that is already in motion—can never impel a heavy thing as fast as it is itself moved; but even in a vacuum, the impulse would always be diminished in a **geometric proportion**<sup>a</sup>. <margin>10</margin> Indeed, things that are diminished by two or more causes in a geometric proportion are diminished by all of them as if by a single cause that would diminish them in a geometric proportion, and the same calculation always returns. Likewise, even if some other cause should restrain [the motion] by an **arithmetic force**, <margin>15</margin> a diminution in geometric proportion will always arise.

If, however, some other force should impel [the body] always in a geometric proportion, acting simultaneously with that which is geometrically diminished, it will finally reach a point where the Geometric ceases and only the Arithmetic remains, increasing the motion, as <margin>20</margin> it was said a soul would do in a vacuum<sup>b</sup>. Finally, if the impulse should increase geometrically and be diminished or even increased arithmetically, the speed will increase to infinity in a **composite proportion**, which can be explained by the spaces encompassed by the help of a triangle and a hooked line of proportionals <margin>25</margin> in this manner *(fig. I noticed a box <note>original: "pyxidem"; likely a small vessel or container</note> that was very tightly sealed, in which there had been scented water throughout the entire winter; when I opened it in the spring, <margin>5</margin> the water burst out with a certain force. This was because, in winter, dense particles had been introduced into it by the cold, which the heat of spring did not so easily expel; and therefore that water was, as it were, compressed inside. I think the same thing happens in almost all things: since the heat of spring does not easily rarefy those <margin>10</margin> things which were thickened in winter, it achieves this with a certain force once it has increased enough to prevail. I believe this force contributes to the origin of those things which are generated in the springtime. <insert>Springtime</insert> <note>original: "Verno tempore"; written above "spring" in the manuscript</note>

While new wines or beers bubble, this happens from <margin>15</margin> the opposition of motions which exist between their parts, <margin>Hippocrates says that "contrary things folded together at the same time even burn one another."</margin> <note>original: "Contraria simul complicata se invicem etiam etiam comburere, dicit Hippocrates." This marginal note appears to have been present in Descartes' original manuscript.</note> which consequently require a larger space, and admit fluid particles between themselves, as if in the angles of contact; from this, heat arises. This is also how the digestion <note>original: "concoctio"</note> of food occurs in the stomach of animals. Just as lime and water <margin>20</margin> are neither of them hot separately, so also wine drawn immediately from the grapes would not bubble, except for the fact that it is steeped for some time with the clusters; from whose...

# EXCERPTS I, 92-94.

...receives this heat through a contrary nature, by the agitation of which it is afterwards more perfectly mixed, and therefore can be less easily corrupted; for it borrows, as it were, certain fibers <note>original: "nervos"; literally "nerves" or "sinews," here meaning structural strength</note> from the hardness of the grape-stalks, by which the fluid matter <margin>5</margin> is strengthened, and is defended against the motions of the surrounding air which tend toward corruption.

We say that the air corrupts many mixed things rather than generating them; on the other hand, we say the sun generates them rather than corrupting them. This happens because <margin>10</margin> the motion of the air is weak and directed into different parts, or is disordered; and consequently, those things which have been altered by it do not have the faculty of preserving themselves in the same state, and therefore we do not say they have perfect forms, but are only corrupted things. On the contrary, the motion of the sun <margin>15</margin> is uniform or ordered and stronger; and consequently, those things which have received their form from it generally have a more durable one, although this varies frequently according to the dispositions of the subject.

Old men have white hair, and animals born in cold regions have white fur; on the contrary, Ethiopians have the <margin>20</margin> blackest. The same is also true of the skin. This happens because, when the heat is greater both inside and outside, those excrements <note>original: "excrementa"; in early modern science, this refers to any byproduct of the body, including hair and sweat</note> exiting from the body more frequently interrupt their flow: which interruption produces a black color. It also causes the Moors to have twisted and very soft hair. On the contrary, in <margin>25</margin> other regions, a lesser heat emits thicker particles; each of which, since they are transparent, are only interrupted enough to produce a white color, not black, and thick hair, not thin like that of the Moors.

# ANATOMICAL NOTES

It is certain that hair becomes curly because the cuticle <note>the outermost layer of the skin</note> is proportionately denser than the skin itself; and since the roots grow in the skin, they are bent obliquely as they pass through the cuticle. It is evident that Ethiopians have this denser cuticle <margin>5</margin> because it is dried by the hot air. In old age, however, the passages of the cuticle are enlarged, and often those who had curly hair in their youth no longer have it in old age; on the contrary, it can happen that when hair has fallen out due to illness, that cuticle becomes denser and the hair grows back curly, even if it had previously been completely straight; <margin>10</margin> which I have observed in a certain person <note>original: "in quodam observavi"</note>. — Eyelashes grow while in the womb because they have suitable material there, namely cartilage that has not yet hardened; but they do not grow afterwards, because that hardened cartilage <note>original: "cartilago"; corrected in the manuscript from "cartilagine"</note> is no longer suitable <margin>15</margin> for emitting hair, unless perhaps it is loosened by old age. The material of hair is that sticky or dry substance secreted from the brain or glands and similar underlying parts; the eyelashes testify <note>original: "testantur"</note> that cartilages are of this nature at their beginning.

Tears are the sweat of the eyes: which is evident from the fact <margin>20</margin> that everything heating the eyes draws out tears. Sweat does not differ from that material which exhales from the body through insensible perspiration, except in quantity, rawness, and saltiness: because, when the passages of the skin are more relaxed, what would otherwise be air becomes water; but the wax <margin>25</margin> in the eyes is the stickiness of sweat, just as hair and dandruff sweat *thickly*, since the glands and the brain sweat much, and that which exudes is stickier and thicker.

# EXCERPTS I, 96-98.

Urine is the same part of the blood filtered through the kidney, just as sweat is through the skin, except that it is a little thicker.

<margin>5</margin> | From milk, three things are separated: the whey, the fat or butter, and the dry <insert>curd</insert> <note>original: "caillé"; the French term for curdled milk</note>.

Sugar is quite sticky; and if that which is sticky were removed from the sugar, what remains would be salty. Blood is sweet in the same way, and whatever in it is sticky goes into the flesh; therefore, the remaining sweat <margin>10</margin> is salty. Truly, sweat is salty for this reason: since it is that part of the blood which does not turn into flesh, and because no salt is attached to the flesh on account of its dryness (by which it would rather corrode the flesh), therefore all the salt existing in the blood overflows into the sweat and into the urine.

<margin>15</margin> *Miscellaneous Problems.* — Why ice does not melt by softening gradually like *wax*. <note>Leibniz adds here: "Nothing further was written, nor do other problems follow."</note>

# EXCERPTS
->FROM<-
# FATHER KIRCHER ON THE MAGNET.

This title is followed by several notes found at the bottom of leaf 10 of the preceding manuscript, 12 lines on the front and 4 on the back. (See above, p. 607, note *c*, and p. 611, note *b*.) They relate to the reading Descartes did of the work by Father Athanasius Kircher <note>A Jesuit polymath (1602–1680) known for his vast interests in the sciences and oriental studies</note>, which he mentions in a letter to Huygens dated January 31, 1642. (Volume III, p. 521-522.) The pages he refers to are those of the 1st edition, 1641. Descartes had found there, he said, only one new experiment, and he indeed recalls it in his *Principles of Philosophy*, Part IV, article 170. (Volume VIII, p. 301-302.) For everything else, he judges the author severely: "There is," he says, "none of his reasons that is worth anything." Yet (could it be a mere coincidence?) he enumerates up to thirty-four properties of the magnet (*Ibid.*, p. 284-287), and Kircher before him enumerated thirty-three. But these are not the same properties for both; and if for some Descartes agrees with Kircher, for at least one, which he had noted while reading him, he opposes him (p. 636 below, note *c*). Likely, in 1642, he already had his opinion formed on the magnet, based on the works of Gilbert <note>William Gilbert, author of 'De Magnete' (1600)</note>, Cabeo <note>Niccolò Cabeo, a Jesuit philosopher who studied magnetism</note>, or his own observations, or even from communications such as that of Mersenne at the beginning of 1640 (vol. III, p. 46, and p. 51-52), which is found again in the *Principles* (vol. VIII, 20th property of the magnet, p. 286 and p. 300-301).

As for what he says, page 7, that burnt crystal gives as much weight in ash as there was before ^a.

---

a. <note>original: "Si crystallus comburatur, nihil humidi resudare videbis, tantùmque cineris, quanta prius erat crystalli quantitas, generari comperies."</note> "If crystal is burned, you will see no moisture sweat out, and you will find that as much ash is generated as the quantity of crystal was before." (A. *Kircher's The Magnet, or On the Magnetic Art*, 2nd edition, book I, part 1, p. 6.)

# MISCELLANY

Glowing iron is attracted by a magnet. <margin>a</margin>

177. A huge magnet, which can barely pull a small needle joined to it, moves compass needles <note>original: "versoria"</note> at a distance of one foot: something which smaller, much stronger magnets do not do. <margin>b</margin>

617. He describes a method of raising a wind by the fall of water through a long channel—wider at the top than at the bottom—into some closed vessel. In this vessel, he says the air is thus agitated and reproduced: specifically, as the water escapes through a hole in the lower part of the vessel, the air (generated from the vapors of the water) blows through a hole in the upper part of the vessel. He notes that he has seen metalsmiths <note>original: "malleatores," literally 'hammerers' or 'forgers'</note> who draw iron into rods using this machine to continually blow on the fire. From this, he gives a reason why wind perpetually exits from certain caverns, and rightly so. <margin>c</margin>

---

a. "Theorem XXXI: A magnet attracts ignited iron just as well as cold iron." (*Ibid.*, p. 140.)

b. "Note also in this place that a very large magnet, notwithstanding the weaker power it possesses in pulling, nevertheless establishes a larger Sphere of Activity than a stronger magnet that is smaller than it. For I have a huge magnet which, though it barely pulls a needle joined to it, nevertheless moves compass needles at a distance of a geometric foot; there are others, smaller in bulk, which are most effective in pulling and holding, yet they yield to the larger one in the Sphere of Activity." (*Ibid.*, book I, part 1, p. 169.)

c. "Another way of artificially raising winds is done by the compression of air, in the following manner. Let there be flowing water at place A. You will allow this to flow into a channel A B, which you shall construct thus: let a channel of any number of feet be made from 4 long planks (note, however, that the longer the channel is, the more vehement the future wind will be), in a pyramidal shape, as figure A B C shows. # EXCERPTS

Electrical bodies <note>In the 17th century, "electrica" referred to materials like amber that could hold a static charge.</note> heated by friction attract; moved near a fire, they do not attract: indeed, in order to attract, something must go out that then returns. <margin>a</margin>

As he says <margin>b</margin> elsewhere that he observed in a large, round dining room—

> » ...should have a vessel or receptacle E D, into which it is inserted; and you will have the instrument prepared. If, therefore, you wish to stir up vehement winds,
> » you will allow the water A to flow into the channel A B; which, having been cast down with vehement force into
> » the receptacle E D, will push the air in the vessel E D with the greatest violence through
> » the mouth V of the channel V X; for since the falling water carries a great
> » portion of air down with it, and the water itself, worn down and diminished by the vehement
> » commotion and striking, is changed into air, there will never
> » be a lack of a huge agitation of air in the receptacle D E, and consequently a
> » perpetual blast erupting through V. I myself have seen in many places metalsmiths <note>original: "Malleatores"</note>
> » in Vulcan’s workshops <note>A poetic reference to smithies or forges.</note> for drawing iron out into rods, who use a skillful construction of channels of this kind
> » instead of bellows to perpetually blow upon the fires.
> » Moreover, a wind of this kind is so vehement that almost nothing can be
> » placed before the orifice that is not cast a long distance through the air like an arrow,
> » by the sole vehemence of the blast. » (*Ibid.*, book III, part II,
> » chapter 3, pp. 543-544.)

> « From this it is also clear why... a huge wind continually blows out from certain
> » mountain caverns? I remember in the Lipari or Aeolian Islands <note>original: "Vulcanijs Inſulis"</note> that a certain
> » hole in a cliff was shown to me, from which a continuous wind breaks out so cold
> » that water placed there freezes into ice in a short time. »
(*Ibid.*, pp. 544-545.)

a. « But someone will object at this point: if electrical things <note>original: "electrica res"</note> emit effluvia when heated by friction,
» why do they not do so by the sun, fire, or other heat? For it is
» certain that electrical bodies exposed to fire, coals, or a vehement sun, are so far
» from attracting that they rather suspend all their action in the presence of these things,
» as if they were sworn enemies of their power. To this I respond that amber <note>original: "electrum"</note>
» does not attract when fire is moved near it, because... Whence it ought not to have heat, except
» that produced only by motion and light friction, and as if it were its own, not
» introduced from other bodies... » (*Ibid.*, book III, part III, chapter 3, p. 568.)

b. *Ait* [he says] is a conjecture, instead of *et* [and] (MS.). Unless *ait* is
understood, and one ought to read: *ait et alibi* [he says also elsewhere]. Kircher’s text: « From this
» cause it is also gathered why in vaults and round dining rooms <note>original: "cœnaculis"</note>, in
» opposite places, any words, even those uttered in the lowest voice, are
» perceived. I remember once discovering a thing of this kind at Heidelberg in the Palace of the Prince Palatine, in
» a certain large round dining room, the diameter of which equaled almost a hundred feet:
» it was built with such skill that from one side, voices however lowly uttered are
» rendered so clearly in the diametrically opposite part, with an ear applied to the wall—

# EXCERPTS II, 210-211.

...are observed. From this it is clear that even the most common foods can easily transform into a harmful force.

I would believe that the skin of the stomach <note>original: "ventriculi cutem"</note> is loose and porous, and through it a serous humor <note>A "serous humor" refers to a clear, watery bodily fluid, similar to saliva or lymph, which early modern physicians believed played a key role in digestion.</note> flows into it from the whole body. 
<margin>5</margin> This is evident from the fact that when hungry people see food, this humor overflows even into the palate, because those passages are loosened by the power of the imagination. This is because that humor is useful for digesting food, just as hay, if it is stored after being sprinkled with water, will grow warm and rot <note>Descartes uses the fermentation of damp hay as an analogy for how moisture and heat break down matter in the stomach.</note>.

<margin>10</margin> From this, a reason can easily be given for many astringents <note>Medicines that shrink or constrict body tissues.</note>, such as *verdigris* <note>original: "ver de gris"; a green pigment or rust formed on copper, used historically in small, controlled medicinal doses.</note>, all bitter fruits, service berries, medlars, etc. It is certain that these close up those passages; on the other hand, Mercury ☿ and Antimony ♁ <note>The text uses the alchemical symbols for these elements.</note>, which are cold and humid—like plums, cassia, apples, etc.—loosen them; and for that reason, they are 
<margin>15</margin> purgatives.

However, other things can be purgatives or astringents for other reasons; but I think this is the principal one. For those things which are quickly corrupted in the stomach, such as foods more delicate than usual, etc., seasonal fruits, etc., indeed 
<margin>20</margin> render the feces soft, but they do not for that reason purge from the rest of the body; likewise those things which are astringent, but only by accident.

It should be noted that almost all astringents help digestion <note>original: "concoctionem"; the process of "cooking" or breaking down food in the stomach.</note>. For the less serous humor there is in the stomach, the more the heat is kindled. From which it happens, that

## II, 211-212. MISCELLANY.

Certain astringents <note>Substances that constrict or shrink body tissues.</note>, when taken after a meal, accidentally loosen the stomach because they accelerate digestion, such as quince jelly <note>original: "cydoniacum"; a common medicinal preserve in the 17th century used to aid digestion.</note>.

<margin>5</margin> The stomach presses upon the food enclosed within it and adapts itself to the quantity of the contents. Hence, when hungry people see food, they compress the stomach through the power of the imagination before the food has even entered; this causes fluids to rise to the mouth. There are, however, perhaps certain purgatives which prevent this compression, such as Mercury <note>original: "☿"; the alchemical symbol for the element mercury.</note>, which perhaps relaxes its 
<margin>10</margin> nerves; this would be extremely dangerous.

A powder made from the whole Goldenrod plant <note>original: "Virgæ aureæ"</note>, drunk in the weight of a dram; likewise the seed of the Broom plant <note>original: "geniſtæ"</note>, crushes stones in the bladder and kidneys.

Some things purge by softening the feces, such as mallow; others 
<margin>15</margin> by lubricating the intestines, such as butter; others by compressing the feces, such as quince after a meal; others by scouring the intestines, such as salt water or even fresh water; others by cutting through and opening the pores, such as cream of tartar <note>original: "<image-desc>alchemical symbol for tartar</image-desc>ri"; cream of tartar was used as a mild laxative.</note>; others by relaxing the 
<margin>20</margin> nerves serving the retention, such as Mercury. But things can also purge in a thousand other ways, such as by blocking the orifices of the veins, by hindering digestion, etc.

Indeed, I have even experienced at times that a drink of Spanish wine purged me, namely by heating the mass of the 
<margin>25</margin> blood, so that many vapors from it slipped down into the stomach and, like fresh water, were mixed copiously with the feces. This was manifest to me because on another occasion, when the same wine was taken in the morning, it promoted much urine, transparent and tasteless like honey, then...

# MISCELLANY.

## ON REFRACTION.

For glass whose refraction is as 7 to √113, if the diameter is C, the thickness will be 1/36 C or thereabouts, namely — 7/2 C + √(49/4 CC + 49/256 CC); and the height of the machine for polishing <margin>5</margin> it is 4 C, and the focal length is nearly 9 C.
The refraction in glass, according to the experiments of Mr. de Beaune <note>Florimond de Beaune (1601–1652), a mathematician and friend of Descartes who studied the properties of lenses.</note>, is nearly as 1181 to 768.
The refraction from air to water is less than from air to <term>oil of salt</term> <note>original: "⊖"; a historical term for hydrochloric acid or a related preparation</note>; this is less than to <term>oil of rosemary</term> <note>original: "°°° rosmarini"</note>, this <margin>10</margin> less than <term>oil of sage</term> <note>original: "salviæ"</note>, this less than <term>oil of thyme</term> <note>original: "thymi"</note>, this less than <term>oil of cloves</term> <note>original: "caryophyllorum"</note>. Furthermore, the refraction which occurs in oil of cloves nearly equals that which occurs in solid glass.
In <term>water</term> <note>original: "∇"</note> it is nearly the same as in common water, and likewise <margin>15</margin> in salt water (*I am surprised*). But in hot water it is less (often tested) than in cold<sup>a</sup>.
In spirit of wine <note>Ethanol or highly distilled alcohol.</note> a much greater refraction occurs than in common water; but the experiment must be repeated.

---

a. Note the use of characters from old chemistry: the inverted triangle ∇ to designate water, *aqua*; the same sign with an attached F, aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>; the three small circles arranged in a triangle °°°, to designate an oil or essence, *oleum*: essence of rosemary (*rosmarini*, refractive index: 1.475), of sage (*salviæ*: 1.475), of thyme (*thymi*: 1.483), of cloves (*caryophyllorum*: 1.495). The first oil or essence indicated, with the sign ⊖, is oil of salt, *oleum salis*, of which Descartes speaks, vol. VI, p. 263, l. 31, and p. 668. See *Commentaries on Alchemy* by <small>ANDREAS LIBAVIUS</small> Part I, ch. vi, p. 86-7. (Frankfurt, 1606.)
