# EXCERPTS

## Witelo calculates the angles of refraction as follows:

| Angles of Incidence | Refracted from air to water | Refracted from water to glass | Refracted from water to air | Refracted from air to glass |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| <margin>5</margin> 10 | 7.45 | 9.30 | 12.5 | 7.30 |
| 20 | 15.30 | 18.30 | 24.30 | 13 |
| 30 | 22.30 | 27 | 37.30 | 19.30 |
| 40 | 29 | 35 | 31 | 25 |
| <margin>10</margin> 50 | 30 | 42 | 65 | 30 |
| 60 | 34.30 | 30 | 79.30 | 34.30 |
| 70 | 38.30 | 49 | 94.30 | 38.30 |
| 80 | 42 | 30 | 110 | 42 |

<note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285) was a Polish friar and physicist whose work "Perspectiva" was the standard medieval text on optics. Descartes is here scrutinizing Witelo's data tables.</note>

When he calculates the refraction from water to air based on the complement of that which is from air to water, he necessarily <margin>15</margin> errs. For since the refraction at entry and exit is equal <note>Descartes refers to the principle of reversibility: light traveling from A to B follows the same path as light from B to A.</note>, if the angle of incidence being 30 degrees results in a refracted angle of 22.30, then conversely, from water to air with an angle of incidence of 22.30, the refracted angle will be 30 degrees; and <margin>20</margin> consequently, with an angle of incidence of 30 degrees, the refracted angle will be more than 37.30. But these entire tables are false.

<note>Descartes is pointing out mathematical inconsistencies in Witelo's tables. He argues that if the light path is reversible, Witelo's specific values for the transition between air and water do not align logically with his other measurements.</note>

# DESCARTES ᵃ <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>

---

> The wise man enjoys good things as long as they are present, and is not saddened by the fact that they might depart. <note>original: "Sapiens gaudet bonis quamdiu adſunt, nec triſtatur ex eo quòd poſſint abîſſe."</note>

> Understanding is to the mind as motion is to the body, and will is as shape: we deflect from one understanding to another, just as from one motion into another ᵇ. <note>original: "Intellectio eſt ad mentem ut motus ad corpus, & voluntas ut figura : deflectimus ex unâ intellectione ad aliam, ut ex uno motu in alium."</note>

a. Royal Library of Hanover. Manuscript of Leibniz. Cataloged by Eduard Bodemann, p. 54 of his work cited on p. 549 above, note *a*, with the indication: “*Leaves 19-22, without heading, faulty copy, 7th part corrected by Leibniz.*” <note>original German: "Bl. 19-22, ohne Ueberſch., fehlerhafte, 7. Th. von L. corrig. Abſchr."</note>

This manuscript copy fills two large sheets, each of which is folded in two: making in all four leaves, or eight pages of writing. It comprises two very distinct parts, of which only the second bears a title: *Annotations which it seems Mr. Descartes wrote on his Principles of Philosophy* <note>original Latin: "Annotationes quas videtur D. des Cartes in ſua principia Philoſophiæ ſcripſiſſe"</note>. This second part begins at about the third of the 6th page, and continues until the end of the 8th. All that precedes, pp. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 (the first third of the latter), is composed of detached thoughts or reflections, each of which is separated from the next by a sign: two small horizontal lines, crossed by two small vertical lines. (The same sign further separates the second part from the first.) This first part bears only at the head the name, written after the fact and in pencil, of DESCARTES. The eight pages are in the same handwriting, which is no longer that of Leibniz; but the latter has made, by his own hand, some corrections in faulty places. The fact that he himself corrected this text shows that he attached a certain importance to it, and that he undoubtedly believed it to be by Descartes. Is it, however, truly an authentic text by our philosopher? We would not dare to assert it. However, in the first part, the date of an astronomical observation, 20 *Sept.* 1642 (p. 650), would be a favorable argument, as would some references to the *Principles*, in the second part. (See above, p. 545.)

--- Page 684 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page's collection of detached philosophical reflections found in the Leibniz manuscript, likely attributed to Descartes. This page explores the relationship between mind and body, the nature of free will, and a psychological explanation for the interpretation of dreams.</meta>

# EXCERPTS

-> <-

If the mind were perfectly united to the whole body, just as it is to that part in which it forms the images of things <note>referring to the pineal gland, which Descartes believed was the seat of the soul</note>, it could render that body capable of penetrating other bodies, invisible or transparent, impassible <note>incapable of suffering or injury</note>, and capable of all those similar qualities which are attributed to glorified bodies <note>the "glorified body" is a theological term for the perfected human form after resurrection</note>. <margin>Leibniz corrected the original phrasing here from "similar things" to "capable of similar qualities."</margin>

It is possible that I may see something to be true and yet not affirm it; but it is impossible that I should affirm something as a thing to be followed or desired, and yet desire the opposite. To affirm that something <margin>Leibniz corrected "when" to "something" here.</margin> is desirable is an act of the will, no less than the desire itself.

What is the freedom of the mind? Surely it is to will in such a way that we do not feel there is anything that hinders us <margin>The manuscript originally read "not," corrected to "us."</margin> from willing the exact opposite, if it should seem right to us. If this definition is accepted, no one can deny that we are free. If, however, we define freedom in such a way that it is not within my will if there be any power by which—even without my noticing—my will could be so inclined toward this or that that it certainly wills that thing and no other: freedom so defined is incompatible with a created being, given the omnipotence of the Creator. Just as the universe of bodies is the object for the eyes, so God is the proper object for the intellect. <margin>The manuscript originally read "Let it be," corrected to "Just as."</margin>

The interpretation of dreams seems to have originated chiefly from this: if by chance something happens during the day similar to those things which appeared to us in sleep, the parts of the brain—having been bent into such an image during rest—immediately and easily recall the appearance of that dream and present it to our minds, which we otherwise would never have remembered. Thus, while we forget almost all other dreams except those which a similar occurrence somehow forces us to remember (it is no wonder if we think all dreams contain something similar to what happens later), or we remember preceding things in the same way, whence we know that other things often follow—and rightly so, because the parts of the brain are more easily shaped into that form which they have already taken on before. There remain dreams arising from the body... <note>The manuscript has a gap here; the text is corrupted.</note> whence certain stronger impressions during the day strike the imagination most forcefully; and from the very fact that these occur rarely, superstitious people immediately judge them to have something of the divine.

<summary>This page contains philosophical fragments regarding the mind's potential power over the body, a definition of free will compatible with divine omnipotence, and a naturalistic explanation for why people believe dreams are prophetic.</summary>
<keywords>mind-body dualism, glorified bodies, free will, divine omnipotence, dream interpretation, psychology of memory, Leibniz manuscript, Descartes</keywords>

--- Page 685 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the freedom of the mind and the relationship between the soul and the body, these notes further explore the distinction between sleep and wakefulness, the nature of memory, and a refutation of the soul as a mere "harmony" of the body.</meta>

# MISCELLANY

We distinguish sleep from wakefulness because in sleep the mind is passive toward whatever images occur, whereas in wakefulness it is not merely passive, but active. From this it follows that if something sad occurs to me in my sleep, I easily wake myself up; for then the mind, which <gloss>which: an addition by Leibniz</gloss> wishes to be active, rouses itself.

The true art of memory is to know things through their causes; for he who understands the causes of things, even if the things themselves or their mental images <term>phantasmata: the sensory images or "ghosts" of objects stored in the brain</term> have slipped away, will easily have them formed anew by the intellect in our brain through the impression of the cause.

A great argument for why we should not be distressed by coming miseries is that they pertain to us no more than those already passed, the recollection of which often helps rather than afflicts us.

It is demonstrated that the soul <gloss>soul: a correction; the manuscript originally read "mind"</gloss> is not a "harmony" of the body <note>The "harmony" theory, famously discussed in Plato's Phaedo, suggests the soul is just a result of the body's tuning, like music from a lyre</note>. For if the soul were diffused <insert>< through ></insert> this harmony, and wherever there was some correspondence of parts, there also some part of the soul would be; it would correspond <gloss>it would correspond: the manuscript originally used a passive form</gloss> to the individual parts of the body, so that if one part of the body were removed, that part of the soul which arose from it would also be removed—just as in a lute <term>cythara: a stringed instrument like a lyre or lute</term>, if certain strings are removed, certain voices are also removed. But on the contrary, we see in man that even when arms, feet, ears, and similar parts are amputated, the soul remains so whole that someone can have an arm cut off and yet not even know it <gloss>See volume 8, page 320</gloss> <note>This refers to the phenomenon of the "phantom limb," which Descartes used to prove the soul is not spread out through the limbs</note>. Thus it must necessarily be admitted that the whole soul, in order to have clearly all the same thoughts it possesses—I say even the same sensations of the individual parts of the body—does not require the whole body. Therefore, it is not diffused through that whole as harmony is diffused in strings. Furthermore, it is clear that the soul is not the harmony of a single part, namely the brain alone; because if this were so, its actions would correspond either to the brain alone or at least chiefly to the affections of the brain. On the contrary, however, we see that we hardly ever feel any pain or pleasure as being in the brain, but rather in all the other members. If you were to say that the affections of the brain are not pain or pleasure, but all the other things that fall under thought, the counter-argument is that these have nothing to do with the body, or certainly no more to do with the brain than with other bodies. Consequently, either the soul would be diffused through the whole body, or I would certainly have many souls in each of my parts.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the nature of the soul and memory, these excerpts transition into definitions of virtue, the role of natural instinct versus artifice, and specific astronomical observations from 1642.</meta>

# EXCERPTS

Virtue is the firmness of mind in accomplishing those things which are shown to be better by the intellect judging correctly. If this is practiced regarding the dangers and evils of the body, it is called **fortitude**; if regarding the pleasures of the body, it is **temperance**; if regarding wealth and external goods, **justice**; and finally, if regarding any other matters whatsoever, it is **prudence**.

Dialectic <note>The art of logical argumentation</note>, Rhetoric, Poetics, and similar arts—just like the art of gladiatorial combat—often do more harm than good while they are being learned; for they remind us that we do not know those things which, by the force of nature, we would do perfectly if we did not doubt ourselves. A distinction must be made between those things which we cannot pretend not to know, such as the manner <margin>Perhaps read as "motion"?</margin> of swimming: about which beasts do not doubt, but we, being doubtful, must learn the art of swimming in order to swim; yet animals themselves, if they once experienced that they could not emerge from some water, would afterwards swim poorly. But there are other things which we do with nature as our guide, such as reasoning, persuading, defending ourselves, etc.; to these, no arts should be applied unless they are converted back into a kind of nature through very long practice. Finally, there are things which cannot be done at all without art, such as the art of playing the lute <term>cithara: a stringed instrument similar to a lyre</term>.

If we compare the modes of the mind with the modes of the body <margin>See previously, p. 647, note b.</margin>, we might say that perception of nothing is like rest in the body; the perception of a thing is like motion; the perception of a thing through understanding is like circular motion; through doubting, like a trembling motion; through desiring, like forward motion; through hating, like backward motion, etc.; extension is like the magnitude of the thing thought; and duration in both cases is a relationship in both cases.

To observe whether any parallax <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points; here used to test the Earth's motion around the sun</note> appeared in the fixed stars due to the annual motion of the earth, no star seemed more suitable than the second-to-last in the tail of the Great Bear <note>original: "Ursae majoris", commonly known as the Big Dipper</note>: above which I saw a certain tiny star standing, which seemed to be barely 12 minutes distant from it—that is, 1/3 part of the diameter of the moon—and it was situated in a straight line with the second-to-last star of the tail of the Great Bear and that which is in the bend of the tail of the Dragon <note>original: "Draconis", the constellation Draco</note>, as I have marked it on my globe. However, the star nearest to the square of the tail, which is noted as being of the second magnitude, appeared much smaller than the others; and I was able to notice it many minutes near the lower sequence of the same square, as is noted on globes; and this I have now observed for several continuous days, in the month of September, on the 20th day, in the year 1642.

# MISCELLANY

The reason why an inverted ear of grain <note>original: "spica inversa"</note>, when placed between the sleeve and the arm, moves upward by the motion of the arm, is easily explained.

We see that apples and pears—when covered with oats, or tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers</note>, or wax, or another solid body—and likewise liquids, when oil is poured over them, are preserved from the rot that would arise from the air. This is because these solid substances remain at rest, whereas air is in motion according to its smallest parts.

Human bodies, when placed in dry locations, are eventually changed into ashes without rotting; this is because the parts that were in motion eventually depart, and nothing remains except the parts resting among themselves, mixed with dry air—that is, ashes.

It should be noted that the bones and nerves of animals, the spines of fish, the fibers of herbs, the interior of almost all woods, and indeed almost all <insert>flesh</insert> <margin>The original manuscript likely intended "almost" (ferè) rather than "truly" (verò)</margin>, and generally whatever things grow from the motion of heat in such a way that they are sufficiently refined and perfected by it, are white. However, all blood is red, as if it consisted of parts still ignited and mixed with much soot. But milk and semen, as they possess a greater degree of this refinement, are white. All herbs and leaves are green because of the moisture existing within them; likewise <margin>The manuscript originally read "the same," but was corrected to "likewise" by Leibniz's hand</margin>, they are yellowish when a refracted light is admitted through a transparent medium <note>Leibniz is observing how light interacts with the internal fluids of plants</note>, and their roots are sometimes <margin>The manuscript was incomplete; Leibniz added the suffix to complete the word "sometimes"</margin> found to be whitish. Truly, nothing is more changeable in colors than external features, such as flowers, the rinds of fruits, the feathers of birds, and the fur or hair of other animals; all of these have attained their nature not from a slow concoction <note>A term in early science for the "cooking" or ripening process of nature</note> or an ordered maturity arising from seeds, but are merely external and in a way accidental, like the excrements of nature <margin>Leibniz corrected the grammar here from "nature" to "of nature"</margin>. Even stones arising from the earth, but <margin>The text is corrected from "as" to "but"</margin> mixed at random and not arising from specific seeds, vary greatly in their colors. Metals are the most opaque.

And so, if an object is perceived by one eye as red, but by the other eye as white, it will be perceived by the **common sense** <note>original: "sensu communi"; the faculty that integrates different sensory inputs into a single perception</note> <margin>The word was first written as an abbreviation, then written out in full.</margin> as a more diluted red, or as a mixture of white and red. From this, it is demonstrated that the perception of color occurs only in the common sense or the imagination, and not in the eye itself; therefore, in the eye, color can be nothing other than a certain kind of contact. For if the sensation occurred in the eye, then I would see a double object located in the same place—namely one white and another red—rather than a single one. It is necessary, however, that the glass be very transparent; <margin>The word "velatio" is suspect; perhaps read "vel alio" (or to another [eye])</margin> also, let a glass of another color be placed before the other eye, but one with no <margin>"Nullius" (none) was added by Leibniz's hand to fill a gap in the manuscript.</margin> obscurity. Otherwise, the object would be seen by the free eye in such a way that the rays of the other eye would be stopped in the glass and would not pass through to the object.

The diversity of the senses is not only to be sought from the diversity of touches, but especially from the fact that <margin>The manuscript reads "quid," but "quod" (that) is conjectured.</margin> they carry information to the mind by different paths.

**Amber** <term>Succinum: fossilized tree resin</term> melts spontaneously if it is placed alone in a covered pot over a sufficiently violent fire for the space of half an hour or thereabouts; if then, after being removed from the fire, oil of turpentine is poured in little by little until it becomes clear, it will become a **varnish** most suitable for gilding metals.

It should be noted that we can know nothing (that is, have certain knowledge of it) except whatever <margin>The manuscript is missing words; Leibniz supplied "whatever is most clear."</margin> is most clear and evident; wherefore we ought to gird ourselves to discourse about all things in such a way that we only deduce those things which can be concluded without difficulty, obscurity, labor, or uncertainty; for such things alone are what truly generate **science** <note>original: "scientiam"; here meaning systematic, certain knowledge</note>.

How much richer is he who, whenever it pleases him, can claim for himself whatever belongs to others, than those who indeed possess things but are accompanied by a perpetual fear of losing them: such are those who retain the sciences only in their memory. But those who possess the **foundations** of them can find for themselves, whenever they please, everything that is derived therefrom. And indeed, the general principles of any science are few in number...

Diseases of the body are more easily recognized than diseases of the mind: because we have more frequently experienced the correct health of the body; but of the mind, never.

Seed, both in plants and in animals, is the final work of the nutritive faculty or of growth. Indeed, while the power of the previous seed is first excited by external heat (that is, by the foreign parts which are in it by a specific motion), they then produce not <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "non"; the manuscript reads "eo" (in that), but "non" is conjectured for the sense of the sentence.</note> something similar to themselves, but something else, in which nevertheless the whole similarity to themselves remains, but mixed with other dissimilar things: just as a plant arises from a pea, in which the whole likeness of the pea is contained, but with many other foreign things besides. Crystals made from tartar become whiter with well water than with rain water.

The motion of parts in fire is diverse; therefore different fires often have different effects <gloss>c</gloss> <note>original: "effectus"; the manuscript reads "affectus" (affections). It is a great argument for truth, whatever cannot but be conceived; and for falsehood, that which cannot be conceived: such as a vacuum <note>a space entirely empty of matter</note>, the indivisible <note>the atom</note>, a finite world, etc. For these imply that some things exist, and others do not.

It is a strong conjecture for affirming something that, if it is posited, God is understood to be greater or the World more perfect: as for example, that the determination of our will toward local motion always coincides with a bodily cause determining the motion; that miracles agree with natural causes, etc.

Concerning those things which involve a contradiction, it can be said absolutely that they cannot happen; although meanwhile it must not be denied that they could be done by God, namely if he changed the laws of nature. We ought never to suspect that he has done this, unless it has been revealed by him: as concerning an infinite, eternal World, concerning atoms, the vacuum, etc.

When one has a positive reason which persuades one of something, those metaphysical doubts to the contrary are not to be admitted, which are put forward supported by no reason at all: such as whether perhaps God willed to annihilate the mind whenever its body is destroyed.

Nor should we think about those things of which we can have plainly no knowledge as to whether they are or are not.

From evident experience, but not sufficiently weighed by the examination of reason, a false conclusion is often drawn.

# LINES 60-64. VARIOUS MATTERS.

...we should consider only this: that we often conclude the opposite of what we would conclude if we weighed the entire cause. It is as in arithmetic: if we omit something, a number that was even becomes odd, and it turns out entirely different than it ought to be.

| From the freedom of choice <note>original: "libertas arbitrii"</note> it follows that rewards and praises, or punishments, are due to us; from this, religion also follows.

To comprehend something, it is not required that we see each and every perfection of a thing; it is only required that what we know matches our thought, or that the thought extends as widely as the thing known. Thus, I comprehend the extension of one foot, even though I perhaps do not see each and every one of its properties, because my thought can match it. And so, we know nothing that we do not comprehend, except for the infinite and all those things which, for the very reason that they are not comprehended, I call "indefinite": such as the extension of the universe, the divisibility of the parts of matter, etc.

I understand the idea of God to be in us in no other way than the ideas of all self-evident truths. Specifically, I do not understand them to be always actually depicted in some part of our mind, as many verses are contained in a book of Virgil, but only potentially, like various figures in wax. That is to say: just as wax—because it encounters other bodies in this or that way—finds this or that figure within itself, | so too the mind—because it is applied to considering this or that, either by itself or by other causes—notices that this or that idea of what it considers is within itself. Nevertheless, innate ideas differ from adventitious <note>ideas coming from the outside via the senses</note> and made or fictitious ideas, because the action of the will concurs in fictitious ones, the senses in adventitious ones, and the perception of the intellect alone in innate ones.

Many things can be understood by a finite mind, both concerning God and also concerning any infinite thing, about which it is permitted to dispute. But there are many other things which we experience cannot be understood except with a certain comprehension or "finitization" of the infinite, such as this: whether a thread of infinite length wound into a ball would fill an infinite space, and similar things. Concerning these, it does not seem to me that they should be discussed, except by those who think their own mind is infinite.

I think it is of the essence of the mind to be actually thinking, just as it is of the body to be actually extended.

# EXCERPTS
### I, 64-68.

Nothing is absolute in motion, except for the separation of two moved bodies from one another. However, that one of these bodies is said to move and the other to rest is relative, and depends on our concept, just as the fact that such motion is called "local" <note>pertaining to change of place</note>. Thus, when I walk upon the earth, whatever is absolute or real and positive in that motion consists in the separation of the surface of my feet from the surface of the earth, which exists no less in the earth than in me; and in this sense I have said that there is nothing real and positive in motion that is not also in rest <gloss>a</gloss>. But when I said that motion and rest are contraries, I understood that in respect to the same body—namely, that it behaves in a contrary way when its surface is separated from another body than if it were not separated.

We shall find no difficulty in the **indefinite extension of the World**, if we only consider that by calling it "indefinite," we do not deny that it might perhaps be finite in actual truth, but we only deny that any of its ends or extremities can be grasped by our intellect. This opinion seems to me much more flexible <gloss>b</gloss> and safer than the opinion of those who, by asserting the World to be finite, dare to prescribe limits to the works of God. And so, for us who assert <gloss>c</gloss> the infinite, the burden of solving the contradictions usually proposed concerning it does not fall upon us; rather, we are freed from all difficulties by this candid and most true <gloss>d</gloss> confession: that we acknowledge our <gloss>e</gloss> intellect is not infinite, and therefore incapable of grasping such things as pertain to the infinite. Nor shall we fear lest, by philosophizing about the indefinite extension of the World, we seem to establish its infinite duration; for we do not call the World infinite, and its duration is indefinite in respect to us: that is, it is most certain that it cannot be defined by us through natural reason when it ought to have been created. Furthermore, because even if perhaps some natural reasons might prove it to have been created from eternity, since faith teaches otherwise, we know well that those reasons are in no way to be listened to, as is clear from article 76 of the first part <gloss>f</gloss>.

Motion and rest differ truly and modally <note>a "modal" distinction refers to the difference between a thing and its state or "mode" of being</note>, if by motion one understands—

# PROJECT FOR AN ACADEMY

## IN STOCKHOLM

### February 1st, 1650.

---

> “...The Queen, who intended nothing less than to inconvenience him,
> ” obliged him, in the height of the Ambassador’s illness <note>referring to Pierre Chanut, the French Ambassador to Sweden</note>, to
> ” return again to the Palace in the afternoon for several days,
> ” to share with her the communication of a plan for a Confer-
> ” ence or Assembly of Scholars <note>original: "Sçavans"</note>, which she wished to establish in the form
> ” of an Academy, of which she was to be the head & the protectress. She
> ” regarded Mr. **Descartes** as the man of the best counsel that one
> ” could listen to regarding this establishment, & she chose him to draw up
> ” the plan & to make the regulations. He brought her the memoir
> ” that he had made of it, on the first day of February, which was the last
> ” that he had the honor of seeing the Queen. Here are the articles that he
> ” had set down there, containing the regulations or statutes of this Acade-
> ” my in French:”

I. Each of those who shall be received into this Assembly, shall have his turn, as much for proposing the question, as for explaining it. And all shall always maintain the same order among themselves, in order to avoid confusion.

<margin>5</margin> II. But there shall only be the natural Subjects of this Crown <note>meaning Swedish citizens</note> who may have their rank there, because it is for them alone that it is instituted.

III. If it pleases her Majesty to permit some Foreigner to attend, it shall only be to be a listener,
<margin>10</margin> or at most to give his opinion after all the others, & when it shall be specifically requested of him.

# PROJECTS

<margin>5</margin>
IV. The person who speaks first in each circle <note>term: <term>circle</term> (original: "cercle") refers to the formal seating arrangement and the order of debate</note> shall be the same person who previously proposed the question to be examined; and he shall explain all the reasons he judges capable of proving the truth of what he has undertaken to support.

<margin>10</margin>
V. The others shall then endeavor, each in their turn, to resolve the same difficulty, adding all the reasons they have to prove what they have put forward; but they shall take care that none of them begins to speak until the person preceding him has entirely finished.

VI. They shall listen to one another speak with gentleness and respect, never showing contempt for what is said within the Assembly.

<margin>15</margin>
VII. They shall not study to contradict one another, but only to seek the Truth.

<margin>20 25 30</margin>
VIII. However, because the conversation would be too cold if each person said nothing other than what he had previously premeditated: after they have all finished speaking, the person who first gave his opinion shall be permitted to say what he judges appropriate to defend it against the reasons of those who proposed another; and these others shall also be permitted to answer him, each in their turn, provided that this is done with great civility and restraint, without exceeding three or four replies. It shall be permitted in the same manner for the second person and all those following, each in their turn, to modestly defend their opinion against those who spoke after them, until the time for the conference has expired.

IX. When it shall please her Majesty to end the circle,

# ADDITIONS

---

## I.

### AUTOMATA. <note>Self-operating machines, often hydraulic, which were popular marvels in Renaissance and Baroque gardens.</note>

#### Page 212.

The quotation from Olivier de Serres, at the bottom of this page, ends as follows in the first edition:
> "...just as such miracles are seen in many places, even
> » at Tivoli? And most naturally at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, where the King has
> » newly constructed such and other magnificences,
> » admired by all those who contemplate them." (*The Theater of Agriculture and Management of the Fields*, by OLIVIER DE SERRES. At Paris, 1600. By Jamet Metayer, ordinary Printer to the King. Seventh part: *Of Water and Wood*. Chapter I, p. 751.)

Therefore, when Descartes speaks of the machines that can be seen "in the gardens of our Kings" (p. 130, l. 25), one should understand Saint-Germain-en-Laye rather than Fontainebleau.

A Florentine Italian, whom Henry IV requested from the Grand Duke of Tuscany, Thomas Francini, came to France at the end of the 16th century. As early as 1602, he is described as "Engineer to the King and superintendent of his fountains, residing ordinarily at Saint-Germain-en-Laye," or else "superintendent of the King's fountains and grottoes," or finally "superintendent of the waters and fountains of the houses, castles, and gardens of Paris, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, Fontainebleau and others generally whatsoever," letters patent of February 28, 1623, registered on July 24. (*Thomas Francini, general superintendent of the waters and fountains of France, 1572-1651*, by E. Coüard, *Meeting of the Societies of Fine Arts of the Departments*, 1894, p. 1459-1492.)

<note>original: "Automates, Olivier de Serres, Theatre d'Agriculture, Descartes, Thomas Francini, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, Fontainebleau, Henri IV, ingénieur du Roy, fontaines, 17th century"</note>

<summary>This page identifies the royal gardens at Saint-Germain-en-Laye as the likely inspiration for Descartes' descriptions of automata, highlighting the work of the Italian engineer Thomas Francini.</summary>
<keywords>automata, René Descartes, Olivier de Serres, Thomas Francini, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, hydraulic engineering, royal gardens, Henry IV</keywords>

## II.

### DESCARTES AND DIGBY.

Des Maizeaux, in his *Life of Saint-Evremond*, (written as a *Letter to Mr. Bayle*, dated London, Nov. 15, 1706), provides the following curious information:

> "Mr. de Saint-Evremond also sought out the company of the most
> distinguished men of letters in England. He often conversed
> with Sir Kenelm Digby <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665) was an English courtier, diplomat, and natural philosopher known for his 'powder of sympathy' and his interest in the works of Descartes.</note>, and with the famous Hobbes... One day
> when Mr. Digby and he were speaking of Philosophy, the Knight
> told him that having read the writings of Mr. Descartes, he resolved to travel
> to Holland to see him. He went to find him in his retreat at Eg-
> mond<sup>a</sup>, and after having reasoned with him for a long time without
> making himself known, Mr. Descartes, who had seen some of his
> works, told him that he did not doubt that he was the celebrated
> Mr. Digby<sup>b</sup>. *And you, Sir,* replied Digby, *if you were*
> *not the illustrious Mr. Descartes, you would not see me coming expressly*
> *from England for the pleasure of seeing you.* Mr. Digby then said
> to this Philosopher: that our speculative knowledge was
> indeed beautiful and agreeable, but that after all it was too
> uncertain and too useless to be the sole occupation of man; that
> life was so short that one hardly had the time to properly understand
> necessary things; and that it would be much more worthy of him, who
> understood the construction of the human body so well, to apply himself
> to researching the means of prolonging its duration, rather than attaching
> himself to the simple speculations of Philosophy."

---

a. <margin>Descartes did not live in Egmond (du Hoef) until May 1643. However, Digby appears to have been interested in his philosophy as early as 1638 (see vol. II, p. 192, 271, 336 and 398).</margin>
b. <margin>"Mr. Digby, a zealous Roman Catholic, wrote several works of
Controversy and Philosophy. His *Discourse on the Sympathetic Powder* <note>The 'powder of sympathy' was a form of sympathetic magic or medicine popular in the 17th century, believed to heal wounds by applying the remedy to the weapon that caused the injury rather than the wound itself.</note>
caused a great stir. Mr. Baillet was mistaken, in the *Life of*
*Mr. Descartes*, when he said (vol. II, p. 244) that Mr. Digby was an
Earl and a Knight of the Garter. He confused him with Lord Digby,
Earl of Bristol, who died in 1677. He was also unaware that Sir
Digby went to Holland to see Mr. Descartes." — See vol. III,
p. 89-90, of this edition.</margin>

It also includes bibliographical corrections regarding Digby's identity and titles.</summary>

# DESCARTES AND DIGBY.

> "Mr. Descartes assured him <note>Sir Kenelm Digby, a natural philosopher who visited Descartes</note> that he had already meditated on this matter, and that while he did not dare promise to make man immortal, he was quite sure he could make his life equal to that of the Patriarchs <note>Biblical figures like Methuselah, said to have lived many centuries</note>."

> "When Mr. de Saint-Evremond <note>A French soldier and writer</note> informed me of this detail, he added that it was well known in Holland that Descartes flattered himself with having made this discovery. He had heard it spoken of by several people who had known the Philosopher; Descartes' friends in France knew it as well. The Abbé Picot, his disciple and his martyr <note>Meaning a devoted follower</note>, being persuaded that he had found this great secret, refused to believe the news of his death. When he was no longer permitted to doubt it, he cried out: *It is finished; the end of the human race is coming!*"

> "It is certain that Descartes believed he had found the means to prolong human life. 'I have never taken such great care,' he said to Mr. de Zuytlichem <note>Constantijn Huygens, a Dutch diplomat and scientist</note>, who had asked him what he was busy with... ^a. Mr. Baillet informs us, in the *LIFE OF MR. DESCARTES*, that the Abbé Picot, having accompanied him to Holland in 1647, conformed to his dietary regimen during the three months he stayed with him at Egmond. He was so pleased with it that upon his return to France, he seriously renounced the grand feasts of which he had previously been a fan. He wished to restrict himself to Mr. Descartes' institute, believing it to be the only way to make the secret succeed—the secret he claimed had been found by our Philosopher—to make men live FOUR OR FIVE HUNDRED YEARS ^b. This Abbé, Mr. Baillet says further, was so persuaded of the certainty of Mr. Descartes' knowledge on this point, that he would have sworn it would have been impossible for him to die as he did at fifty-four years old; and that without a foreign and violent cause (like that which disrupted his machine <note>Descartes viewed the human body as a biological machine</note> in Sweden) he would have lived FIVE HUNDRED YEARS, after having found the art of living for several centuries ^c."

> "He was, however, quite far from this rare secret, if it is true, as Mr. Goris claims, that he killed himself by trying to treat himself according to the Principles of his Medicine. This Philosopher,

---

<meta>WORKS. VI.</meta>

book, for which he had brought the manuscript to the philosopher as early as the month of June 1645. The latter had strongly advised against its publication <gloss>a. <note>original: "Voir t. IV, p. 238..." referring to earlier correspondence where Descartes expressed his disapproval.</note></gloss>. But Regius ignored this, and the book appeared in 1646 (dedication dated August 10/20), under the title *Foundations of Physics* <note>original: "Fundamenta Physices"</note>.

Descartes had plenty of reasons to be wary. He himself had only published, in his *Principles* <note>original: "Principia"</note> of 1644, a portion of his philosophy (or his physics, for they were one and the same): he still had to treat the subjects of plants, animals, and man. Was Regius not about to preempt him and provide, before his master, the entire body of doctrine that the latter had promised <gloss>b. <note>original: "Huygens en jugea ainsi..." Christiaan Huygens noted this risk in a letter to Mersenne.</note></gloss>? Indeed, of the twelve chapters contained in the *Foundations of Physics*, the first six correspond roughly to Descartes' *Principles*, and the last six have titles such as, notably, *On Plants* <note>original: "De Stirpibus"</note>, *On Animals* <note>original: "De Animalibus"</note>, and *On Man* <note>original: "De Homine"</note>—that is to say, precisely the subjects that the philosopher had not yet released to the public, and on which he continued to work.

The reader was therefore in danger of being misled on these final questions, and of receiving as the pure doctrine of Descartes what was not that at all. Regius included many things of his own making; or he did even worse: Descartes claims that regarding the animal, in particular, Regius used manuscript notes that he himself had written for his own use, and shared only with a few friends. And Regius used them clumsily: he gives, in fact, and on two occasions, an explanation of the movements of the muscles which the philosopher claims as his own; but, as he had not been given the diagrams, he imagined some that no longer fit the text, rendering the explanation faulty <gloss>c. <note>original: "Tome IV, p. 517..." citations to specific passages where Descartes critiques Regius's errors.</note></gloss>. Now, this explanation was of the highest importance: it concerned only a specific case, the movement of the eye; but it could be extended to all the movements of our "machine" <note>Descartes famously viewed the physical body as a complex biological machine.</note>, and it was the action of the soul upon the body that was being addressed in the question thus generalized.

Descartes does not use the word plagiarism. It was one, however, at least on this point, and perhaps likewise for the rest of the physics. It is enough, indeed, to leaf through this volume of the *Foundations of Physics*. The diagrams there are numerous: now, there are...

# ADDITIONS.

There are very few [illustrations] that are not borrowed, or to be more precise, transported exactly as they were, from the volume of the *Principles* <note>original: *Principia*, published by Descartes in 1644</note>, published in 1644, or else from the *Dioptrics* and the *Meteors*, which date back to 1637. One would think that the same printing plates, or rather the same woodcuts, were reused; and in fact, the two works of 1646 and 1644 were printed by the same bookseller, Louis Elzevier, in Amsterdam, who could easily have obtained the woodcuts of 1637 from his colleague, Jean Maire, in Leiden. Regius did not devise any new figures himself, except for the one we just mentioned regarding the movement of the eye: in which he was not very successful. And if the figures belong to Descartes, the text they accompany undoubtedly does not reproduce the philosopher's words word-for-word, but it merely restates in other terms and summarizes roughly the same doctrine, with varying degrees of accuracy.

There is one part, however, where Regius differs; and this difference must have been even more noticeable to Descartes than the resemblances—which were, all things considered, flattering to him, since he was named as the inspiration for the book in the dedication. Regius's physics is entirely Cartesian; but the same is no longer true of his metaphysics. Regius does not believe that one can demonstrate that God exists, even though such a demonstration is, for Descartes, the very foundation of certainty. Thus, Regius no longer aspires to demonstrative or mathematical certainty: he contents himself with probability <note>or "likelihood"</note>, based solely on the testimony of the senses. This was the exact opposite of what Descartes maintained. And Regius relegates to the end of his work, after the physics proper, in the twelfth and final chapter, *On Man* <note>original: *De Homine*</note>, the small amount of metaphysics intended to complete it. But this inversion of subject matter alone is a complete reversal of Descartes's system<sup>a</sup>. The latter never ceased repeating that his physics was founded solely on his metaphysics, and that, for lack of the latter, the former would entirely collapse. And here his declared disciple—the one whom he himself had proclaimed as such—presents an entire physics, quite similar if not identical to his own, which stands all by itself and is self-sufficient. Only at the end does he superimpose a bit of metaphysics; and even then, what a metaphysics! The most opposed imaginable to that which the master considered as—

### DESCARTES AND REGIUS

absolutely necessary. At the distance we are today, we might not think that Regius was so wrong, theoretically: the solid part, the part that remains of Descartes's work, is indeed the physics as he understood it—that is, the application of mathematics to physics. No doubt, there was no need for so much metaphysics for that, and especially not a metaphysics like Descartes's. But for him, that was his own specific work, and the reform he brought to the scientific world; this new metaphysics, the foundation of a new physics, was simultaneously his revolution and his renovation of philosophy and science. That the disciple should have denied his master precisely on this point must have been the sharpest disappointment for the latter.

Descartes's correspondence leaves no doubt on this subject. Whether he is writing to Princess Elisabeth, Father Mersenne, or Constantijn Huygens on the day after the publication of Regius's book, one finds the same complaints everywhere, and they are quite bitter: the physical part is acceptable, but it comes from him, Descartes; the metaphysics is worth nothing, and therefore it is entirely by Regius<gloss>a</gloss>. The philosopher did not stop at private letters: the following year, in 1647, in a Preface he included in the French translation of his *Principles*, he publicly declared what he thought of the *Foundations of Physics* <note>Original Latin title: *Fundamenta Physices*</note><gloss>b</gloss>.

Regius was undoubtedly wounded by this public disavowal, and especially by the reproach that he understood nothing of metaphysics. Thus, before the end of that same year 1647, he published, in the form of a broadside, a *Program* <note>Original Latin title: *Programma*</note>, which we have seen in Volume VIII (2nd part), pp. 342-346, where he sets out a series of theses, all in contradiction with the doctrine of Descartes. The latter replied immediately with a small booklet titled *Notes on a Program* <note>Original Latin title: *Notæ in Programma*</note>, which we have also seen, *ibid.*, pp. 346-369; and things remained there for some time.

Descartes's biographer, Adrien Baillet <note>Baillet wrote the definitive 17th-century biography of Descartes</note>, asserts that after this final passage of arms between the master and the disciple,
> "Mr.
» Descartes resolved to no longer speak of Mr. Regius
» except in terms of civility & esteem, to show that he wished
» to forget the ingratitude of this Philosopher. Thus he made it known,
» after he was in Sweden, that he remembered nothing else
» about Mr. Regius but his merit<gloss>c</gloss>."

...since he invokes in the margin the testimony of a "manuscript letter <note>original: "let. MS."</note> from Creighton to Regius." But one certainly does not find similar sentiments in the latter's work, far from it. Four years after Descartes's death, in 1654, Regius released a second edition of his 1646 book; however, he changed the title from ***Foundations of Physics*** <note>original: *Fundamenta Physices*</note>. Perhaps he wanted to mislead the reader, who had been all too well warned by Descartes's 1647 preface; he therefore chose the new title of ***Natural Philosophy*** <note>original: *Philosophia Naturalis*</note>. Bibliographers were even deceived by this: because this *Natural Philosophy* of 1654 was presented as a second edition, they imagined a first edition under the same title in 1651, which never actually existed<sup>a</sup>. The only true first edition is that of the *Foundations of Physics* in 1646. But beyond the title, many other things underwent changes.

First, while the dedication to the Prince of Orange, Frederick Henry, was reproduced in 1654 with the same date of August 10/20, 1646, Regius spitefully removed Descartes's name from it, as Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier was Descartes's friend and literary executor who worked to preserve his legacy.</note> would rightly reproach him for two years later, in the preface to Volume I of the *Letters* in 1657<sup>b</sup>. Then, in a "Notice to the Reader" dated April 5, 1654, Regius insinuated that he was the first to have presented this philosophy to the public, "**I was the first to present [it] in our century**" <note>original: *seculo nostro primus exhibueram*</note>: meaning the first even before Descartes, since he, Regius, had been teaching it for seventeen years (since 1637), "**approximately seventeen years ago**" <note>original: *abhinc annos præter propter septendecim*</note>, whereas the philosopher's publication—a partial publication—only dates to 1644; Regius had, moreover, completed it eight years prior, "**eight years ago**" <note>original: *ante octennium*</note>, in his 1646 work which included the whole universe, "**the whole Universe of things**" <note>original: *tota rerum Vniversitas*</note>. Finally, in a poem in his praise, following the custom of the time, he is proclaimed the "king of philosophers," both ancient and modern, through a pun on his name, Regius <note>Regius is the Latinized form of his Dutch name, "de Roy," which means "of the King."</note>. And perhaps, indeed, Henri de Roy naively imagined that he was not unworthy of this title of honor.

He then revisits, in the same order, the subjects presented in 1646, though with many enrichments, "**a fruitful edition, much richer than the former**" <note>original: *fecunda editio priore multò locupletior*</note>. He organized them no longer into twelve chapters, but into five books, each subdivided in turn. In the final book, ***On Man*** <note>original: *De Homine*</note>, he adds in the appropriate place a rather long development on the passions, ***On the Passions*** <note>original: *De Affectibus*</note> (ch. XI, p. 413-432). Descartes's small book dealing with this subject had only been published at the end—

However, the main addition to this Book V is in Chapter 1, pages 334-360, corresponding to pages 245-252 of the first edition—that is, twenty-six and a half pages compared to only seven and a half. This Chapter 1 is titled: ***On the Human Mind, or the Rational Soul*** <note>original Latin: *De Mente humana, sive Anima rationali*</note>, which is precisely the title of the *Program* <note>The *Programma* was a broadsheet published by Regius in 1647 that summarized his disagreements with Descartes, prompting Descartes to write a public rebuttal.</note> of 1647. The philosopher’s name is not mentioned; but there is no lack of criticism against him, using hurtful expressions aimed at him personally: "**Their boastings are vain and empty...**" <note>original Latin: *Vanæ & inanes eorum sunt gloriationes...*</note> "**As some wrongly believe...**" <note>original Latin: *Ut quidam perperàm existimant...*</note> Thus, not only does Regius sharpen his opposition, which is his right, but he adds unpleasant behavior, seen again a bit later when Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’s friend and the editor of his posthumous works.</note> asked him in vain to share the letters he must have kept from Descartes. Clerselier ironically reminded this disciple that he was not exactly acting toward his master’s memory as the motto on his portrait in the 1654 edition seemed to promise: "**Candidly and Generously**" <note>original Latin: *Candidè & Generosè*</note> ᵃ.

It seems Regius had come to believe, in good faith, that he was the primary author of the new philosophy. Descartes had indeed, no doubt, indicated the principles in private conversations. He had even given the public a few samples of what could be drawn from them in his *Essays* of 1637. But who was the first to deduce the entire body of the doctrine? Who had presented it publicly? None other than Regius, in his lectures at the University of Utrecht since 1637—long before, consequently, Descartes had published a part of it in his 1644 work <note>Descartes published his *Principles of Philosophy* in 1644.</note>. And this, Descartes himself had acknowledged in 1642, in his *Letter to Father Dinet*: an entire page is devoted there to Regius, who had succeeded—by reading the *Dioptrics* and *Meteors* and meditating on the principles of true philosophy—in composing for himself an entire Physics in just a few months (he called it a "**Physiology**" <note>original Latin: *Physiologiam*. In the 17th century, "physiology" referred generally to the study of nature or physical science.</note>), such that Descartes could endorse it in advance as his own ᵇ. # ADDITIONS.

To the Benevolent Reader <note>original Latin: "Benevolo S.", where S. stands for *Salutem*, a common greeting meaning "health" or "greetings"</note>, with this new date: *Utrecht*, April 5, *Year* 1654. Here is the beginning:

> The entire Universe of things, which I had clearly deduced from the clear, sufficient, and unique principles of Nature some seventeen years ago, and was the first to show to our century: was brought into public light in print eight years ago by certain learned men. However, since it pleased so many that, all copies having been sold, I was invited by many to a new edition, I have increased, polished, and filed down the work, having brought it back to the anvil... <note>original Latin: "Tota rerum Vniverfitas, quam ex claris, ſufficientibus, & unicis Naturæ principiis... ad incudem revocatum, auxi, limavi, deſcobinavi..." The "anvil" is a classical metaphor for revising a piece of writing.</note>

Next comes a beautiful portrait, with this inscription below: *Henry Regius of Utrecht, Physician and Philosopher, and Professor of Medicine in the Academy of his homeland.* "Painted by H. Bloemaert. Engraved by T. Natham." Motto above: *Candidly and Generously.*

Verses by A. Caesellius on this portrait. We read there:

> ...This is the vivid form of the man, who, before others,
> opens the way with a bright torch to the hidden secrets of things...
> Therefore, among the wise men of old, and among those of today,
> He is a King, and deservedly bears the name of King.
> <note>The poet is making a pun on the author's name: "Regius" is Latin for "Royal" or "Kingly," and the Latin text uses "Rex" (King) to emphasize his mastery of philosophy.</note>

The work is no longer divided into twelve chapters, as in the 1st edition, but into five books.

**BOOK ONE.** — On the Principles of natural things, and common properties and differences. (XV Chapters, pages 1-70.)
**BOOK TWO.** — On the Structure of the Visible World. (XIV Chapters, pages 71-141.)
**BOOK THREE.** — On those things contained in the Earth, lacking life. (X Chapters, pages 142-221.)
**BOOK FOUR.** — On those things contained in the Earth that are living but lack reason. (XVI Chapters, pages 222-333.)
**BOOK FIVE.** — On Man. (XII Chapters, pages 334-441.)
**EPILOGUE.** — (Pages 441-442.)
Quarto <note>A book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>, 442 pages, plus 38 unnumbered pages.

Descartes also especially reproaches Regius for having omitted the most important part of his explanation, “which is that the animal spirits <note>In 17th-century physiology, "animal spirits" were thought to be extremely fine fluids that transmitted motion and sensation through the nerves.</note> which flow from the brain into the muscles, cannot return by the same paths through which they come” (Vol. IV, p. 626, l. 17-20). Did Regius himself feel this omission? In any case, at the end of the 1646 volume, in the *errata* <note>a list of corrections for printing errors</note>, one finds this significant note:

> Page 235, l. 14, *after the word "convertant," add this article*:
> « *The reason why—when some valve of the partition* <note>original Latin: "mediastini"</note> *of the nerve wall is opened—the spirits are able to flow through it from only one side into the other muscle, and not from both sides indiscriminately, nor by turns, now into this muscle and now into that, is this: that the pores of that partition wall, which these valves govern, are formed in such a way that the part of the pores which can be closed by the valves is wider, and is gradually narrowed into a tighter and finally the tightest passage, ending in the other nerve. And from this, an easy passage is given to the spirits from the wider part of the pores into the opposite nerve; but from the other part, which is narrower, the passage is difficult or non-existent.* »

The corresponding passage from Descartes, *Treatise on Man*, is found above, p. 133, l. 20, to p. 137, l. 20.

->D.<-

In the 2nd edition, the first chapter of Book V is titled: *On the Human Mind, or the Rational Soul* <note>original Latin: "De Mente humana, sive Anima rationali"</note>. This is precisely the title of Regius’s broadside <note>A "placard" or "programma" was a single large sheet of paper printed on one side, often used for public notices or academic theses.</note>, printed in 1647, and on which Descartes immediately published notes: *Notes on a Certain Program* <note>original Latin: "Notæ in Programma quoddam"</note>. (Volume VIII, 2nd part, p. 341-369.) The broadside (*Programma*) includes twenty-one THESES. Almost all of them are found, word for word, in the 1654 volume, except for some variations or additions that we will provide here in italics. The order is not always the same.
THESIS I (vol. VIII, p. 342), already appearing, or nearly so, in the 1st edition (1646): « *Thought is that by which thinking actions are first performed by a human.* » (Page 245.)

**THESIS II** (Vol. VIII, p. 342-3), in the 2nd edition only (1654):

> » can be either a substance; or a certain mode of corporeal substance;
> » or, if we follow some other philosophers who establish
> » that extension <note>In Cartesian philosophy, "extension" refers to the essential attribute of matter: occupying space.</note> and thought are attributes which exist in certain substances
> » as subjects: since these attributes are not opposites, but
> » distinct, nothing prevents the mind from also being a certain
> » attribute, meeting in the same subject with extension in man,
> » although one is not contained in the concept of the other.
> » For whatever we can conceive rightly, or clearly and distinctly,
> » that, at least by divine power, can exist: but, that the mind
> » be one of these, can be rightly conceived; for none of these
> » implies a contradiction. Therefore, it can be one of these. »
(Page 335-336.)

<summary>This page details Henricus Regius’s departure from Descartes's strict separation of mind and body, arguing instead that the mind could potentially be a physical mode or attribute of the body. Regius defends this position by challenging Descartes's logic and utilizing the limits of human certainty to suggest that "distinct" concepts are not necessarily "opposite" substances.</summary>

» ...doubt, now, through divine revelation in the Sacred [Scriptures], is indubitable. » (Page 341-342.)

**THESIS VI** (Vol. VIII, p. 343-344), thus reproduced: « *The human mind, although it is a substance really distinct from the body, nevertheless in performing all its actions, as long as it is in the body, is—in my judgment and that of many philosophers debating this very common question—organic, or in need of corporeal organs: so that it can perform absolutely no actions without corporeal organs...* » (Page 342.) However Regius, as if reconsidering, adds this further on: « *Yet it does not follow from that organic constitution of the mind that the mind is not a substance, but is only a mode of the body; and that the body uses the mind as its mode. For not everything that uses instruments is a mode. Nor are actions ascribed primarily to the instruments, but to the [agents] themselves, as they are called, the underlying subjects <note>original: "suppositis"; in scholastic philosophy, the individual substance that acts</note>, or the more principal causes using the instruments, which here is the rational soul.* » (Page 344.)

**THESIS VII** (ibid., p. 344), thus developed: « *...its essence, however the body may be disposed, always remains unchanged and incorruptible: since this [essence] is of a nature clearly different from the form of the human body—or from its temperament and conformation arising from the fitting motion, rest, position, shape, and size of its parts—inasmuch as it consists in the faculty of thinking alone, and cannot arise from that arrangement of parts...* » (Page 345.)

**THESIS VIII** (ibid., p. 344): « *And since the mind, which we know from divine revelation to be a substance distinct from the body, has no parts nor any extension <note>The property of taking up space, which Descartes attributed only to matter.</note> in its concept: it is asked in vain whether it is whole in the whole [body], and whole in each of the parts...* » (Page 346.)

**THESIS IX** (ibid., p. 344): « *...Hence it seems manifest that our mind can be affected in perception just as clearly by imaginary things as by true ones; and that therefore, for one seeking not moral <note>In this context, "moral" certainty refers to a high degree of probability sufficient for practical life, but not absolute proof.</note> or probable and likely knowledge, but an exquisite, accurate, and indubitable knowledge of truth, it is—by the nature of the mind already proposed—doubtful and uncertain whether any true bodies or only imaginary phantasms are perceived by us...* » (Page 347.) And almost immediately [comes] this jab, which aims directly at Descartes: « *Therefore, the boastings of those who claim to have, or to be able to have, an apodictic <note>original: "apodicticam"; meaning demonstrably or absolutely certain</note> and indubitable knowledge of things from nature are vain and empty: since nothing beyond likelihood can be obtained from it, as is clear from what has been said.* » (Page 347.) And Regius makes the same declaration as in Thesis IX: « *But for those who have understanding and are not [stubborn] toward faith like the mule and the horse, all this doubt is removed by divine [revelation] in, with, and concerning...* »

<summary>This page lists Regius's Theses VI-IX, where he argues that while the mind is distinct from the body, it is "organic" and requires bodily organs to function. He concludes by attacking Descartes's claim to certain knowledge through reason, arguing that only divine revelation provides absolute certainty about the existence of the physical world.</summary>

> » The revelation made to us in the Sacred Scriptures <note>original: "Sacris Literis nobis facta revelatio"</note>, by which it is indubitable that God created heaven, and earth, and everything contained within them, and even now preserves them... » (Page 348.) 

There follows a critique of Descartes, in particular, of his argument regarding divine veracity—the idea that God is not a deceiver—which Descartes held as the necessary and sufficient condition for our mind to reach perfect certainty: 

> « *Nor* » *is it an obstacle if someone says it is established through nature that God exists, and that He cannot deceive...* <note>original: "Nec obstat, si quis dicat per naturam constare, Deum esse, eumque non posse fallere..."</note> » (Page 349.)

**THESIS X** (*the same*, p. 344), reproduced word for word. (Page 351-352.)

**THESIS XI** (*the same*, p. 344-345), slightly expanded in these terms:
> « But, since the soul is a substance, as we have already proven through divine revelation, and is produced anew during generation: those who maintain that the rational soul is produced by immediate creation from God during generation, and is substantially united to the body in that manner, as I have already said, seem to judge most correctly... <note>original: "Sed, cùm ea sit substantia... animam rationalem per immediatam creationem à Deo in generatione produci..."</note> » (Page 353.)

**THESIS XII** (*the same*, p. 345), taken up with greater force: 
> « ***The mind,*** » ***or the human faculty of thinking, does not need any innate ideas, notions, or axioms to think...; but it alone is sufficient for itself to carry out all thoughts, both prior and subsequent, without any such innate help...*** <note>In this passage, Regius explicitly rejects the Cartesian doctrine that certain ideas, like those of God or geometry, are "hard-wired" into the soul from birth.</note> » (Page 353.)

**THESIS XIII** (*the same*, p. 345), originally two lines, which here become:
> « Nor is there any reason to say that any engraved <term>notions</term> <note>original: "notiones... inculptas"; these are basic principles or "common notions" like "the whole is greater than the part."</note>, commonly called "common," are innate to our mind for the proper performance of its actions. Instead, we have formed all those, and any other similar ones, for ourselves from the observation of things—first through the perception of individual objects, and then through the collection of many individuals and the induction made from them, which allows us to infer universal notions; or we have received them from others through tradition... » (Page 354-355.)

**THESIS XIV** (*the same*, p. 345) : 
> « *Indeed, the very idea of God implanted in our minds—that is, the one that does not come from divine revelation—is not innate, but has arisen in us from the observation of things, through the senses, memory, imagination, and our own judgment...* <note>original: "Imo ipsa idea Dei... ea non est innata, sed ex rerum observatione... in nobis est orta"</note> » (Page 356-357.)

Finally, **THESIS XV** (*the same*, p. 345), which is so significant, is found presented thus: 
> « However, this concept of God, or idea of God, produced in our mind and existing in it, is not a sufficiently valid argument to prove the existence of God, as some wrongly believe. Since not all things exist for which ideas or concepts are observed in us, and this idea—being conceived by us and that imperfectly—does not surpass our own powers of thinking any more than the concept of any other thing does... <note>Regius here strikes at the heart of Descartes’s "Ontological Argument," which claims that the mere presence of an idea of an infinite Being in a finite mind proves that the Being must exist to have placed it there.</note> » (Page 357.) 

Then Regius critiques, for three consecutive pages, the proofs that Descartes

gives of the existence of God, and ends thus: 

> “And since it is now clear from this how imperfect that faculty of our mind is, by which we form the idea of God in our souls, it is in vain that some pretend—using that faculty which they wrongly call the 'idea of God' to plaster over their errors and find new escapes—that the most valid argument of all for proving God's existence can be produced from it. <note>original: "Cùmque hinc jam pateat... ideam Dei appellant..."</note> For since this faculty of the mind has such imperfection that it can comprehend nothing of that infinite being positively, but only negatively, and even that which it does comprehend positively is meager and imperfect: therefore, a sufficiently valid argument for proving the existence of that most perfect being clearly cannot be drawn from this source; for this faculty, like our other imperfect faculties, could belong to us through our own nature, or have been given by some other imperfect nature.” <note>original: "Cùm enim hæc mentis facultas tantam habeat imperfectionem... nihil infiniti positivè... comprehendere possit..."</note> (Page 360.)

The remaining six theses, which in any case do not have the same metaphysical importance as the preceding ones, are developed in the following chapters.

## DESCARTES AND ROBERVAL.
### 1648.

...and that could only be known in Paris through Florin Périer's letter <note>Florin Périer (1605–1672) was the brother-in-law of Blaise Pascal; he is best known for carrying out the famous barometric experiments at the Puy-de-Dôme.</note>, written on the 22nd. This long letter from Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675), a prominent French mathematician and physicist who often clashed with Descartes.</note> (which must not be confused with a first letter from the same to Des Noyers, which had been printed the previous year, 1647), has only just been discovered and published by Messrs. > "And yet such a space would be extended in length, width, and depth: therefore it would be a body." <note>original: "Atqui tale spatium extenderetur secundùm longitudinem, latitudinem & profunditatem : ergo corpus esset."</note>
> "This was indeed the objection of a certain person <note>Referring to René Descartes, whose "New Physics" identified matter with extension.</note> who seemed to himself to be wiser than others, and had published a 'New Physics' built upon a rotten foundation of this kind." <note>original: "Hæc sane fuit instantia cujusdam qui præ cæteris sibi sapere videbatur..."</note>
> "— I, however, first laughed at the man's empty sophism. Then I replied: that he was deceived in this, because he thought the essence of a body was constituted by extension; however, that is far from the formal concept of a body." <note>original: "id autem longè abesse à formali corporis conceptu."</note>
> "— 'Indeed, whatever is extended in itself, I call a body; nor do I recognize anything extended except that which is a body,' said he."
> "— 'Do you not see,' I said, 'that you are misusing names, while you call "body" that which others are accustomed to call "space," or "mathematical solid," or simply "extension"?'"
> "— 'But what other real thing do you think exists in the nature of things,' he asked, 'besides such space or such extension?'"
> "— 'Besides God and created spirits,' I said, 'I recognize whatever moves within such space, or within such extension. While meanwhile such space, by its nature, remains entirely immobile, and receives me and you and the other bodies moving freely within it (add: within itself), so that we now occupy that part of it in which we exist while we speak, soon to occupy another after we have departed from each other, and finally to recover the same part if we should ever be brought back to this same place in which we now stand; meanwhile we shall have passed through innumerable parts of that same space. This extended thing, therefore, which moves in this way—not being God or a created spirit—I, along with the whole School <note>The "School" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian philosophy taught in universities, which Roberval is defending against Cartesian innovation.</note>, call "body." But that other immobile extended thing in which motion occurs, by the name accepted by all, I call "space," or "extension," or, as the geometers do, a "solid." And in this regard, both truly agree: that it is a real extended thing, divisible, and measurable; but it differs most greatly in that space is immobile...'"

# DESCARTES AND ROBERVAL.
87
<meta>WORKS VI.</meta>

> "...and [space] receives moving things that penetrate it and allows them to move through its parts; however, a body is a movable thing that does not allow itself to be intimately penetrated by another body according to its dimensions. I am not unaware that such space, or a 'mathematical solid,' is called a 'body' by some; but they misuse the name 'body' and make it ambiguous <note>original: "æquivocum"</note>, because they use the same name for two beings of entirely different natures: space and physical or material body. Although both are considered by the mathematician and the physicist, the method of consideration is very different for each. For the mathematician considers space first and for its own sake, as something extended, measurable, and divisible: so that its parts, depending on the position of their boundaries, take on different shapes and have different relations and proportions to one another. However, that same mathematician considers the physical body only secondarily and by accident, namely as it is extended in such a space according to any dimensions and shapes, but not according to the differences of matter and form. Hence the common saying: *the mathematician abstracts from matter* <note>original: "mathematicus abstrahit à materia"</note>. The physicist, on the contrary, considers the physical body first and for its own sake, as it is material and movable, changeable or unchangeable, corruptible or incorruptible, and so on. But the physicist considers mathematical space only secondarily and by accident, specifically as the physical body is extended and moved within and through it, and as such a body, in acting and being acted upon, performs its operations. See then," *I added*, "how different those things are which you confuse, whose formal concepts are distinct, as are their properties."
>
> "Indeed," *he said*, "I truly have cause to boast, when I see that in my MEDITATIONS <note>Refers to Descartes’ *Meditations on First Philosophy* (1641), where he argues that the mind can clearly perceive the essence of matter as extension.</note> I have been raised so far above the limits of common science that I clearly and distinctly see and know that body and space are one and the same thing—the very thing which you, by some blindness of intellect, believe to be two distinct entities."
>
> "At this point, I (for I felt the man was gripped by an all-too-charming disease <note>original: "sensi enim nimiùm amabili morbo detineri hominem." Roberval uses this medical metaphor to suggest Descartes is suffering from a delusion of grandeur or intellectual vanity.</note>): "I praise you," *I said*, "and I do not envy such happiness; indeed, I pray with the greatest possible fervor that it may remain yours forever. Furthermore, please forgive our 'blindness' which has resulted in us—having read those sublime MEDITATIONS of yours attentively more than once, and not only by myself, but also by many of our friends, men of the highest talent, and after gathering our opinions together—having nonetheless failed to notice that excellent point. Instead, nothing appeared to us but mere thoughts and empty sophisms, to our great [unfortunate information]..."

<summary>In this passage, Roberval recounts a debate with Descartes regarding the distinction between mathematical space and physical matter, mocking Descartes' claim that his "Meditations" allow him to see they are the same. Roberval argues that mathematicians study extension while physicists study the properties of matter, and to conflate the two is a fundamental philosophical error.</summary>
<keywords>Roberval, Descartes, extension, matter vs space, mathematical solid, physical body, Meditations, philosophy of science</keywords>

### MANUSCRIPTS FROM THE ROYAL LIBRARY OF HANOVER.

->(Leibniz Papers: IV. Volume I. 4. b. *Excerpts from Descartes*.)<-

The Hanover manuscripts relating to Descartes were sent to us for review in Nancy, thanks to the kindness of the Librarian, Professor Karl Kunze, successor to Eduard Bodemann (who passed away on September 23, 1906). We have conducted a final and scrupulous <term>recension|A critical revision of a text or a systematic survey of manuscripts</term> of them, which allowed us to correct many remaining errors in previous readings. What follows is material that could not be included in the already printed portion of our text.

The right diagram shows a biconvex lens with vertices A and A' placed between two vertical parallel lines. A dashed double-headed arrow between these lines is labeled 'c', representing the distance between them.

sees by calculation that the thickness $e = BD$ of the lens is given by the equation:

-> $e^2 + 2 \frac{7}{2} ce - \frac{49}{256} c^2 = 0.$ <-

From which

-> $e = - \frac{7}{2} c + \sqrt{\frac{49}{4} cc + \frac{49}{256} cc}.$ <-

(Note provided by the kindness of Mr. Henri Vogt, professor of applied mechanics at the University of Nancy.)

On the following line, lines 6-7, regarding the experiments on <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, like glass.</note> sent by Florimond de Beaune to Descartes, see two letters dated February 20 and April 30, 1639 (Vol. II, p. 512, line 14, and p. 542, lines 3-4).

# PARALLAX.

->Page 650.<-

> *To observe whether parallax...* <note>original Latin: "Ad observandum an parallaxis..."</note>

Here is an interpretation of this passage, provided by Mr. Gaston Floquet, professor of mathematical analysis at the University of Nancy.

Among the methods for determining <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in the position of a star when viewed from different points in Earth's orbit, used to calculate its distance.</note>, there is one that requires two conditions: a first star, large enough—that is to say, bright enough; and a second, smaller or fainter, but positioned quite close to the first.

Let us consider the Great Bear <note>Commonly known in North America as the Big Dipper.</note>, composed, as everyone knows, of four stars in a square: α, β, γ, and δ, with three others following:

<image-desc>Two astronomical diagrams. On the left is the constellation "DRACO" (The Dragon), showing a series of stars connected by dashed lines forming a winding path. On the right is the "GREAT BEAR" (Ursa Major), commonly known as the Big Dipper. It shows four stars in a box labeled α, β, γ, and δ, with a handle or tail of three stars labeled ε, ζ, and η. A tiny star labeled 'g' is positioned very close to the star ζ.</image-desc>

ε, ζ, η, representing a tail. Let us examine two of these seven stars: ζ and g.

The next to last of the tail <note>original Latin: "penultima caudæ"</note>, which is to say ζ, which is also called *Mizar*, meets precisely these two conditions: first, it is bright enough; furthermore, it has in its vicinity a fainter star, a "little star" <note>original Latin: "stellula"; this refers to the star Alcor</note>, and quite close, since it is only
