<header>PARALLAX.</header>

distant by only 12' (exactly 11' 48''), or a little more than a third of the Moon's apparent diameter. This small star, *g*, also called "the postilion" <note>A nickname suggesting a rider on a horse, with Mizar being the horse.</note>, or *Alcor*, is located on the straight line joining *Mizar* and the star λ of the Dragon's tail.

On the other hand, neither of the two conditions is met for another star in the Great Bear (which had, no doubt, also been considered): the star of the square closest to the tail <note>original Latin: "stella quadrati caudæ proxima"</note>, that is to say, star δ. First, it is not bright enough: although noted as being of the second magnitude <note>original Latin: "secundæ magnitudinis"</note>, it appears much smaller than the others <note>original Latin: "multo minor aliis apparuit"</note>. Furthermore, the star that follows, on the lower side of the square, namely star γ, is not close enough; it is, in fact, distant by "many minutes." Here we correct *multam minutam* <note>original Latin: "a many minute" (grammatically incorrect in the MS)</note>, the reading in the manuscript, to *multis minutis* <note>original Latin: "by many minutes"</note>. Additionally, the manuscript gives: *et et multam minutam*; the second *et* <note>Latin for "and"</note> might only be a repetition of the first, through a copyist's error, or a misreading by that same copyist, and the misread word could be *eam* <note>Latin for "it"</note>, written as an abbreviation, replacing "star of the square..." from the previous sentence. We would have a satisfactory meaning by reading: *et eam multis minutis advertere potui inferioris sequentiæ ejusdem quadrati vicinam*,

> "and I was able to notice 
> "that it was distant by many minutes (*and consequently* 
> "*too far away*) from the next (read *sequentis*, rather than *sequentiæ*) 
> "lower one of the same square."

The manuscript being only a copy filled with errors, such corrections carry their own excuse and justification.

Star δ must therefore be set aside, as it does not meet the required conditions. There remains star ζ, *Mizar*, which does satisfy them. It seems suitable for revealing an effect of <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in the position of a star when viewed from different points in Earth's orbit, used to calculate its distance.</note>, because of its proximity to *Alcor*. Indeed, since the latter is very faint, it is probably much further away in the sky, and consequently without any perceptible parallax, so that it can be regarded as a fixed reference point. Therefore, because of the proximity, any parallactic displacement of *Mizar* could be easily observed.

See, however, article 40 of the third part of the *Principles* <note>Refers to René Descartes' "Principia Philosophiae" (Principles of Philosophy), 1644.</note>, vol. VIII, p. 151, and vol. IX (2nd part), p. 121.

<header>ADDITIONS.</header>

# DESCARTES' THE WORLD.

## TREATISE ON LIGHT.

->Pages 3-118 above.<-

*The World* which is published here on pages 3-118 is not the complete work that Descartes had composed under this title: it is only a part of it—perhaps an incomplete sketch, or at most a first draft left unfinished, or one whose subsequent parts have been lost. However, the text is undoubtedly authentic. To convince ourselves of this, and to determine its importance and value, we have three means of verification against which it should be compared. These are, first, the indications given in his *Correspondence* on this subject from 1629 to 1634; second, a complete summary that Descartes published of his work in the *Discourse on the Method* in 1637; and finally, the *Principles of Philosophy* <note>original Latin: *Principia Philosophiæ*</note> of 1644—or at least certain parts of the *Principles* where the same subjects are developed further.

As soon as he settled in Holland, during the first nine months of his stay, Descartes occupied himself with a small Treatise on Metaphysics. However, he was interrupted by research into Dioptrics <note>The study of the refraction of light, especially by lenses.</note>, and especially by the study of a phenomenon brought to his attention in the summer of 1629: the Parhelia <term>Parhelia: also known as "sun dogs," these are optical illusions where bright spots appear on either side of the sun, caused by ice crystals in the atmosphere.</term> observed in Rome on the previous March 20th. To properly account for them, the philosopher thought he should examine all "Meteors" <note>In the 17th century, the term "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rainbows, wind, and rain, rather than just space rocks.</note> in order (Oct 8, 1629, Vol. I, p. 23, l. 6-7), and this led him back to the study of the whole of Physics (Vol. I, p. 70, l. 8-11). He then decided to publish his Physics before his Metaphysics, keeping the latter to himself. In less than a month, it seems, he conceived the project of an entire and complete work; he even found the most convenient angle, or the most favorable light, under which to present it to the public. His Physics would take the form of a *Treatise on Light*, without losing anything in the process: all the phenomena of nature—the fixed stars and the Sun, the Comets, the Planets, and the Earth, and even Man—would find a place there, and it would truly be a *Treatise on the World*.

The draft that remains for us consists first of fifteen chapters, the fifteenth of which is unfinished. The first five serve as an introduction, and the work does not truly begin until the sixth.

where Descartes explains what he calls "the Fable of his World":
an expression that appears for the first time in a letter from

Chapter I emphasizes the difference between the objects themselves
that we see, touch—in a word, that we sense—and the
sensations we have of them: two things that have nothing in
common, despite common prejudice. Descartes gives as an

in a letter of November 20, 1629, he does indeed discuss language regarding
a project for a universal language (vol. I, pp. 76-82). He then gives
the example of sounds and what causes them outside of ourselves (vol. XI,
p. 5, l. 3-20); many of his letters from 1629 and 1630 also contain
remarks on sounds, in response to questions from
Mersenne or passages from Beeckman's letters.

Chapter II deals with Fire, which burns, heats, and illuminates—
three facts that Descartes explains, not through more-or-less
occult "qualities" <note>Scholastic philosophers often explained properties like heat by saying an object possessed a "quality" of heat; Descartes rejected these as circular and unscientific.</note>, in the manner of the scholastics, but according to his own
principles: through the movements of particles of matter (vol. XI,
pp. 7-10). Chapter III similarly explains how certain bodies
are hard and others are liquid (by which he also means fluid),
without having any further recourse to "qualities" of hardness
or liquidity (vol. XI, pp. 10-16). Now, in January 1630 and on the following
February 25, he wrote to Mersenne that he had drawn up a list of qualities,
with the help of Bacon <note>Francis Bacon (1561–1626), the English philosopher whose works cataloging natural phenomena influenced Descartes' early methodology.</note>, and that this was one of the first things he would try
to explain: which would be easy, he adds, once the foundations
were laid (vol. I, p. 109, l. 21-27). These foundations or principles are
none other than the Subtle Matter <term>Subtle Matter: In Cartesian physics, a very fine, fluid matter that fills all space, as Descartes did not believe a true vacuum could exist.</term>, which he also mentions to Mersenne for
the first time around this date, recommending a degree of
secrecy (vol. I, p. 119, l. 20-21). And this question is linked for him
to that of the Void, which he resolves, as we know, by suppressing it: the
letter of June 2, 1631, is quite explicit on this subject (vol. I, pp. 205-208);
but well before this date, Descartes had already made up his mind, and he
lets it be glimpsed as early as October 8, 1629 (vol. I, p. 25, l. 9-12). Thus
Chapter IV, on the Void (vol. XI, pp. 16-23), immediately follows
Chapters III and II, on Hardness and Liquidity, and on the qualities of
Fire. Finally, Chapter V naturally ends this introduction
with a theory of the three Elements (vol. XI, pp. 23-31). There are only
three, in fact, and not four <note>Descartes replaced the traditional four elements (earth, air, fire, water) with three sizes of particles: "fire-matter," "air-matter," and "earth-matter."</note>: Descartes demonstrates this, or
imagines he demonstrates it. He thinks he knows these things, he wrote to Mersenne,
by demonstration (vol. I, p. 120, l. 1-2). And in the same letter of
February 25, 1630, we find the comparison of a sponge full

But more importantly, later, in a letter dated January 9, 1639, Descartes no longer wishes to hide his theory of the three Elements from Mersenne, and he summarizes it in a note very similar to the essential passage of chapter V (vol. XI, pp. 24-25, and vol. II, pp. 483-484, and p. 564, l. 11-16).

With chapters VI and VII, the work truly begins. One deals with Matter, which Descartes explains through the indefinite extension of the geometers, without needing the "forms" or "qualities" of the School <note>The "School" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval philosophical system based on Aristotle that Descartes sought to replace with mechanical explanations.</note> (vol. XI, pp. 31-36); the other deals with Motion and the Laws of Motion, which he calls the Laws of Nature (pp. 36-48). He also calls them Eternal Truths (p. 47, l. 12): in a letter of April 15, 1630, he announces that he will speak of these in his *Physics* within a fortnight (vol. I, p. 146, l. 10-11), and he returns to them in two subsequent letters from May 1630 (p. 149 and p. 151). As for Matter, since he also declares on May 27, 1630, that he is in the process of explaining in his *Treatise* what will become of the "forms and qualities" of the Scholastics (vol. I, p. 154, l. 9-13), we can believe that he was then writing chapter VI as well as chapter VII.

Chapters VIII, IX, and X, which follow, deal successively with the Fixed Stars, including the Sun (vol. XI, pp. 48-56), then Comets (pp. 56-63), and finally the Planets, including the Earth and the Moon (pp. 63-72). Descartes explains their formation in this World, the history of which he tells like a fable or a novel. And as he has left the real world far behind him, he moves at ease through imaginary spaces and freely follows the Copernican system <note>The Copernican system placed the Sun at the center of the universe; Descartes framed his book as a "fable" about a new world to avoid potential religious censorship regarding the Earth's movement.</note>. On December 23, 1630, he writes to Mersenne that he is in the middle of unraveling Chaos to bring forth Light (vol. I, p. 194, l. 15-24)—that is to say, undoubtedly, the bodies that produce light to our eyes, the Fixed Stars and the Sun: he adds that almost all of Physics is comprised in this matter (l. 15-17). Later, on May 10, 1632, after he has seemingly already explained the Comets and the whole of his imagined world theoretically, he considers finding his footing in reality again and asks for a collection of observations made on comets that have actually appeared (vol. I, pp. 250-251). And he does not despair of explaining the cause of the positions of the Stars, even though they appear quite irregularly scattered here and there in our Sky (vol. I, p. 250, l. 20-23): has he not already attempted to do so in his imaginary Heavens, and does he not think he has succeeded (vol. XI, p. 105, l. 23, etc.)?

After chapter X, on the Earth and the Moon, one naturally finds a chapter XI, on Gravity (vol. XI, pp. 72-80), and a chapter XII, on the Ebb and Flow <note>The "ebb and flow" refers to the tides.</note> (pp. 80-83). Now, in October 1631, Descartes wrote to Mersenne that he would, within a few days, have to explain the cause of gravity in his *Treatise* (vol. I, p. 222, l. 13-16). And he speaks of it again in a subsequent letter, from October or November 1631: he will try to explain <term>what gravity, lightness, and hardness are</term> <note>original Latin: "quid sit gravitas, levitas, durities"</note>, in the two chapters he promised to send at the end of that year (p. 228, l. 10-14). Later, he opened up about it to Debeaune <note>Florimond de Beaune (1601–1652), a mathematician and early follower of Descartes.</note>, in a letter dated April 30, 1639 (vol. II, p. 544). Regarding the question of the ebb and flow, Descartes only mentions it a little later, in two letters from Nov. or Dec. 1632 and August 14, 1634, but only to say that he had explained it in his *World*, like Galileo, by the motion of the earth—and this before having read Galileo, and in a way entirely different from his own (vol. I, p. 261, l. 21-26, and p. 304, l. 7-11). Much later still, he went further: on August 6, 1640, he communicated to Mersenne, in confidence, his explanation of the ebb and flow as he gave it in his *World*, that is, before the revisions he later made to adapt it, in the *Principia* <note>*Principia Philosophiae* (Principles of Philosophy), published in 1644.</note> of 1644, to a hypothesis different from that of Copernicus; and this explanation communicated in 1640 is the same, except for a few sentences, as that of chapter XII (vol. XI, p. 80-83, and vol. III, p. 144-146).

The following two chapters, XIII and XIV, are the essential chapters, on Light (vol. XI, p. 84-97) and on the Properties of Light (*ibid.*, p. 97-103). If Descartes does not speak of them explicitly anywhere in his letters, one can just as well say that he thinks of them every time he speaks of his *World*, since the latter is nothing other than a *Treatise on Light*.

Finally, after chapters VI and VII, which laid the foundations, and chapters VIII to XIV, which built the edifice, Descartes would have shown, in chapters XV, XVI, and XVII, that this edifice is not at all imaginary, and that it is entirely similar to the real world we inhabit. But he only began this final task: at least we only have the beginning, a part of chapter XV, where he speaks of little else but Comets, and their "hair" <note>Historically, the "coma" or glow around a comet was called its hair (from the Latin *coma*).</note>, and their tails... (vol. XI, p. 104-118); we are missing chapters XVI and XVII. Did Descartes write them, and how? It is impossible to say. From then on, he encountered many obstacles. First, there was the explanation of "forms" and "qualities," no longer in general (such as heat and cold, dry and moist, hard and liquid, heavy and light), but in the different bodies that present themselves

But what were two years, especially if one considers the ambitious project that Descartes reveals to us almost at that same date, May 10, 1632: no longer merely guessing <term>after the fact</term> <note>original: "à posteriori"</note>, and by their effects, the various forms and essences of terrestrial bodies; but knowing them <term>from the cause</term> <note>original: "à priori"</note>, by deducing them from the order of the Fixed Stars in the Heavens (vol. I, p. 250, l. 21, to p. 251, l. 2). This was the dream of astrologers, and it is curious to find it for a moment in our philosopher. He excuses himself for it: this science, he recognizes, exceeds the reach of the human mind; and yet he is so unwise that he cannot help dreaming of it (vol. I, p. 252, l. 12-15). By 1637, he had frankly given it up (vol. VI, p. 64). And perhaps he did not linger too long, being hurried to return to anatomy for the study of man.

Indeed, in the month of June 1632, in order to finish his *World*, he speaks of adding something regarding the nature of Man (vol. I, p. 254, l. 11-12): not that he wants to describe, as he had first thought, how the <term>generation of animals</term> <note>In the 17th century, "generation" referred to the biological process of reproduction and the development of the embryo.</note> occurs, which would be too long (p. 254, l. 5-9) and undoubtedly too difficult; but he will explain at least, as he would say in November or December 1632, all the principal functions of man (vol. I, p. 263, l. 1-8). This was to be a second part of the *Treatise on the World*: the first, concerning inanimate bodies, was completed—Descartes says so on several occasions, May 5, 1632 (vol. I, p. 248, l. 6-9), and in the following June (p. 254, l. 9-10). Let us understand by this that a first draft was on paper: it remained to make a clean copy, which would perhaps bring about many modifications. This draft is undoubtedly the one that has been preserved for us, and which we place at the beginning of the present volume.

Descartes did not publish his *World* at all: the condemnation of Galileo, in 1633, prevented him. But, in 1637, in the *Discourse on the Method*, he gave, at the beginning of the fifth part, a complete summary of his great work. He could do no better, he declares, than by saying here "summarily" what this work contains (vol. VI, p. 41, l. 24-25). He first indicates its design: to explain "the Nature of Material things" (l. 26-27). But for that, he took the approach of treating Light (p. 42, l. 4-5). This indeed encompasses everything: the Sun and the Stars, which produce it; the

# ->THE WORLD OF DESCARTES.<-

Heavens, which transmit it [light]; the Earth and the Planets, which reflect it; all bodies, which are either colored, or transparent, or luminous; and finally Man himself, who is the spectator (l. 5-13). He took yet another approach, so as not to offend the <term>learned</term> <note>original: "doctes"</note> (meaning the Theologians as well as the Philosophers): and that was to leave this real world to their disputes or controversies, and to create, through thought, a new world specifically in <term>imaginary spaces</term> <note>original: "espaces imaginaires". Descartes used this hypothetical framework to present his radical physics as a "fable" to avoid potential condemnation by the Church, similar to what had happened to Galileo.</note> (ibid., l. 13-27). And here we are precisely brought back to Chapter VI of *The World*, as it has been preserved for us (vol. XI, p. 31).

From this moment on, if one follows, phrase by phrase, the text of the *Discourse on the Method*, and if one takes up, chapter by chapter, the text of *The World*, one notices that each phrase corresponds exactly to a chapter, and that the order is the same (or nearly so) on both sides.

The first phrase, indeed: "I described this matter..." (vol. VI, p. 42, l. 27, to p. 43, l. 5), could serve as a title for Chapter VI, itself titled: "Of Matter" (vol. XI, pp. 31-36); and on one side as on the other, the emphasis is on the essential point, namely how easily one can do without the "forms" and "qualities" used in <term>the School</term> <note>original: "l'École", referring to Scholasticism, the Aristotelian philosophy and theology taught in universities during the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.</note>.

The following phrase speaks of the Laws of Nature (vol. VI, p. 43, l. 5-12), and this is also precisely the title of Chapter VII (vol. XI, pp. 36-48), which discusses Movement first, then the Laws of Movement, with their universal character.

The third phrase (vol. VI, p. 43, l. 12-19) recalls how, from primitive Chaos or Matter, the Heavens, the Earth and the Planets, the Comets, the Sun, and the fixed Stars were formed as a result of these laws. And it is, in reverse order, what Chapters VIII, IX, and X of *The World* explain (vol. XI, pp. 48-56-63-72).

The fourth phrase (vol. VI, p. 43, l. 19-25) teaches us that Descartes then expanded upon Light and its Properties. This is also (skipping over XI and XII) the subject developed in Chapters XIII and XIV (vol. XI, pp. 84-97-103).

The fifth phrase emphasizes the perfect resemblance between the new world thus explained and the real world in which we live (vol. VI, p. 43, l. 25, to p. 44, l. 1). The same emphasis, and for the same purpose, is found elsewhere in Chapter XV, which is otherwise unfinished (vol. XI, pp. 104-118).

But what comes next in the *Discourse on the Method* perhaps allows us to supplement the end of this Chapter XV, as well as the two following chapters, XVI and XVII, which are entirely missing. First

### ADDITIONS.
<page-num>704</page-num>

Descartes mentions his explanation of **Gravity** (vol. VI, p. 44, l. 2-6), then 그of the **Tides** <note>original: "Flux et le Reflux"</note> (l. 6-10); and these are chapters XI and XII of our *The World* (vol. XI, p. 72-80-83), although their positions have been changed slightly. Descartes then treated various subjects: the Winds in the tropics; the formation of Mountains and Seas, of Springs and Rivers, of Metals in mines, and of Plants in the countryside (vol. VI, p. 44, l. 10-29). Finally, he concluded with an explanation of Fire, and one of its most curious effects, the production of Glass (p. 44, l. 29, to p. 45, l. 3).

None of these things survived in our version of *The World*; but they can be found, in English translation from the original Latin, in the IVth part of the *Principles of Philosophy* <note>original: "Principia Philosophiæ"</note>. The order is no longer exactly the same, it is true; yet there are series of articles that correspond well to specific questions in the *Discourse on the Method*. Thus, Gravity is treated from article 20 to 27 inclusive (vol. VIII, p. 212-217), and the Tides a little further on, from 49 to 56 (p. 232-238). These two questions even acquire a particular importance here: we see how Descartes treated them within his new hypothesis, which was close to that of <term>Tycho Brahe</term> <note>A 16th-century astronomer who proposed a model where the Sun orbits the Earth while other planets orbit the Sun; Descartes adopted a version of this to avoid the theological controversy of a moving Earth.</note>; and we can compare this with what he had said initially while following the system of <term>Copernicus</term> <note>The astronomer who first argued that the Earth revolves around the Sun.</note> (vol. XI, p. 72-80-83, and vol. III, p. 144-146). Between these two questions, in the *Principles*, he had spoken of Mountains and Seas, art. 44 (vol. VIII, p. 230); and a little later, of Springs and Rivers, art. 64 to 70 (p. 242-246); and of Metals and Mines, art. 71 to 76 (p. 246-248).

But where the concordance appears most clearly is regarding Fire: the sentence in the *Discourse on the Method* (vol. VI, p. 44, l. 19-29) enumerates, point by point, what is found on the same subject in the articles of the *Principles*. "I applied myself," says Descartes <note>original: "Je m'étudiay"</note>, to making understood very clearly everything that belongs to the nature of Fire, and this is the title of art. 80 (vol. VIII, p. 249-250); how it is made, see art. 81 to 89 (p. 250-254); how it is fed, art. 83 (p. 250); how it sometimes has heat without light, art. 92 and 93 (p. 256-258); and sometimes light without heat, art. 90 and 91 (p. 254-256); ... how it melts some bodies, art. 118 (p. 267-268), and hardens others, art. 119 (p. 268); finally, how it forms glass. Descartes declares that he had taken particular pleasure in describing the <term>transmutation</term> <note>The process of changing one substance into another, such as turning ash into glass through extreme heat.</note> of ash into Glass; indeed, in the *Principles*, this fills no fewer than eight articles, 124-132 (vol. VIII, p. 270-275). Only one subject perhaps pleased him even more, and that is the magnet: he develops it from article 133 up to article 183 inclusive (*ibid.*, p. 275-311). Yet he had not said a word about it in the *Discourse on the Method*, and we find nothing of it...

...trace in the fifteen chapters of our *The World*: Descartes appears to have had the intention to speak of it for a moment, in a letter dated November 4, 1630 (vol. I, p. 176, l. 15-19); but he quickly gave it up, it seems, according to a letter of November 25 (p. 180, l. 15-17). Aside from this novelty, many articles in the *Principles* <note>original: "Principia"</note> merely took up subjects already treated in the final chapters of *The World*.

This is true for the fourth part of the *Principles*, and it is no less true for the third and second parts. We find there the same general questions which are the subject of the other chapters of *The World*, and which the *Discourse* of 1637 listed.

Thus, the second part of the *Principles* treats the <term>Void</term> <note>The concept of a vacuum or space containing no matter; Descartes famously argued that a true vacuum is impossible because extension is the essence of matter.</note>, art. 5, 6, and 7, and art. 16 to 20 (vol. VIII, p. 42-44, and p. 49-52), which corresponds to the entirety of Chapter IV (vol. XI, p. 16-23); the infinite or indefinite **Extension** of the World, and its Nature or its Essence, art. 21, 22, and 23 (vol. VIII, p. 52-53), which is the subject of Chapter VI (vol. XI, p. 31-36); **Motion**, art. 24-33 (vol. VIII, p. 53-59), and the **Laws and Rules of Motion**, art. 36-53 (p. 61-70), which is Chapter VII (vol. XI, p. 36-48); finally, **Hard and Liquid Bodies**, art. 54-63 (vol. VIII, p. 70-78), which is—returning slightly backward—Chapter III (vol. XI, p. 10-16). Aside from this transposition, and another involving Chapter V which we will encounter below, the order followed is the same; these are also, with some additional developments, roughly the same ideas, and sometimes the same expressions. To the three great laws of motion, Descartes added, it is true, seven rules, art. 46-52 (vol. VIII, p. 68-70); but he had already indicated them in a few words in Chapter VII of his *The World* (vol. XI, p. 47, l. 4-9). Let us also note that the three great laws are not presented in the same way in the two works: in the *Principles*, the second law of *The World* becomes the third, and consequently, the third law of the latter becomes the second.

The third part of the *Principles* begins with an introduction: an overview of celestial phenomena, art. 4-14 (vol. VIII, p. 81-84), and an account of the different astronomical hypotheses that claim to explain them; Descartes develops his own, after having recalled <term>Ptolemy</term>, <term>Copernicus</term>, and <term>Tycho</term> <note>Reference to the three major models of the universe: Earth-centered (Ptolemy), Sun-centered (Copernicus), and a hybrid model (Tycho Brahe).</note>, art. 15-41 (vol. VIII, p. 84-98). Then he clearly marks the starting point of his deductions, art. 43-47 (p. 99-103), and immediately begins the series. We then find the theory of the three **Elements**, art. 48-52 (p. 103-105), which is to say Chapter V (vol. XI, p. 23-31), which was set aside a moment ago. We also find the explanation of the Sun and the

**Fixed stars**, articles 53-118 (vol. VIII, pp. 106-168), which correspond to chapter VIII (vol. XI, pp. 48-56). However, the changes here are considerable: Descartes inserts into these articles his theory of **Light**, art. 55-64 (vol. VIII, pp. 108-116), where we find chapters XIII and XIV (vol. XI, pp. 84, 97, 103); but above all, he presents a theory of <term>grooved particles</term> <note>original: "parties cannelées." These are screw-shaped particles of matter that Descartes hypothesized to explain magnetism and the movement of celestial bodies through the "ether."</note>, art. 87-93 (vol. VIII, pp. 142-147), and expands upon **sunspots**, their causes, and their effects, art. 94-118 (vol. VIII, pp. 147-168). We find a more exact correspondence in what follows: art. 119 and art. 126-139 on **Comets** (vol. VIII, p. 168, and pp. 174-192), with chapter IX (vol. XI, pp. 56-63); art. 140-148 on the **Planets**, particularly art. 149-153 on the **Earth and the Moon** (vol. VIII, pp. 192-197 and pp. 197-200) with chapter X (vol. XI, pp. 63-72).

If one then examines the *Principles* <note>original: "Principia"</note>, chapters III, IV, VI, and VII of *The World* <note>original: "Le Monde"</note> which have been preserved for us, are found in the second part, "On the Principles of Natural Things" <note>original Latin: "De Principiis rerum naturalium"</note>; chapters V, VIII, IX, X, and also XIII and XIV, and even XV, are found in the third, "On the Visible World" <note>original Latin: "De Mundo adspectabili"</note>; finally, chapters XI and XII, as well as XIII and XIV (at least as an indication), and undoubtedly the two missing chapters, XVI and XVII, are found in the fourth part, "On the Earth" <note>original Latin: "De Terrâ"</note>.

Of course, a fundamental difference remains between the *Principles* and *The World*. The <term>Copernican system</term> <note>The astronomical model placing the Sun at the center of the universe. Descartes famously suppressed "The World" after the Catholic Church condemned Galileo for supporting this view in 1633.</note> regarding the motion of the earth, unfolds in the latter with total freedom and is displayed, one might say, naively. In the later work, it gives way to a hypothesis that disguises it—a sort of compromise Descartes settled upon, and an indirect approach he felt necessary to take: all the rest of the doctrine is modified here and there because of it. However, with this reservation made, the essentials are found without too many changes, and the whole of Cartesian Physics receives triple and quadruple confirmation from the *Correspondence* (1629-1634), the *Discourse on the Method*, part 5, in 1637, and the compared texts of *The World* (1629-1632) and the *Principles* (1644). We can therefore be assured that the *Principles* are merely a reworking of *The World*, as Descartes himself warned Huygens in a letter dated January 31, 1642:

> » My *World* <note>Descartes is making a play on words here: "Mon Monde se fera bientost voir au monde" — "My [book] The World will soon be seen by the world."</note>
> » will soon be seen by the world, and I believe it would be so
> » presently, were it not that I wish first to teach it to speak
> » Latin; and I shall have it named the *Summary of Philosophy* <note>original Latin: "Summa Philosophiæ"</note>. » (Volume III,
> p. 523, l. 14-17.)

-># ERRATA.<-

### PAGE 534, NOTE *b*. — PAGE 694, *fig.* No. 2.

The two figures, indicated in note *b* of p. 534 under the number XV, are in reality figures XXII and XXII *bis* <note>original: "bis"; a Latin term used in cataloging to indicate a second version or addition to a numbered item, similar to "22a".</note> of the plate inserted between pp. 639 and 641, as already stated on p. 694, rectification. (At this last location, read: *p. 595, and not 594*.)

### PAGE 642, L. 19, AND PAGE 694.

*Fruits of the hour* <note>original Latin: "Fructus horarii"</note>. It is indeed *horarii* <note>meaning "of the hour" or "pertaining to the hour"</note>, in fact, that one must read. Foucher de Careil had wrongly conjectured: *of the gardens* <note>original Latin: "hortorum"</note>. The meaning is this: "fruits which have just been picked *on the hour*, fresh fruits." Even today, in Athens, one hears fishmongers crying in the streets: "I have fish of the hour." <note>original Greek: "Ἔχω ψάρι τῆς ὥρας"</note> "I have fresh fish." (Note sent from Greece by Mr. Gaston Colin, professor at the University of Caen.)

### PAGE 687-690.

Regarding the dispute between Descartes and Fermat, Roberval having taken the latter's side, here is an important document, the existence of which was known, but which could not be found until now. It is a letter from Desargues to Mersenne, dated April 4, 1638. We had mentioned it in volume II of this edition, pp. 114-115. The autograph (signed DESARGUES, with a G interlaced very legibly in the initial D: <term>GIRARD DESARGUES</term> <note>Girard Desargues (1591–1661) was a French mathematician and engineer, considered one of the founders of projective geometry and a friend of Mersenne and Descartes.</note>) now belongs to the City Library of Lyon: MS., D, 16, pp. 252-255. The discovery was made by Lieutenant-Colonel H. Brocard, of Bar-le-Duc, who very obligingly shared it with us immediately. And the manuscript was sent to us for review, no less obligingly, by the Librarian of Lyon, Mr. Richard Cantinelli.

> "My Reverend Father,
> "Being on the point of going for a tour of the countryside for a few
> "days, I have decided to return to you the latest papers that you
> "received from Mr. Descartes, at least those that you did me the hon-
> "our of entrusting to me. On which matter I shall tell you at length whatever
> "has come to my knowledge until now."

# ERRATA. VIII

» something outside the ordinary way of thinking in Geometry, and which
» has some conformity with thoughts that I have only brushed upon myself.
» Paper will fail me, but not the will to be
» always

->» My Reverend Father, <note>original: "Mon R. P." (Mon Révérend Père). A standard address for Marin Mersenne, who was a priest in the Minim order.</note><-
->» Your very affectionate servant,<-
->» G. DESARGUES. »<-

« *To the Reverend Father M. Mersenne, Minim Friar at the Place Royale, in Paris.*

->» At Paris, this 4th of April 1638. »<-

The same Lieutenant-Colonel H. Brocard, to whom we are indebted for this autograph by Desargues, gives us the key to the four initials *D. A. L. G.*, which are found in the *Examination of the book of Mathematical Recreations* <note>A popular 17th-century work, *Récréations Mathématiques*, which contained puzzles and mathematical problems.</note> (published by Mydorge in 1630), and which remained inexplicable to us. (Volume X, p. 546-551.) Already a scholar, A. Aubry of Beaugency, had proposed to read the first three letters *D. A. L.* as *Des Argues Lyonnois* <note>original: "Des Argues Lyonnois." This identifies the author as Desargues of Lyon.</note>. There remained the fourth letter *G*. There was little likelihood that it was the initial of the first name *Girard*: why, indeed, would it be placed at the end? Mr. Brocard correctly proposes *Geometer* <note>original: "Géometre." In this period, "geometer" was often used as a synonym for "mathematician."</note>. The same letters are found under the title of another work by Mydorge in 1631, *D. A. L. G.* (Volume I, p. 257.) And elsewhere still, Desargues had designated himself under similar initials, *S. G. D. L.*, *Sieur Girard Desargues Lyonnois* <note>original: "Sieur Girard Desargues Lyonnois." Lord/Sir Girard Desargues of Lyon.</note>. (Volume I, p. 360, note *b*.)

<keywords>Girard Desargues, Marin Mersenne, H. Brocard, Claude Mydorge, D.A.L.G., mathematical history, 17th-century geometry, Lyon</keywords>
